sens: Brother of Jesus, son of Mary and Joseph
Son of Mary, a supporter of Jesus' ministry
G2500G.detail:
1. Joses is presented as one of the brothers of Jesus, child of Mary and Joseph. Mark mentions him among the four brothers of Jesus (James, Joses, Jude, and Simon) that the inhabitants of Nazareth knew, before being astonished at his wisdom and miracles (Mark 6:3).
2. A Joses is also mentioned as the son of Mary, a woman who followed Jesus and watched from a distance during his crucifixion, also present at the burial (Mark 15:40, 47). This Mary is distinct from the mother of Jesus.
G2500G.origine: The name Joses is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Joseph (Yoséph). In Greek, it can receive variable endings (Ἰωσῆς, Ἰωσήφ). The meaning of the Hebrew name is "God increases" or "God adds." It is a very common name in the genealogies and Jewish families of the first century.
G2500G.emploi: Joses appears three times in the Synoptic Gospels, all occurrences found in Mark. First in Mark 6:3, he is named as the brother of Jesus, alongside James, Jude, and Simon. Then, in Mark 15:40 and 15:47, a different Joses is mentioned as the son of Mary (a woman who followed Jesus), during the crucifixion and burial. These two characters should not be confused: the first is a member of Jesus' family in Nazareth, the second is the son of another Mary among the disciples.

sens: Righteous man of Nazareth, husband of Mary and adoptive father of Jesus
Ancestor of Jesus in the line of David
Son of Jacob in the Old Testament
Other people bearing this name in the New Testament
G2501G.detail:
1. Joseph of Nazareth is the husband of Mary and the legal adoptive father of Jesus. He is a righteous and obedient man: when he learns that Mary is expecting a child, an angel commands him to take her as his wife and to name the child Jesus (Matthew 1:19-20, 1:24). He flees to Egypt on heavenly warning, then returns to establish his family in Nazareth (Matthew 2:19). He represents paternal protection and trust in God in the face of the unexpected.
2. Joseph appears in the genealogy of Jesus according to Matthew and Luke, legally linking Jesus to the royal house of David (Matthew 1:16; Luke 3:23). Although he is not the biological father, this genealogical link establishes Jesus as the heir of the messianic promises made to David.
3. In the Old Testament, Joseph is the favored son of Jacob, whose extraordinary life (sold into slavery, exaltation in Egypt, reconciliation with his brothers) serves as a model of faithfulness despite trials (Acts 7:9, Hebrews 11:21-22).
4. Other people bear this name in the New Testament: an ancestor of Jesus (Luke 3:24), a member of the Sanhedrin named Joseph of Arimathea who buried Jesus (Matthew 27:57), and possibly a brother or son of Mary (Matthew 13:55, 27:56).
G2501G.origine: The Hebrew name יוֹסֵף (Yossef) literally means "God adds" or "May God add," expressing a wish for multiplication or family blessing. This name was common in Second Temple Judaism. The Greek form Ἰωσήφ (Iōsēph) faithfully reproduces the Hebrew pronunciation. The name evokes trust in divine providence in the face of uncertain circumstances.
G2501G.emploi: Joseph appears mainly in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, particularly in the accounts of the birth and childhood of Jesus (Matthew 1-2; Luke 1-2). Matthew emphasizes his legal role as husband of Mary and adoptive father, establishing the genealogical connection to David. Luke portrays him as a faithful father who fulfills the obligations of the Law (Luke 2:4: he goes to Bethlehem for the census). John mentions Joseph as what is believed to be the father of Jesus (John 1:45; 6:42), highlighting the paradox that Jesus is this without truly being so. In Acts and the Epistle to the Hebrews, Joseph son of Jacob from the Old Testament is recalled as an example of perseverance and trust in God during trials.
G2501G.portee: Joseph manifests the virtue of prompt obedience to God and the ability to embrace what is not initially understood (the incarnation). For the believer, he embodies responsible fatherhood, discreet righteousness, and the protection of what has been entrusted. His silent acceptance of a divine plan that surpasses him serves as an example to those seeking to serve without seeking recognition.

sens: One of Jesus' brothers according to the flesh
One of the sons of Mary mentioned among Jesus' close relatives
G2501H.detail:
1. Joseph is one of the brothers of Jesus named in the Gospel of Matthew. When the people of Nazareth are astonished at Jesus' miracles, they list his family: "Isn't this the carpenter's son? Isn't his mother called Mary? And aren't his brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Jude?" (Matthew 13:55). This Joseph grew up alongside Jesus in the house of Mary and the carpenter Joseph (his legal father).
2. Another mention places him among the sons of Mary present at the crucifixion: "Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph" (Matthew 27:56). This mention confirms that he was indeed a recognized member of Jesus' family.
G2501H.origine: The name Ἰωσήφ (Iōsēph) derives from the Hebrew יוֹסֵף (Yoséph), which means "God adds" or "God increases" — a common blessing name in Israel. This Joseph of the Gospels should not be confused with Joseph son of Jacob (the patriarch), nor with Joseph of Arimathea who buried Jesus, nor with the other Josephs mentioned in the genealogies (such as the one in Luke 3:24 or 3:30).
G2501H.emploi: Joseph appears twice in the Gospels according to Matthew as a brother of Jesus. Matthew 13:55 explicitly names him among the four brothers publicly recognized in Nazareth. Matthew 27:56 mentions him again alongside James, while Mary and the other women remain near the cross. The Gospels provide no further details about his life, actions, or fate. He simply represents an ordinary member of Jesus' family before and after his death.
G2501H.portee: The mention of Joseph reminds us that Jesus grew up in an ordinary human family, with brothers and sisters. For Protestants, these brothers are biological children born after Jesus. This detail shows the true incarnation of Jesus: far from being isolated or superhuman from childhood, he experienced the common life of a sibling. The Gospel's discretion regarding Joseph also emphasizes that it is not familial ties that define spiritual importance.

sens: Member of the Sanhedrin, counselor of Jesus in Jerusalem
A good and righteous man, secret disciple of Jesus
He who requested Jesus' body from Pilate after the crucifixion
He who buried Jesus in his own tomb
G2501I.detail:
1. Joseph of Arimathea was a counselor (member of the Sanhedrin, the assembly of Jewish notables): he is an influential and respected man in Jerusalem, as noted in Mark 15:43 and Luke 23:50.
2. He is described as a "good and righteous man" (Luke 23:50), and as a disciple of Jesus, but who believed "secretly for fear of the Jews" (John 19:38) — he followed Jesus in his heart without publicly admitting it.
3. After Jesus' death on the cross, Joseph dared to present himself before Pilate (Mark 15:43) to request the body, a courageous act that finally revealed his faith (Matthew 27:57-59).
4. He took the body of Jesus, wrapped it in a clean linen shroud, and placed it in his own new tomb, thus fulfilling the final funeral honors (Matthew 27:59).
G2501I.origine: The name Joseph comes from the Hebrew Yossef, formed from a root meaning "to add" or "to increase" — it expresses a wish for blessing and offspring. Arimathea is a town in Judea, identified with Ramathaim-Zophim. This Joseph of Arimathea, distinct from other Josephs mentioned in the New Testament (the husband of Mary, the ancestors of Jesus, the brothers of Jesus), carries his hometown for clear identification.
G2501I.emploi: Joseph of Arimathea appears only in the accounts of the Passion and Burial: six references in the four gospels (Matthew 27:57, 59; Mark 15:43, 45; Luke 23:50; John 19:38). Each evangelist depicts him slightly differently: Mark emphasizes his status as a prominent counselor, Luke on his goodness and righteousness, John on the secret nature of his faith. But all show him making a decisive and dignified gesture in burying the body of Jesus, fulfilling a messianic prophecy (Isaiah 53:9: "they made his grave with the wicked"). His intervention marks the moment when even a hidden character out of fear dared to confess his faith.
G2501I.portee: Joseph of Arimathea teaches Christians that authentic faith does not require the absence of fear or caution, but the honesty of the heart. His final act — requesting the body and burying it with respect — shows how to honor Jesus in a concrete way. It also reminds us that great confessions of faith can arise at decisive moments, when love for the Lord prevails over fear of others.

sens: Son of Jacob, ancestor of Israel
Ancestor of Jesus (son of Matthias)
Ancestor of Jesus (son of Joram)
Husband of Mary, mother of the Lord
One of the brothers of Jesus
Joseph of Arimathea, who buried Jesus
G2501J.detail:
1. The most well-known Joseph of the Old Testament, son of Jacob and Rachel, sold into Egypt by his brothers, who became governor of the land and saved his family from famine (Acts 7:9-14, Hebrews 11:21-22).
2. An ancestor of Jesus according to his genealogy by Luke, son of Matthias (Luke 3:24).
3. Another ancestor of Jesus according to the same genealogy, son of Joram (Luke 3:30).
4. The husband of Mary, mother of Jesus, a carpenter from Nazareth who welcomed the Child into his family (Matthew 1:16, Luke 1:27, John 1:46).
5. One of the brothers (or cousins) of Jesus, mentioned in the gospels (Matthew 13:55).
6. Joseph of Arimathea, a notable Jew who, after Jesus' death, requested his body from Pilate and buried it in his own new tomb (Matthew 27:57-59, Mark 15:43, Luke 23:50, John 19:38).
G2501J.origine: The name Ἰωσήφ (Iōsēph) comes from the Hebrew יוֹסֵף (Yosef). It means "God adds" or "he whom God adds," composed of the root "to add" and the divine name. It is a name borne by several important figures in biblical history and in the gospels.
G2501J.emploi: The name Joseph refers to several people in the New Testament. The most famous is the husband of Mary and earthly father of Jesus, who appears mainly in the childhood narratives of Jesus in Matthew and Luke. Joseph of Arimathea, a disciple of the Lord, plays a crucial role at the time of the Passion, ensuring the honorable burial of Jesus. The New Testament also mentions ancestors of Jesus bearing this name, as well as a brother of Jesus. In Acts and the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Joseph of the Old Testament is recalled as a figure of faith and divine providence.
G2501J.portee: The name Joseph reminds us that God accompanies His own even in trial and exile. Joseph, husband of Mary, embodied justice, quiet faith, and responsibility for the family entrusted to him by God. Joseph of Arimathea shows that at the very moment when the disciples fled, hidden believers acted courageously to honor Jesus. These accounts comfort Christians by showing that God uses ordinary men to accomplish His purpose.

sens: Son of Jacob and Rachel, one of the twelve patriarchs of Israel
Ancestor of Jesus according to Luke's genealogy
Righteous man, husband of Mary, mother of Jesus
Brother or supposed relative of Jesus according to some witnesses
Pious man from Arimathea, secret disciple of Jesus
G2501L.detail:
1. Joseph, son of Jacob and Rachel, is one of the major figures of the Old Testament: sold by his brothers, he became a slave in Egypt, interpreted Pharaoh's dreams, and became governor (Genesis 37–50). He is the patriarch from whom two tribes of Israel, Ephraim and Manasseh, descended.

2. In the genealogy of Luke 3, Joseph appears as "son of Simeon, son of Judah, son of Joseph, son of Jonam": this link in the family tree establishes a continuity of 77 generations between Adam and Jesus, and this is the Joseph referred to.

3. Joseph of Nazareth, husband of Mary and legal father of Jesus: he receives the angel's announcement without doubt, raises Jesus in the fear of the Lord, and quietly disappears from the Gospel after the childhood of Christ.

4. Matthew 13:55 mentions him among "the brothers of Jesus" (Matthew, Mark), which has led to various interpretations: son of a previous union of Mary, or simply relative according to Semitic culture.

5. Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy notable of the Sanhedrin, secret disciple of Jesus, who dares to ask Pilate for Jesus' body and buries it in his own new tomb, thus testifying to his faith despite social pressure.
G2501L.origine: The Hebrew name יוֹסֵף (Yôsēph) means "God adds" or "may God add" (from יָסַף, "to add"), recalling Rachel's wish at Joseph's birth in Genesis 29:24. It is a very common name in Israel, evoking divine blessing and increase. The Greek Ἰωσήφ simply transcribes the Hebrew name without alteration.
G2501L.emploi: Joseph is a name borne by several people in the Bible, and this entry concerns the Joseph in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke 3:30. However, the context of the New Testament primarily highlights two major Josephs: first, the patriarch ancestor of the People of Israel, recalled in Hebrews 11:21-22 as a model of faith; secondly, Joseph of Nazareth, the carpenter of Galilee who raises Jesus, absent from the fourth Gospel but central in Matthew and Luke for anchoring the incarnation in real human history; finally, Joseph of Arimathea, who symbolizes hidden faith waiting for the Resurrected One. The name is a constant reminder of God's hand that adds, multiplies, and blesses.
G2501L.portee: The different Josephs in the Bible offer lessons in practical faith: Joseph the ancestor shows how God transforms even injustice into good; Joseph of Nazareth teaches humble obedience and vigilant protection of what is entrusted to us; Joseph of Arimathea demonstrates that one can be courageous in faith without being publicly known. For a believer, these models remind us that God adds His strength, wisdom, and blessing to those who trust Him, even in trials.

sens: Disciple candidate for the replacement of Judas among the apostles
G2501M.detail: 1. Joseph Barsabbas is a believer from the first church in Jerusalem, proposed alongside Matthias as a candidate to replace Judas Iscariot among the Twelve apostles (Acts 1:23). The name "Barsabbas" means "son of Sabbas." He also bears the Latin nickname "Justus," which means "just."
G2501M.origine: The name Joseph comes from the Hebrew Yossef, which means "God adds" or "may God add." It is a very common name in the Old Testament (the son of Jacob, notably) and in the New Testament. The nickname Barsabbas follows the Aramaic custom of designating someone by their father's name (bar = son).
G2501M.emploi: Joseph Barsabbas appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 1:23. After the Ascension, the apostles and disciples gather in Jerusalem to fill the vacancy left by Judas's suicide. Peter proposes two candidates: Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias. The other disciples pray and cast lots, and Matthias is chosen. Therefore, Joseph does not become an apostle and disappears from the biblical narrative.
G2501M.portee: This story reminds us that not all believers receive the same responsibilities in the church, even if they are worthy. Joseph Barsabbas was indeed qualified, but the Lord chose Matthias. This invites us to humbly accept the place that God assigns us and to serve faithfully, whatever it may be.

sens: son of Jacob, sold into Egypt where he became a powerful minister of Pharaoh
one of Jesus' ancestors in his genealogy
the husband of Mary, mother of Jesus
a brother of Jesus according to the flesh
a disciple or member of the early Christian community
G2501N.detail:
1. Joseph, son of Jacob, is the hero of the Old Testament whose story occupies a large part of Genesis. Sold by his jealous brothers (Acts 7:9), he was taken to Egypt where God blessed him and elevated him to become minister of Pharaoh. His brothers recognized him during a famine (Acts 7:13), and he brought his entire family to Egypt (Acts 7:14). Jacob, before dying, blessed Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh (Hebrews 11:21-22). The New Testament mentions him to show that God has always guided him and to recall the story of salvation.
2. Several men named Joseph appear in the genealogy of Jesus: one is the son of Matthias, the other the son of Joram (Luke 3:24, 3:30).
3. Joseph of Nazareth, husband of Mary, is the adoptive father of Jesus according to the flesh. He is the man God chose to protect and raise His incarnate Son.
4. A brother of Jesus bears this name (Matthew 13:55), being from the same mother.
5. Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the Sanhedrin, is the one who, after the crucifixion, asked Pilate for the body of Jesus and placed it in his own new tomb (Matthew 27:57-59).
G2501N.origine: The name Joseph comes from the Hebrew יוֹסֵף (Yoséph), which literally means "God adds" or "may God add." It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the name of God, expressing a prayer or a promise from the parents. In the Old Testament, Rachel, the mother of Joseph, calls him this by saying: "God has taken away my reproach... May the Lord add me another son" (Genesis 30:23-24).
G2501N.emploi: The name Joseph designates eight different figures in the New Testament. The most important is Joseph, son of Jacob, whose holy story is recalled in several books (John, Acts, Hebrews, Revelation) to illustrate divine providence and God's faithfulness through generations. The New Testament cites Joseph of Egypt to show how God elevates the righteous and prepares salvation. Joseph of Nazareth, the adoptive father of Jesus, appears mainly in the gospels of Matthew and Luke, particularly in the infancy narratives. Joseph of Arimathea appears in all the passion narratives as the respectful witness who honors the Lord's body after His death. Other Josephs appear in a minor way in genealogies or as the brother of Jesus.
G2501N.portee: The name Joseph, repeated throughout the biblical history from Abraham to Jesus, reminds the reader that God "adds" always: He adds His blessings, His protection, His promised offspring. The example of Joseph of Egypt shows that even injustice and exile cannot stop God's plan. Joseph of Nazareth teaches humble obedience and righteousness: he is a just man who accepts what God asks of him, even beyond his understanding. These figures embody trust in divine providence and the importance of remaining faithful in trials.

sens: Man who received the nickname Barnabas among the early Christians
G2501O.detail: 1. Joseph, nicknamed Barnabas by the apostles, is a Levite from Cyprus who played an important role in the early church of Jerusalem (Acts 4:36). His nickname means "son of encouragement," which shows that he distinguished himself by his gift of encouragement and consolation among the brethren.
G2501O.origine: The name Ἰωσήφ (Joseph) comes from the Hebrew יוֹסֵף (Yosef), which literally means "God adds." It is a very common name in Israel, borne by several important figures in Scripture. This Joseph is known by his Greek nickname Βαρνάβας (Barnabas), which was his name of use among the disciples.
G2501O.emploi: This Joseph appears in Acts under his nickname Barnabas. He is presented as a Cypriot Levite who engaged in the communal life of the early Christians: he sold a property and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet (Acts 4:36-37). Later, he became a major collaborator of Paul in the expansion of the Church, particularly during the first missionary journey. His main role in the New Testament is to encourage Christians and promote unity among the disciples.
G2501O.portee: Barnabas embodies the Christian who puts his resources and talents at the service of the community. His example shows that encouragement and exhortation are essential gifts for building the Church. He also teaches us that the disciples did not need to wait for the end of the world to start sharing brotherly, but that generosity was at the heart of church life from the beginning.

sens: king of Judah in the 7th century BC
G2502.detail: Josiah is a king of Judah, an ancestor of Jesus according to the genealogy of Matthew. He appears in the list of kings preceding the birth of Christ, inscribed in the messianic lineage: "Amon begot Josiah; Josiah begot Jeconiah" (Matthew 1:10-11). He is an important link in the chain connecting David to Jesus, showing that the Messiah descends from the royal dynasty of Judah.
G2502.origine: The Greek name Ἰωσίας transcribes the Hebrew name יֹאשִׁיָּה (Yō'ashiyyāh), which means "Yahweh heals" or "Yahweh supports." Josiah was a notable historical king of Judah, known in biblical history for his religious reforms and practices.
G2502.emploi: Josiah appears twice in the Gospel of Matthew, exclusively in the genealogy of chapter 1. He is mentioned as the son of Amon and the father of Jeconiah, marking his place in the succession of kings. Matthew reproduces the dynastic line of the people of Judah, thus establishing the genealogical link between the promised royalty and Jesus, the son of David.

sens: the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet
a tiny, minuscule thing
G2503.detail:
1. The iota is the letter י (yod) of the Hebrew alphabet: the smallest of the letters, so minuscule that it can barely be seen. Jesus refers to it in Matthew 5:18 to illustrate the most minute detail.
2. Figuratively, the iota denotes a microscopic, seemingly negligible thing. In the same verse, Jesus asserts that not a single iota will disappear from the Law — indicating that God preserves every detail, even the smallest, of His Word until its final fulfillment.
G2503.origine: The Greek word ἰῶτα directly transcribes the Hebrew name of this letter, י (yod). In Greek, the iota is also the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, corresponding to our 'i'. Jesus chose this word because it was recognizable to His Jewish listeners: the Hebrew letter and its Greek equivalent share the same name and symbolize infinitesimality.
G2503.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 5:18. Jesus uses it to affirm the absolute integrity and indestructibility of God's Law. By associating the iota with 'a stroke of a letter' (the smallest mark of writing), He emphasizes that the divine Word is trustworthy in all its details, not just in its general principles. This assertion responds to false teachers who claimed to annul certain commandments: Jesus guarantees that everything will be fulfilled.
G2503.portee: This word teaches the believer to respect the entire Word of God, even the seemingly insignificant details. It also assures that God governs history until the complete fulfillment of His promises: nothing will be lost, nothing will be omitted.

sens: In the same way as, according to the mode or manner indicated by what precedes
Just as, exactly in the same way
G2505.detail:
1. This word introduces a comparison or conformity: it means 'in the same way as' or 'according to'. In Matthew 27:10, the apostle Jeremiah reports that he acted 'as' the Lord had commanded him — that is, by exactly imitating the received order, obeying its precise terms.
2. It is a conjunction of comparison that establishes a parallel or equivalence: 'just as' or 'just so'. It connects two actions or states by showing that they correspond or resemble each other.
G2505.origine: The word comes from the contraction κατά ('according to', 'in accordance with') and ἅ (the relative pronoun 'what', 'which'). It combines the idea of conformity (κατά) with that of reference or standard (the relative pronoun). In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew אֲשֶׁר ('who') or כְּ ('as'), small words that mark a relationship or resemblance between two elements.
G2505.emploi: This word appears once in the Gospel according to Matthew (27:10) and once in a textual variant at the beginning of Luke (1:2, according to some manuscripts). It is always a conjunction of comparison used to establish a relationship of conformity or resemblance: one acts 'as' one has been commanded to act, or one describes things 'as' they have occurred. It is a rare word in the New Testament; Greek generally prefers other forms like ὥς or καθώς to express this idea.
G2505.portee: This small conjunction reminds us of the importance of exact obedience to the Word of God. When we act 'as' God has commanded, we leave no room for improvisation or personal interpretation: we faithfully submit to His will. It is a lesson in precision and respect in our relationship with the Lord.

sens: Action of overturning, demolishing a structure
Abolition, suppression of a force or power
Annihilation or ruin of a person or work
G2506.detail:
1. The word first evokes the physical act of demolishing, overturning fortified buildings: Paul speaks of 'overthrowing strongholds' (2 Corinthians 10:4), a powerful image of the collapse of a solid structure.
2. It also designates the cancellation, the abolition of an established power — not by brute force, but by the power of God that disarms and annihilates what opposes Him. It is the opposite of edification, the patient construction of faith (2 Corinthians 10:8 and 13:10).
3. Finally, it can mean total ruin, the spiritual or physical death of a person or cause; here, apostolic authority may be used for 'destruction' if correction becomes punishment without mercy.
G2506.origine: The word comes from 'cathairein', which means 'to take away downwards', composed of 'kata' (downwards) and 'hairein' (to take away, seize). The basic image is one of an action that removes, snatches, makes fall — hence the idea of destruction by lowering. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often uses this word to translate 'haras', which means to break, demolish.
G2506.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Paul's letters to the Corinthians. In 2 Corinthians 10:4, it metaphorically designates the overthrow of the 'strongholds' of pride and unbelief by spiritual weapons — not carnal weapons. In 2 Corinthians 10:8 and 13:10, Paul plays on the contrast between 'edification' (building faith) and 'destruction': the authority he has received from the Lord is meant to build the Church, never to destroy it. The word thus underscores the stakes of all spiritual power: it can build or ruin depending on how it is used.
G2506.portee: This word reminds the Christian that true power does not destroy life, but builds it. It overturns spiritual obstacles (pride, lies, rebellion against God), not people. For the believer in a position of authority — pastor, parent, leader — it is a warning: the authority received from God is meant to edify and save, never to crush or humiliate. It is also a comfort: only the power of God can truly overturn the strongholds of evil that oppress us.

sens: To remove something or someone from a high place, particularly from the cross after a crucifixion
To overturn, to bring down something high or someone from their position
To destroy a structure, to demolish a building
To annihilate, to eliminate by force
Figuratively, to refute, to demolish an argument or thought
G2507.detail:
1. The most concrete and frequent meaning in the New Testament is to take a crucified person down from the cross: the technical term used for this funeral practice. Joseph of Arimathea "took Jesus down from the cross" (Mark 15:46), and later "he took him down from the cross, wrapped him in a linen shroud" (Luke 23:53). It literally means to remove a body from a high position.

2. More broadly, to overturn something or someone from a position of power or height. God "has brought down the mighty from their thrones" (Luke 1:52): the word describes the overthrow of an established authority.

3. To destroy a structure, to demolish a building. The rich man says, "I will tear down my barns and build larger ones" (Luke 12:18), contrasting this destruction with construction.

4. To destroy a nation or people through military conquest. God "destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan" (Acts 13:19) to give the territory to Israel.

5. Figuratively, to refute or demolish an argument, a thought. Paul speaks of "taking every thought captive to obey Christ" by "destroying" arguments (2 Corinthians 10:5) — making an intellectual or moral position collapse.
G2507.origine: The Greek word καθαιρέω (kathaireō) is composed of κατά (kata, "down from") and αἱρέω (haireō, "to take, to remove"). The basic image is therefore to take something down, hence the idea of descending, removing, and by extension overturning, destroying. This word belongs to a family of terms that express the action of making fall or reducing to nothing. It translates into Greek Hebrew roots like נָתַץ (natas, to destroy) and פָּרַץ (parats, to demolish), showing that the Old Testament and the New share this notion of destruction or overthrow.
G2507.emploi: The verb καθαιρέω appears 8 times in the New Testament. Its primary use is technical and historical: to take a crucified person down from the cross, a regulated practice that had to be done before sunset. Mark and Luke use the term twice each for Joseph of Arimathea taking Jesus down from the cross (Mark 15:46, Luke 23:53) and once in reference to the removal of Christ (Mark 15:36, Acts 13:29). The word then extends to other forms of destruction: overturning a power (Luke 1:52, Acts 19:27), demolishing buildings (Luke 12:18), conquering nations (Acts 13:19). It also acquires a figurative sense when Paul uses it regarding refuting rebellious thoughts (2 Corinthians 10:5). This progression from the concrete to the figurative shows how the word always retains the idea of making something collapse or fall from an established position.
G2507.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of two important spiritual truths. First, the removal of Christ's body from the cross affirms his true death and true humanity: there is nothing ghostly about the resurrection. Second, the image of overturning "rebellious thoughts" (2 Corinthians 10:5) invites every believer to examine their own reasoning and submit it to the Word of God, rejecting ideas that contradict the Gospel. It is a call to intellectual and spiritual vigilance.

sens: To trim a climbing plant or shrub to remove unnecessary branches
To clean, to purify by removing what clutters
Spiritual perfection through the elimination of the superfluous
G2508.detail:
1. The word refers to the action of trimming a vine or plant to remove branches that do not bear fruit or that suffocate it. It is a concrete agricultural task: the vinedresser examines each shoot and cuts the unproductive one. In John 15:2, Jesus says that the Father "prunes" every branch that bears fruit, so that it may bear more — pruning stimulates fruitfulness.
2. More broadly, the word means to clean or purify by removing everything that is unnecessary or obstructive. It conveys the idea of clearing away, sorting between what remains and what is removed.
3. Spiritually, pruning evokes God's work in the believer's life: He removes what hinders spiritual growth, what absorbs energy without producing fruit. It is never destruction, but grooming aimed at fruitfulness.
G2508.origine: The word comes from "kathara" (pure, clean) and literally means "to make pure." In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "doush" (to tread), the idea of a stick that cleans and orders. Unlike "katharizō" (to purify in a moral or ritual sense), "kathairō" emphasizes the mechanical, concrete action of removal.
G2508.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 15:2, at the heart of Jesus' discourse on the vine and the branches. Jesus uses this agricultural image to explain the relationship between Him, the Father, and the disciples. Pruning is not a punishment, but an act of love: the Father cleans every productive disciple so that he may bear even more fruit. The context suggests that pruning here means removing everything in the believer's life that clutters their relationship with Jesus and their ability to bear spiritual fruit.
G2508.portee: This image speaks to the believer's heart about sanctification. The trials and difficulties of the Christian life are not punishments, but interventions from the Father who wants to make us more fruitful. Understanding this promise comforts and directs: every pain is a grooming, an act of benevolent wisdom. It is an invitation to accept discipline with gratitude, knowing that it serves our growth.

sens: in the same way as
in the same manner as
just as
according to
G2509.detail:
1. The word introduces a comparison: it shows that two things are done in the same way or according to the same model. For example, in 1 Corinthians 10:10, the Israelites complained "as" (in the same way as) some of the former Israelites had complained before.
2. It can also indicate equivalence or correspondence between two parallel realities: in Romans 4:6, David expresses happiness "just as" it applies to all believers. It is an analogy that asserts that a truth extends from one case to another.
3. Sometimes the word connects two situations to show simultaneity or relationship: in 2 Corinthians 3:18, we are transformed "as by" the action of the Spirit of the Lord, that is, under His influence and according to His mode of operation.
4. The word can also introduce a proportion or agreement: in 1 Thessalonians 2:11, the apostles acted toward each of them "as" (just as) a father acts toward his children — the same relationship, the same love, the same role.
G2509.origine: The Greek word κατά (kata) means "according to" or "in accordance with"; ἅπερ (haper) is a relative pronoun ("who"). Together, κατάπερ (kathaper) literally means "according to what" or "just as what." This formula establishes comparisons and parallels between facts or principles: it states that this happens as that does, under the same conditions or by the same logic. In Hebrew, one often finds אֲשֶׁר (asher, "who," "that") to express this idea of conformity.
G2509.emploi: This word appears 13 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Pauline epistles (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, 1 Thessalonians) and in Hebrews. Paul uses it to establish strong theological analogies: David's righteousness prefigures that of believers (Romans 4:6), the body of believers functions "as" one body with many members (1 Corinthians 12:12), we are transformed "as" by the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:18). It is a teaching tool that connects truths and shows how a biblical principle applies to multiple situations. The word also appears to compare behaviors: the murmuring of believers resembles the murmuring of the Israelites (1 Corinthians 10:10).
G2509.portee: This small word reminds the reader that God acts according to a coherence and logic: what He has done in the past sheds light on what He is doing now. The comparisons established by "as" invite reflection on the unity of God's plan and the continuity of His action. They also encourage recognizing biblical analogies: understanding the relationship between a father and his children helps grasp that of God toward His spiritual children.

sens: Fix, place on something
Seize, cling to
Assault, take on
G2510.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to fix or place something onto an object: to attach a garment to someone, to secure an accessory. It is the concrete action of joining two things together.

2. In a middle sense or with the genitive (a less common construction), the verb means to seize, to take hold of something: it is less about placing on than about appropriating, grabbing. In Acts 28:3, the viper "attaches" itself to Paul's hand — it seizes it, clinging with its fangs.

3. By extension, to attach can also mean to assault or take on someone: it is a viper that attacks, a threat that suddenly manifests. The action becomes hostile, an aggression rather than a simple fixation.
G2510.origine: The word is composed of κατά (kata, "on, against") and ἅπτω (haptō, "to touch, seize"). The root ἅπτω evokes the action of making contact, of touching with intention. Together, κατ-ἁπτω means to touch on, to reach directly: first to fix on something, then to seize, then to assault. It is an image of direct and effective contact.
G2510.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 28:3, during Paul's shipwreck on the way to Rome. A viper escapes from the fire and attaches itself to his hand. In this dramatic context, "attach" means both to cling (the viper bites and holds on) and to assault (a sudden aggression). It is a moment of peril where a venomous creature takes on Paul, but where divine protection intervenes — Paul suffers no harm. The verb paints the immediacy and intensity of danger.
G2510.portee: This account recalls the promise made by Jesus: those who believe in his name will crush serpents and be preserved from all poison (Mark 16:18). The viper that attaches itself to Paul symbolizes hostile forces; its powerlessness against the servant of God confirms divine protection over those who serve him. It is an invitation to trust in trials.

sens: Make clean, rid of dirt or filth
Heal someone from leprosy or a disease
Make pure inwardly, cleanse the soul or heart from sin
Make acceptable for worship through a rite or sacrifice
G2511.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes physical cleaning: removing dirt from something. This is why Jesus tells the blind Pharisee to "first clean the inside of the cup and dish" (Matthew 23:26) — it is necessary to clean not just the outside, but what is inside.
2. The word is used for the healing of lepers: when a leper asks Jesus, "If you are willing, you can make me clean," he is speaking of his healing (Matthew 8:2). Once healed, the lepers "were cleansed" as they went to show themselves to the priests (Luke 17:14).
3. Transposed to the soul, the word means to purify from sin: Paul urges the Corinthians to "cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit" (2 Corinthians 7:1). God purifies the heart by faith (Acts 15:9).
4. In Jewish worship, it means to make pure or acceptable for divine service through a rite or sacrifice: "It was necessary that the heavenly things themselves be purified with better sacrifices" (Hebrews 9:23).
G2511.origine: The word comes from the adjective "pure" (καθαρός) and the Greek root that expresses cleanliness. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates the verb "to be pure" (טָהֵר), which originally denoted the absence of cultic defilement. This word is steeped in the biblical vocabulary of purification: adding to it the noun "purity" (καθαρότης) and the accompanying adjective "pure" found in the texts.
G2511.emploi: The verb appears 30 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew and Luke. In the physical sense, it is closely associated with the healing of lepers: Jesus heals the lepers who ask him for this purification (Matthew 8:2-3, Mark 1:40-42, Luke 5:12-13). In the ethical sense, it describes the purification of the soul and heart: it is requested for oneself (2 Corinthians 7:1, James 4:8) or spoken of as God's work (Acts 15:9 for the heart purified by faith, 1 John 1:7 and 1:9 for the blood of Jesus that purifies from sin). In the ceremonial sense, the word applies to ancient worship (Hebrews 9:22-23, 10:2) and to ritual separation (Acts 10:15, 11:9 regarding what is clean or unclean to eat).
G2511.portee: This word shows that Jesus heals both body and soul, and that he fulfills what the Old Testament promised: not only physical health but moral and spiritual purity. For the Christian, it reminds us that true purity comes from God alone — through faith in Jesus Christ, whose blood purifies us from sin (1 John 1:7). It is a call to turn away from what defiles and to ask God for inner purification, not just ceremonial.

sens: action of making pure, cleaning
religious ceremony where one becomes pure in the eyes of the law
ablution or washing prescribed by Jewish law
elimination of sin
G2512.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the concrete action of making something or someone pure: cleaning so that it conforms to what God requires. A healed leper had to undergo a purification (Mark 1:44) — a process prescribed by Moses to mark his return to legal purity.

2. It is also an official religious ceremony, often performed by the priest, who declares someone pure. After her childbirth, Mary underwent the days of purification required by the law (Luke 2:22), fulfilling what Jewish Law mandated.

3. The word can also refer to the vessels and the ablutions themselves: at Cana, there were stone jars "for the purification of the Jews" (John 2:6) — objects and rites that served to maintain ritual purity.

4. From a deeper and spiritual perspective, the purification of sins is the work of Christ (Hebrews 1:3): not an external rite, but the internal and definitive elimination of our faults through his sacrifice.
G2512.origine: The word comes from the verb "katharidzō" (to purify, to clean) and the root "katharos" (pure, clean). The family denotes everything that is purified or cleared of impurity — it is a very concrete image, that of cleaning. In biblical Hebrew, this word often translates "tâhēr" (to be pure, to purify), the root of the complete system of ritual purity in the Law. This notion of purification runs throughout the Old Testament: impurity related to blood, diseases, contact with death — and the rituals to wash away these impurities.
G2512.emploi: The word appears seven times in the New Testament, almost exclusively regarding Jewish law issues. In the Gospels (Mark, Luke, John), it often concerns the legal purification of healed individuals, women after childbirth, or the ritual ablutions that Jews observed (John 2:6 and 3:25). A "dispute" even arises between the disciples of John and a Jew "about purification" (John 3:25) — a question that occupied minds. But in the Epistles (Hebrews 1:3 and 2 Peter 1:9), the meaning transforms: purification becomes the redemptive work of Christ, who erases sin — not through rites, but through his sacrifice. The word thus shifts from legal practice to spiritual reality.
G2512.portee: For the Christian reader, this word illustrates the transition from an external law of purification (ablutions, prescriptions) to the internal and definitive purification given by Christ. Jesus does not abolish the Law — he reveals its deeper meaning: true purity is not a matter of rites, but of forgiveness and heart transformation. This liberates us from guilt: we do not have to perform endless works to "purify" ourselves; Christ has made this purification once for all.

sens: Exempt from physical stain or material impurity.
In accordance with religious law regarding ritual purity.
Innocent, without moral or spiritual guilt.
Sincere, without ulterior motives or hidden intentions.
Unmixed, of absolute quality.
Free from anything that tarnishes, truly holy.
G2513.detail:
1. In the physical sense, the word describes what is clean, without stain or residue: pure water (Hebrews 10:22), the white linen of heavenly garments (Revelation 19:8), the washed body (Hebrews 10:22). It is the purity that can be seen and touched.
2. In a religious context, it refers to what adheres to the purity rules of the Law: clean foods according to Moses (Romans 14:20), or one who has been ritually purified (Luke 11:41). Ceremonial purity opens access to worship.
3. In the moral and spiritual sense for a person, it is the absence of guilt and malice: a pure conscience (2 Timothy 1:3), a pure heart (Matthew 5:8), innocent hands (Acts 20:26). It is one whose heart harbors no evil intention.
4. It is also sincerity, the absence of double-dealing: one who speaks plainly, acts without ulterior motives, and hides nothing. The purity of heart makes one transparent before God and men.
5. It is what is not diluted, mixed, or counterfeit: it is the absolute, the integrity. The Christian's life must be pure, meaning without compromise with anything that would distance them from God.
6. Finally, in an eschatological sense, it is the final state of the believer and the restored creation: pure garments in heaven (Revelation 19:8), pure gold in the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:18), those with a pure heart will see God (Matthew 5:8).
G2513.origine: The Greek word katharos comes from a root meaning "to clarify" or "to make bright." In Hebrew, it primarily translates tahor, which denotes conformity to the rules of Mosaic purity. Related family: the verb katharizō (to purify), the noun katharsis (purification). The image is that of cleaning, removing any obstacle or impurity that veils or tarnishes.
G2513.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, John, Paul, and Revelation. It is first used in the physical sense: water, clothing (Revelation 19:8, 21:18). In a religious context, the Apostle Paul uses it to clarify the rules of dietary purity: all things are pure for one whose conscience is not troubled (Romans 14:20). However, the dominant usage is ethical and spiritual: Jesus promises happiness to those with a pure heart (Matthew 5:8), He purifies His disciples by His word (John 15:3), Paul boasts of having pure hands before the Jews (Acts 20:26). The word becomes the Greek equivalent of holiness in the moral life of the believer.
G2513.portee: This word invites the Christian to purity of heart as a condition for a true relationship with God. Jesus speaks not of external cleanliness or rites, but of inner sincerity, of a guiltless conscience. It is a call to moral transparency and integrity, knowing that the pure in heart will see God. Purity is not an impossible performance, but the fruit of faith and the received word (John 15:3).

sens: State of what is pure, without mixture or stain
Absence of guilt or moral fault
State of ritual consecration, particularly according to the Mosaic law
G2514.detail:
1. Purity is the state of being free from any stain or contamination. In Hebrews 9:13, it refers to the physical purification of the flesh according to the rites of the Law: the blood of sacrifices and the ashes of a heifer provide "purity of the flesh" to Israelites who have become ritually unclean. It is a concrete and legal notion.
2. In the moral and spiritual sense, purity means the absence of guilt, transgression, or malice. It is the state of one whose conscience is clear before God.
3. More broadly, purity denotes consecration to God and the state of one who lives separated from sin and its effects. It is the opposite of spiritual defilement and detachment from God.
G2514.origine: The Greek word "purity" comes from the adjective "pure" (καθαρός), which conveys the idea of being clean, without stain, free from contamination. This root also appears in "to purify" (καθαρίζω). In Hebrew, this word often translates "pure" (טָהוֹר), a key term in the Law of Moses to denote the ritual and spiritual state that allows access to divine worship.
G2514.emploi: The word "purity" appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:13, in the context of the sacrificial and legal system of the Old Testament. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews uses it to explain how the Mosaic rites (sacrifices and ashes of a heifer) provided ritual purification. The word here denotes the legal and physical state of one who had become pure again according to the Law after having committed an impurity. This passage highlights the temporary and external nature of this legal purity, in contrast to the definitive purification brought by Christ.
G2514.portee: This word reminds the believer that the ritual purity of the Old Testament was merely a shadow of the true and lasting purification that Jesus Christ provides. It invites us to understand that our consecration to God no longer rests on external rites, but on the inner transformation of the heart through faith and the Holy Spirit. It is an invitation to seek true spiritual purity, the kind that makes us acceptable before God.

sens: Furniture on which one sits, with or without a backrest
Chair or bench from which an authority teaches or presides
Position of authority or power that derives from it
G2515.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: an object, a piece of furniture where one sits. In the temple of Jerusalem, the sellers of pigeons had seats to sell their merchandise (Matthew 21:12, Mark 11:15) — Jesus overturned these seats to purify the place of worship.
2. By extension, the seat becomes the place from which someone teaches or directs: the scribes and Pharisees "sit in the chair of Moses" (Matthew 23:2). The word no longer simply describes the furniture, but the position of teacher and guide of the people.
3. This second meaning shifts towards the notion of authority and responsibility: occupying the chair means holding the role of interpreter and spiritual leader. The seat symbolizes the right to speak on behalf of the sacred tradition.
G2515.origine: The Greek word καθέδρα comes from two roots: κατά ("according to, down") and ἔδρα ("seat, sitting place"). The initial image is that of an object where one settles, in a stable position. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the same Greek word translates מוֹשָׁב, which also means "seat, place." In the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament), this term describes both ordinary seats and seats of authority — showing that the transition from one meaning to the other occurred naturally in biblical thought.
G2515.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. Twice, it literally designates a material object: the seats of the sellers of pigeons in the temple, which Jesus overturns during His purification of the sacred place (Matthew 21:12 and Mark 11:15, which report the same event). Once, in Matthew 23:2, it takes on a figurative and majestic sense: "the chair of Moses" represents the apostolic succession of Israel's teachers and the legitimacy of their teaching. Jesus acknowledges this chair while criticizing the scribes and Pharisees who occupy it without honoring it through their actions.
G2515.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that the temple is the holy place of prayer, not of mercantile commerce: Jesus purified it so that God's house remains a center of communion with God, not of profit. It also raises the question of spiritual authority: having a chair means having the duty to live according to what one teaches. The Pharisees occupied the chair of Moses, but their lives contradicted their words — which invalidates their moral authority.

sens: To take a seated position, to sit down.
To remain seated in a place, to stay seated.
To occupy a place of power or authority by sitting.
G2516.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply to take or remain in a seated position. John 4:6 illustrates this well: Jesus, tired from his journey, was sitting by Jacob's well — it is the physical posture of rest. Likewise, the angels in John 20:12 are sitting at the tomb's place.

2. The word also describes the act of remaining seated somewhere, staying in that place. Luke 2:46 testifies to this: the young Jesus was sitting among the doctors of the temple, listening and asking questions — he was settled there to learn. Mary in John 11:20 was sitting at home, waiting for Jesus.

3. When it comes to an assembly or a court, the verb takes on a shade of authority and power. Acts 6:15 reports that all who sat on the Sanhedrin fixed their gaze on Stephen — they occupied the places of judgment. This is also what Jesus says in Matthew 26:55: he was sitting among them teaching in the temple, thus exercising his authority as a teacher.
G2516.origine: The word comes from the prefix κατά- (down) combined with ἵζω (to sit). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates יָשַׁב (yashav, "to sit" or "to dwell"), the fundamental verb of rest and dwelling. This root evokes the idea of taking a place, establishing oneself somewhere — hence its extension from physical rest to power exercised from a seat.
G2516.emploi: This verb appears about 91 times in the Greek New Testament, but the word καθέζομαι in particular is used sporadically. Jesus is described as sitting in the temple teaching (Matthew 26:55), at the well tired (John 4:6), among the doctors as a child (Luke 2:46). The disciples and the angels are also presented as sitting (John 11:20, John 20:12). Finally, in a judicial context, the members of the Sanhedrin "sit" to judge (Acts 6:15). The verb can be reinforced by the adjective "alone" or accompanied by a preposition indicating the place: "sitting beside," "sitting on." Each usage emphasizes either physical rest, dwelling, or the exercise of authority.
G2516.portee: This simple verb reminds us that Scripture does not disdain ordinary gestures. Jesus was seated like us, tired, teaching, waiting — he shares our humanity even in his attitudes. For us, "to be seated" can also mean to learn (like the young Jesus at the feet of the doctors), to exercise responsibility with seriousness, or simply to find the rest that labor demands. It is a word of everyday life that anchors faith in real life.

sens: One after another, in an established order
In a coherent and orderly manner, without skipping steps
Then, in the course of time
G2517.detail:
1. The word describes a succession where things happen one after another following a natural order. It is like a list that unfolds point by point. Luke notes that he has investigated "from their origin" and will present the facts "in a successive manner" (Luke 1:3): he will present his account in an orderly way, without skipping steps. Similarly, Paul traveled "successively" through Galatia and Phrygia (Acts 18:23), region by region.
2. The word emphasizes the continuity and clarity of the narrative or exposition. Peter recounts "in a successive manner" how things unfolded (Acts 11:4): he links the events in a logical and understandable way. It is a way of presenting that facilitates understanding.
3. In a broader sense, the word can mark the passage of time or an event that happens after another. "Then," Jesus went through the cities preaching (Luke 8:1): this is what occurred in the course of his ministry.
G2517.origine: The word comes from classical Greek ἑξῆς (hexês), which means "in order" or "in succession." It is composed of prefixes that reinforce the idea of continuity and progression. The root ἔξ (ex) evokes the idea of what flows, of what comes after. The word often translates the Hebrew of the Old Testament when expressing an ordered sequence of events or generations.
G2517.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, mainly in Luke and Acts. Luke uses it to describe his own project as a historian: to write an orderly and continuous account of the events in the life of Jesus. In Acts, it serves to present Peter's speeches and Paul's missionary journey with the same idea of clear and methodical progression. The meaning varies slightly depending on the context: sometimes it is the order of events ("one after another"), sometimes the quality of the presentation ("in an orderly manner"), sometimes simply the passage of time ("then"). But the central idea remains that of a logical and intelligible sequence.
G2517.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith rests on a real and coherent story. Luke takes care to present the events of Jesus' life "in a successive manner," which means we can trust his account: he does not invent, he investigates and orders the facts. For the reader, this invites trust: the Gospels are not disordered tales, but meticulous and ordered testimonies. It is an invitation to read the biblical story in its continuity, seeing how God leads his plan step by step.

sens: natural state of rest for the body during which one loses consciousness
to be in sleep, to gradually fall asleep
to lack vigilance, spiritual attention
state of death or spiritual inactivity
G2518.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simple: it is the natural state of sleep, when the body rests and the mind dozes. Jesus sleeps in the boat during the storm (Matthew 8:24), just as the servants sent by his bridegroom delay and fall asleep while waiting for him (Matthew 25:5).

2. The verb also describes the action of falling asleep, of slipping into sleep: Jesus' disciples in Gethsemane fall back into sleep despite his call to stay awake with him (Matthew 26:40, Mark 14:40).

3. Figuratively, "to sleep" means to be absent, distracted, lacking moral or spiritual vigilance. Jesus reproaches his disciples for sleeping at the crucial moment of his imminent arrest: "You are sleeping now, and you are resting!" (Matthew 26:45). Paul also warns the Christians in Thessalonica: "Why are you sleeping? Get up and pray, so that you will not fall into temptation" (Luke 22:46).

4. The Bible uses "to sleep" as an image of death: Jesus says of Jairus' daughter that "the child is not dead, but sleeps" (Mark 5:39), announcing her resurrection. Paul also speaks of those who are "dead in Christ," who "sleep," awaiting resurrection (1 Thessalonians 5:10).
G2518.origine: The Greek word καθεύδω (katheudō) comes from a root that expresses the idea of stretching out, resting. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew verb שָׁכַב (shakav), "to lie down," and sometimes יָשֵׁן (yashen), "to sleep." It is a very ancient verb, common in the Greek of the four Gospels and the epistles, designating one of the most ordinary vital needs. Its metaphorical use to speak of death or spiritual neglect is already present in the Psalms and the Hebrew prophets.
G2518.emploi: The verb "to sleep" appears 20 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and in Paul's epistles. It first describes ordinary physical sleep: Jesus sleeps during the storm (Matthew 8:24, Mark 4:38), the disciples fall asleep while waiting for the bridegroom (Matthew 25:5), a grain of wheat remains dormant in the ground before sprouting (Mark 4:27). But from the Gospels, the meaning becomes moral and spiritual: to sleep is to lack vigilance at the crucial moment, which Jesus reproaches the three disciples for in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:40-45, Mark 14:37-41). Paul extends this reproach to the entire Christian conscience, urging the faithful to awaken from spiritual sleep (Ephesians 5:14, 1 Thessalonians 5:6-7). Finally, the word takes on an eschatological meaning: to sleep is to die in expectation of resurrection (1 Thessalonians 5:10).
G2518.portee: For the believer, this word cries out a double call: that of trust — Jesus sleeps because he has no worries even in the storm — and that of spiritual vigilance. The Bible warns us that spiritual dormancy and inattentiveness are dangerous; they make us vulnerable to temptation and distance from God. But "to sleep" in the sense of dying in faith is not an end: it is a rest before the resurrection. To watch means to keep one's heart anchored in God and ready for his return.

sens: one who guides, who shows the way
one who directs or teaches a group
master, person who teaches
G2519.detail: 1. The word first evokes someone who walks ahead and guides others — the image is that of a leader who shows the way. 2. In a broader sense, it is one who directs, who has the authority to lead a group toward a goal: in Matthew 23:10, Jesus criticizes those who call themselves "leaders" among the disciples, as this absolute authority belongs only to him. 3. The word also designates a master or teacher, someone who teaches and imparts knowledge — the one to whom one turns to learn.
G2519.origine: The word comes from the verb "kathēgeisthai" which means "to walk before, to guide." The root evokes the idea of preceding: one who goes ahead to show the way. It is a compound formed on an ancient root meaning "to lead" or "to conduct." In Greek, the same family is found in words related to direction, teaching, and command.
G2519.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: Matthew 23:10. Jesus uses it to refer to those who claim to have absolute authority over other disciples. Its use in this passage is critical: Jesus refuses for his disciples to accept such human leadership, as he alone is the true leader, the true master of all. The context shows that Jesus addresses the vanity of the religious leaders of his time who sought titles and prestige.
G2519.portee: This passage teaches Christians an essential lesson about authority: no human leader, pastor, or teacher should take the place of Christ as the supreme director of the believer's life. It invites a healthy vigilance against those who seek to dominate or centralize spiritual power. It is a call to recognize that only Christ truly has the authority to guide the walk of the disciples.

sens: that which is fitting, appropriate, that which naturally imposes itself
that which deserves to be received, accepted, recognized as just
that which is in accordance with order, law, reason
G2520.detail:
1. The word expresses what is fitting, what is suitable for a situation or a person. It is that which naturally imposes itself, that which has its place. In Acts 22:22, when the crowd cries that a man is not "worthy" to live, they assert that he does not deserve to continue existing — he does not have the required quality for that.
2. Worthy also means that which deserves to be received or accepted. It is that which has the weight, the sufficient value to be considered acceptable or just.
3. In Romans 1:28, the "unworthy things" are acts that do not fit, that are contrary to what is right, to the natural order or to the law of God. The word describes what does not align with what should be.
G2520.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to descend" or "to arrive at." The idea is that of what "fits" or "returns" to someone — literally, what "comes" to its place, what corresponds to one's rank or condition. In ancient Greek, the word has shifted from the meaning of "to come" to that of "to be appropriate." The corresponding Hebrew in the Greek Old Testament often is the verb meaning "order" or "fittingness" (as in Leviticus 5:16).
G2520.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament in the provided passages. In Acts 22:22, it is used in the negative affirmative: a man is "not worthy" to live, meaning he does not deserve to live. In Romans 1:28, it is used in the neuter plural with negation, "the unworthy things" — acts that do not fit, that are repugnant or contrary to justice. In both cases, the word judges whether something or someone has the quality, merit, or appropriateness required.
G2520.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what truly deserves our commitment and respect. It emphasizes that dignity is not given arbitrarily, but rests on criteria — merit, appropriateness, alignment with just order. For the Christian, this reminds us that our lives should reflect what truly fits: a conduct in accordance with justice and the will of God, and not the repugnant acts that the Bible condemns.

sens: To occupy a seated position on a seat or place
To sit as an authority, notably a judge or a sovereign
To remain, reside in a place
To be in a state, a condition (figurative sense)
G2521.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning: to take or remain in a seated position, on a seat or a place. John 2:14 shows the money changers seated in the temple, engaged in their trade. Mark 16:5 describes the young man seated on the right in the tomb.
2. To sit with authority: to be placed in a position of honor or power, particularly to render justice. Matthew 27:19 speaks of Pilate seated on the judgment seat, a position that symbolizes his authority as a judge. Revelation 4:2 uses this image to describe the one who is seated on the heavenly throne, an expression of his absolute sovereignty.
3. To inhabit or dwell: to remain established in a place. Acts 2:2 indicates that those who were seated (established) in Jerusalem received the gift of the Holy Spirit. The word then evokes the idea of stability and residence.
4. Figurative state or condition: Matthew 4:16 uses the word metaphorically to describe a people seated in darkness, meaning immersed in ignorance and distance from God. It is an image of the spiritual state of people.
G2521.origine: The word comes from an ancient form of Greek (the perfect form of the verb καθέζομαι, to sit). In Hebrew from the Old Testament, it primarily translates יָשַׁב (yashav), which fundamentally means to sit, but also to inhabit, dwell, reign. This dual richness of the Hebrew word explains why the Greek κάθημαι encompasses both the physical action of sitting and the ideas of residence or authority.
G2521.emploi: The verb appears 89 times in total in the New Testament, particularly frequent in Revelation where it describes celestial beings around the throne. In the Gospels, it is used in very varied contexts: Jesus seated to teach (Matthew 13:1-2), the calling of Matthew seated at the tax booth (Matthew 9:9), the women seated at the tomb (Matthew 27:61, Mark 16:5). It can be accompanied by prepositions that specify the place (on, beside, near) or the relative position. The word slightly changes nuance depending on the context: simple seated position for a tax collector or a disciple, but a position of power when it concerns a judge, a king, or God himself.
G2521.portee: This word reminds us that the seated position in Scripture is never neutral. It can evoke rest, teaching, authority, or judgment. When Jesus returns to the idea of being seated at the right hand of God (Matthew 26:64), it means not only that he is exalted, but that he exercises sovereignty. For the Christian reader, this word also emphasizes that our condition can be transformed: from seated in darkness, we can move to a new position through the light of Christ.

sens: That occurs every day, each day
That recurs regularly, habitually
G2522.detail:
1. Daily refers to what happens or repeats day after day, without interruption. The Greek word is formed from the expression "each day": it paints the image of an action or thing that is part of the routine of passing time. In Acts 6:1, it refers to the distribution of food or aid to widows that took place every day, regularly and without exception.
2. By extension, daily can describe what is habitual, what belongs to everyday life. It is what is ordinary and predictable, as opposed to what is exceptional or rare.
G2522.origine: The Greek word kathēmerinos comes directly from the expression "kath'hēmeran" (κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν), which literally means "according to the day" or "per day". The root hēmera denotes the day. This formation well reflects the fundamental idea: what is measured and organized day by day. It is an adjective formed to express the routine of daily time.
G2522.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:1. It describes the daily distribution of food to the widows of the Christian community in Jerusalem. This context shows that the early Christians had established a regular system of material aid. The term emphasizes the consistency and organization of this charitable action: it was not a one-time help, but a service that renewed every day, which required organization and dedication.
G2522.portee: This word reminds us that Christian love consists not in words or spectacular gestures, but in regular and concrete acts. The daily distribution to the widows shows that the disciples cared to provide day after day for the material needs of those who were abandoned. For the modern reader, this speaks of faithfulness in charity and the importance of humble and repeated service, which characterizes authentic faith life.

sens: To take position by being seated, to sit down
To remain seated, to stay in a seated position
To occupy an assigned place, notably a seat of authority or judgment
To be established, installed durably in a place
To be placed next to someone in an honorary position
G2523.detail:
1. The most basic meaning: to take a seated position after having been standing. Jesus goes up on the mountain, then sits down to teach his disciples (Matthew 5:1). Peter stands up in the temple, then sits down to listen to Philip (Acts 8:31). It is the action of moving from standing to seated.

2. To remain seated, to dwell in this position: John sends his disciples to Jesus while he remains seated teaching in the synagogue (John 8:2). This describes the state of one who is established in a seated posture.

3. To occupy a place of honor or authority, often a throne or a judgment seat. Jesus tells his disciples that in the coming life they will sit on twelve thrones to judge the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28). The elders of the people sat in the council of the Sanhedrin (Matthew 23:2). It is the seat that confers dignity and power.

4. To settle durably in a place. After the Ascension, the disciples remain in Jerusalem awaiting the gift of the Holy Spirit (Luke 24:49). The apostle Paul established himself in Corinth for eighteen months (Acts 18:11).

5. To be placed at the right hand of someone, the supreme position of honor: God the Father makes the risen Christ sit at his right hand in the heavens (Ephesians 1:20). It is the seat of honor and shared authority.
G2523.origine: The Greek verb καθίζω comes from a root meaning "to cause to pass from one state to another" (the prefix κατά- "downward"), hence "to cause to sit" in a causative sense. In Hebrew, the verb יָשַׁב (yasab), "to sit" or "to dwell," is often translated by this verb in the Greek Septuagint. The family of words includes other compound verbs (ἀνα-, ἐπι-, παρα-, περι-, συν-καθίζω) that nuance the idea of sitting.
G2523.emploi: This verb appears 45 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and Acts. It is first used in the concrete and literal sense: Jesus sits to teach (Matthew 5:1, John 8:2), the apostles sit at the table (Acts 2:3). Then, it takes on a figurative and theological significance: sitting at the right hand of someone becomes the image of exaltation and shared authority (Ephesians 1:20, Hebrews 1:3). The verb is also used for durable installation (Luke 24:49, Acts 18:11), and to express the idea of judgment or governance (Matthew 19:28, Revelation 20:4). Its nuance changes depending on the context: momentary action or durable state, literal or symbolic sense.
G2523.portee: This verb reveals how Scripture unites the concrete with the spiritual. Jesus sitting as a master to teach shows a posture of wisdom and benevolent authority. Above all, the image of Christ "sitting at the right hand of God" (Ephesians 1:20, Hebrews 1:3) affirms his definitive victory and eternal authority with the Father. For the believer, to sit becomes the confident expectation of salvation (Luke 24:49) or rest in faith: being admitted to sit with Christ in heavenly places (Revelation 3:21) is the ultimate promise of communion with God.

sens: To make something or someone go down by letting it slide or fall slowly downwards
To let fall, to lower gradually
G2524.detail:
1. The word describes the action of making something go down by guiding it or letting it slide gradually. This is what happens to the paralyzed man in Luke 5:19: the disciples 'lower' him through an opening in the roof, sitting on his bed, controlling his descent so that he arrives gently before Jesus. This is also what Paul's disciples do in Acts 9:25, lowering him in a basket along the city wall of Damascus.
2. The word can also express a gradual lowering or a deployment downwards. The large sheet in Acts 10:11 and 11:5 'descends' from heaven by 'lowering' slowly, as if it were being gently brought down in Peter's vision: it is a controlled movement, not a fall.
G2524.origine: The word comes from a root meaning 'to send' or 'to let go', combined with the prefix 'down' (katà). The initial image is that of letting something descend gradually, as if sending something down. It is a compound word that emphasizes the action of controlling the descent, not the fall itself.
G2524.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, always in the physical sense of making something go down. In Luke 5:19, it describes the concrete action of the disciples lowering a paralyzed man from the roof. In Acts 9:25, Paul is lowered down a wall. In Acts 10:11 and 11:5, the same word describes the vision of the heavenly sheet that lowers: the verb emphasizes the slowness and majesty of the movement, not a simple fall. In each case, it is a controlled or guided descent.
G2524.portee: This word shows us how the Bible concretizes faith: four friends 'lower' a paralyzed man, a simple act but filled with determination to place him before Jesus. Peter's vision uses the same word for the heavenly sheet: God lowers what is holy to the earth, redeeming what seemed impure. It is a lesson on grace that descends to us, and on the humble and determined action of those who intercede for others.

sens: To place someone or something in a position, place, or state
To entrust a responsibility, power, or task to someone
To constitute, form, or organize something according to an order
To appoint someone to a function or position
To make someone responsible or guilty of something
G2525.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is 'to place' or 'to set in place': to bring someone or something to a specific location or situation. Acts 17:15 illustrates this: the brothers 'established' him in Athens, meaning they brought him there and placed him.

2. 'To entrust' a responsibility to someone means to give them power or a mission to manage. In Matthew 25:21, the master 'will entrust' much to the faithful servant: he entrusts him with his possessions and authority. It is placing someone in a position of trust and power.

3. 'To organize' or 'to put in order' expresses the idea of constituting something according to a plan. Titus 1:5 is an example: establishing elders in the churches means organizing them, structuring them according to apostolic will.

4. 'To appoint' to a specific function: to establish someone as a judge, governor, leader. Luke 12:14: Jesus says he was not established to be a judge. Acts 7:10: Pharaoh established Joseph as governor, officially conferring this title and power upon him.

5. In the passive form, the word can mean 'to be constituted' or 'to be made' in a moral or social state. Romans 5:19: men were 'made' sinners by the disobedience of Adam — established in a condition of sin.
G2525.origine: The Greek word κατα-ἵστημι combines the prefix κατα ('down', 'completely') and ἵστημι ('to make stand', 'to place'). The initial image is therefore 'to place upright' or 'to set in place stably'. The verb ἵστημι, very common in Greek, describes the action of placing, establishing, constituting. The prefix κατα reinforces this idea of definitive placement or order established. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates various Hebrew verbs (פָּקַד 'to entrust', קוּם 'to establish', שׂוּם 'to place') depending on the context, which shows the versatility of the word.
G2525.emploi: The verb appears 21 times in the New Testament, mainly in Luke, Matthew, and Paul. It is used to describe the act of establishing leaders: Titus 1:5 (elders), Acts 6:3 (deacons), Hebrews 7:28 (high priest), Acts 7:10 (Joseph as governor). It also describes the action of entrusting power: Matthew 24:45, Luke 12:42 (servant over people), Matthew 25:21 (entrusting possessions), Luke 12:44. Jesus uses the word to refuse a role: Luke 12:14 ('who made me a judge?'). Paul uses it theologically in Romans 5:19 to say that men have been 'made' sinners. The meaning varies slightly depending on the context, but always remains centered on the action of placing, constituting, or entrusting a responsibility.
G2525.portee: This word reveals how God organizes His world through delegations of power and entrusted responsibilities. It invites the Christian to consider all authority, whether civil, familial, or ecclesiastical, as a charge received and to exercise it faithfully. To establish someone is to trust them; the passage in Matthew 25:21 reminds us that God trusts the faithful servant with little to entrust him with more. It is also a call to recognize that our responsibilities do not come from us, but are entrusted to us.

sens: according to the measure or proportion of something
within the limits of what
by reason of
G2526.detail:
1. The word expresses a relationship of proportion or measure: 'in accordance with', 'according to'. Romans 8:26 uses it to say that the Spirit helps us 'according to' or 'in relation to' our weakness — that is, to the exact measure of our weakness.
2. It can indicate the limit or condition: 'within the limits of', 'to the extent that'. In 2 Corinthians 8:12, Paul says that a gift is acceptable 'by reason of' what one has — that is, in proportion to one's means, not beyond.
3. Sometimes it introduces a cause or basis: 'due to', 'since'. In 1 Peter 4:13, rejoicing 'in' sharing the sufferings of Christ means rejoicing by virtue of this participation.
G2526.origine: The word is formed by the contraction of two Greek terms: κατά ('according to', 'in accordance with') and ὅ (the relative pronoun 'what', 'which'). The literal expression would be 'according to what'; it has solidified into a single adverb. This construction serves to establish relationships of proportion, conformity, or causality between two realities.
G2526.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. In Romans 8:26, it expresses how the Spirit helps us in proportion to our weakness. In 2 Corinthians 8:12, it introduces the criterion of generosity: not according to what one does not have, but according to what one possesses. In 1 Peter 4:13, it indicates the basis of joy: rejoicing due to participating in the sufferings of Christ. The word functions as a logical connector, linking two ideas according to a relationship of measure or causality.
G2526.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God adapts His help to our real needs. He helps us 'by reason of' our weakness, not despite it. The word also invites us to calibrate our generosity and actions based on our true capacity, not on pretensions. Finally, it shows us that Christian joy is founded on our union with the suffering Christ.

sens: In general, overall
Totally or radically
Without restriction, without exception
G2527.detail:
1. The word describes what applies globally, in general, without distinguishing particular cases — it conveys the idea of totality. It is used to affirm something about the entirety of a situation. In Acts 4:18, the apostles receive an absolute order: "they strictly charged them not to speak" means that no context would allow for an exception — the prohibition applies to all cases, without nuance.
2. When one says "not to do something absolutely," it expresses a total refusal, without compromise. It conveys the idea of a radical prohibition or negation. In Acts 4:18, this usage appears: the verb "to charge" with this adverb creates a categorical prohibition.
3. In the strongest sense, the word emphasizes that there are no reservations, no exceptions, no possibility of derogation. It is an emphasis that closes the door to any debate.
G2527.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: "κατά" (according to) and "ὅλος" (whole, all). Literally, it means "according to the whole" or "as a whole." This composition reveals the fundamental idea: one considers the thing in its entirety, without fragmenting it. The word belongs to the vocabulary of generality and universality. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "בִּלְתִּי" (without), which expresses total negation.
