G2527.emploi: This Greek word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 4:18. It reinforces the prohibition that the Jewish leaders impose on the apostles Peter and John: they are absolutely forbidden to speak and teach in the name of Jesus. It is an adverb of absolute negation. The context shows that this order aims to completely stifle the Christian testimony, leaving no room for maneuver. It is a classical word, borrowed from literary Greek, which gives the narrative a legal solemnity.
G2527.portee: This word reminds the reader of the rigor and intransigence of the opposition to the Christian faith in the early years of the Church. But it also illustrates the firmness of the apostles: in the face of an "absolute" prohibition, they will continue to testify (see Acts 5:29). For the Christian today, this contrast shows that obedience to God takes precedence over any human prohibition, even categorical.

sens: To provide someone with complete armor or weapons
To fully equip for battle
Figuratively: to strengthen, prepare to face
G2528.detail:
1. The word describes the action of equipping a warrior with all his weapons and armor — not just giving him a few, but fully clothing him so that he is ready for battle. In Luke 11:21, Jesus speaks of a strong and well-armed man who guards his house: this man has every piece of his war equipment, so he is capable of defending what belongs to him.
2. The image extends to any complete preparation to face a danger or an adversary. One who is thus equipped is considered invulnerable, as long as no one stronger comes to attack him. That is why this strong man can ensure the safety of his house and possessions.
G2528.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "kata-" (completely, from top to bottom) and "hoplizō" (to arm, equip). Hoplizō itself comes from "hoplon," the round shield of the Greek warrior. The prefix reinforces the idea: it is not a partial armor, but one that covers the warrior from all sides. In ancient Hebrew, this notion of complete warrior preparation is found in the verb תָּפַשׂ (taphas), which means to seize or take hold of, as if one were grabbing weapons.
G2528.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:21 (in passive form: "armed"). Jesus uses it in a parable about power: a strong man, properly equipped for battle, successfully guards his house as long as no stronger enemy threatens him. This passage illustrates the necessity of complete preparation, not only materially but spiritually, to repel attacks.
G2528.portee: For the believer, this image reminds us that spiritual life requires complete armor, not just partial. Paul will take up this idea in Ephesians 6 by describing "the armor of God": the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, etc. Being well "armed" spiritually means having donned every piece of protection that God offers, not being negligent or incomplete. It is an invitation to vigilance and intentional preparation in the life of faith.

sens: To perceive distinctly, to see clearly
To understand, to recognize in a sure and evident way
G2529.detail:
1. The word designates the action of seeing or perceiving something clearly and precisely, as if one were looking at it attentively. It is a gaze that does not err, that truly grasps the object before it.
2. Figuratively, it means to understand, recognize, or discern a reality — especially invisible or abstract — with certainty. In Romans 1:20, Paul asserts that God's eternal perfections, although invisible, are "clearly discerned" in the created universe: one can "see" them by observing the creatures, as if they reveal the Creator.
G2529.origine: The word comes from the Greek root οράω ("to see") preceded by the prefix κατά ("downward, intensely"). This composition reinforces the meaning: it is not just to see, but to look toward something with attention and penetration. The image is that of a gaze that descends deeply into reality to grasp its true nature, rather than remaining on the surface.
G2529.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:20, in Paul's argument about general revelation: creatures allow humans to "discern" the invisible and eternal attributes of God. It is a rare word that emphasizes the clarity and obviousness of this perception. Paul uses it to show that knowledge of God through creation is not vague or doubtful, but manifest and perceptible.
G2529.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God has not hidden Himself: He has revealed Himself clearly and perceptibly in creation. This establishes both trust in the goodness of the Creator and the responsibility of those who refuse to see Him. It is an invitation to cultivate a penetrating gaze on the created world, to discern the imprint of the living God.

sens: According to the measure or proportion of something
Given that; due to the fact that; since
G2530.detail:
1. This word primarily expresses a correspondence or proportionality: "according to" or "as". It conveys the sense of "according to the needs of each" in Acts 2:45, where goods were shared according to what each person received.
2. In the New Testament, this word gradually took on the meaning of simple cause: "because", "due to the fact that". This is clearly seen in Luke 1:7, where the absence of children is explained "because" Elizabeth was barren — a reason, not a proportion. Similarly, in Acts 2:24, God raised Jesus "because it was not possible for Him to be held by death" — here it is a pure cause.
G2530.origine: This Greek word is composed of κατά ("according to") and ὅ τι ("what"). Its literal meaning was therefore "according to what" or "as" — an expression of proportion or correspondence. Over time, in late Greek, this conjunction came closer to διότι ("because"), until it became synonymous with cause. The translators of the Greek Old Testament used it to render the Hebrew אֲשֶׁר ("who", "that") in similar contexts.
G2530.emploi: This word appears six times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. In Luke (1:7 and 19:9), it introduces a reason or causal explanation. In Acts (2:24 and 17:31), it is used similarly: to justify or explain a fact. Only twice (Acts 2:45 and 4:35) does it retain its older meaning of "according to", marking a proportional or conditional distribution. This evolution shows how conjunctions evolve in languages: a word that initially expressed measure or proportion eventually expresses cause.
G2530.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp how the Bible explains events and decisions: God raises Jesus, the disciples share their goods — why? This word introduces the reason, the cause that accounts for it. It is a small word, but it anchors faith in logic and responsibility: there is always a reason for what God does and what believers must do.

sens: in the same way as, just as
in the manner of, according to the model of
to the extent that, proportionately to
at the moment when, while
according to what is written
introducing a comparison or proportion
G2531.detail:
1. The most common meaning: "as" introduces a comparison or similarity between two realities. Example: "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up" (John 3:14). Jesus will be lifted up in a manner comparable to what happened under Moses.
2. "As" can mean "in the manner of" or "according to the model of," showing imitation or following. Example: "Therefore welcome one another, as Christ has welcomed you" (Romans 15:7). Christians are to welcome others by imitating Christ's gesture.
3. The word also expresses a proportion or degree: "He spoke the word as the Spirit gave him utterance" (Acts 2:4), meaning to the extent that the Spirit allowed.
4. Sometimes "as" situates in time: "at the moment when" or "while." Example: "You fell asleep as it was fitting" suggests accompanying or temporal coincidence.
5. In scriptural quotations, "as it is written" refers to the ancient text: "And as it was written" (Matthew 26:24), introducing conformity with Scripture.
6. The word can also express equivalence: "as is the custom to bury among the Jews" (John 19:40) means "that is, in the usual manner."
G2531.origine: This Greek word comes from the fusion of "kata" (according to, in the direction of) and "hōs" (as). It is a very common compound conjunction in Koine Greek (the Greek of the New Testament). It appears about 180 times in the New Testament and often translates the Hebrew word "ke" or "kaasher," which have exactly the same role of comparison and conformity. The word belongs to a family of Greek conjunctions: "kathaper" (just as), "katho" (as), "kathoti" (because), but "kathos" is the most common and flexible.
G2531.emploi: "As" appears 180 times in the New Testament, making it a very frequent conjunction. It is used in all types of texts: Gospel narratives, Paul's epistles, letters of John, Acts of the Apostles. It primarily introduces comparisons ("as it is written," "as the disciples did"), models to imitate ("as Christ loved"), and conformities ("as is the custom"). In the Gospels, it connects events in the life of Jesus to announcements in the Old Testament. In the epistles, it introduces ethical principles: Christians must live "as" Christ lived. It can also express a proportion: "I have loved you as the Father has loved me" (John 15:9) establishes a measure. Sometimes it introduces a purpose or consequence clause.
G2531.portee: This word reveals a fundamental biblical principle: the Christian life is one of imitation and conformity. Believers are called to live "as" Christ lived, to love "as" he loved, to forgive "as" he forgave. Furthermore, the conjunction "as" establishes a continuity between the Old and New Testaments: the events of Jesus fulfill what was written. For the reader, this means that faith is not an abstract theory, but a concrete way of life, modeled on the example of Christ and rooted in the history of salvation.

sens: marks the connection between two words or two thoughts of the same nature
joins affirmation to negation
indicates a succession of facts or actions
expresses a consequence
adds a nuance to what precedes, often with slight opposition
marks amplification or intensification
G2532.detail:
1. Kai simply connects two words, two groups, or two thoughts: "Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, Jacob begot Judah and his brothers" (Matthew 1:2). This is the most basic and common link in biblical speech.

2. It can join an affirmative idea to a negation, thus creating tension: "But I say to you, Do not resist the evil one; but if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also" (Matthew 5:39-40) — one might expect "but instead," but the text simply says "and."

3. Kai often links facts that succeed one another in time, especially in narratives: "Jesus went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him" (Mark 5:24). The "and" shows the sequence of events.

4. It can mark a logical or temporal consequence, particularly after an imperative: "Come and follow me" (Matthew 4:19) — the invitation carries the commitment that follows.

5. Kai also plays a more subtle role: it adds something that does not contradict but slightly nuances the previous meaning, as if to say "furthermore" or "moreover."

6. Finally, when repeated ("and... and"), it amplifies and intensifies: "Near the cross of Jesus stood his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene" (John 19:25) — each "and" adds a witness, a presence, accumulating important details.
G2532.origine: Kai is a simple and primitive conjunction in Greek, found even in the earliest texts. It has no complicated root: it is a small pure word, almost an atom of language. It corresponds to the Hebrew וְ ("ve" or "va") in the Old Testament, the most frequent copulative conjunction. Greek translators of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) constantly used kai to render this Hebrew וְ, so that kai has something of the simplicity and recurrence of Hebrew style — which explains why the New Testament, written by authors of Hebrew culture, uses it so liberally and often in a less logical manner than classical Greek.
G2532.emploi: Kai is by far the most frequent word in the New Testament: it appears over 5200 times. It is found in every book and almost every verse. Its usage reflects the popular and direct style of biblical authors, who chain thoughts together with "and" rather than hierarchically organizing them. In the Synoptics (Matthew, Mark, Luke), kai links genealogies, miracle narratives, and the words of Jesus. In Pauline epistles, it organizes theological argumentation. John uses it less densely, but just as decisively. Its meaning varies from the simple enumerator ("and") to a marker of consequence or slight opposition, depending on the context. This plasticity explains why the Segond sometimes renders it as "and," sometimes as "also," "still," "he," or even omits it when it deems the sentence too loaded.
G2532.portee: Learning to recognize kai invites the reader to see how Scripture thinks: it neither opposes nor hierarchizes like scholarly rhetoric, but accumulates, chains, juxtaposes with confidence. This reflects a narrative and contemplative mentality rather than an analytical one. For the Christian, this means that every word counts, that nothing comes by chance: the addition of an "and" in a genealogy, an "and" in a miracle, builds the fabric of meaning. It is the humility of a word that does not shout its logic but allows it to emerge from the simple succession of facts.

sens: High priest of the Jewish people
Father-in-law of Annas, another high priest
The one who presides over the trial of Jesus before the Sanhedrin
The one who unknowingly prophesies that Jesus must die for the people
G2533G.detail:
1. Caiaphas is the high priest, that is, the chief priest of Israel at the time of Jesus. He is the highest religious leader of the Jewish people, responsible for the temple and worship. In Luke 3:2, he is named alongside Annas as one of the high priests during the time when John the Baptist begins his ministry.

2. John 18:13 tells us that Caiaphas is the son-in-law of Annas, who was himself a former high priest. This family relationship shows that religious power was concentrated in a few prominent families in Jerusalem.

3. It is in Caiaphas's house that the religious trial of Jesus takes place before the Sanhedrin (the court of elders and scribes). Matthew 26:57 and John 18:13-14 report that Jesus is brought there after his arrest, where he stands before Caiaphas and the elders.

4. John 11:49 shows that Caiaphas, without truly knowing, prophesies: he says that "it is advantageous that one man die for the people." This man must be Jesus himself, although Caiaphas does not understand the deep meaning of his own words.
G2533G.origine: The name Caiaphas (Greek Καϊάφας or Καιάφας) is the Greek transcription of an Aramaic or Hebrew name. Its exact etymology is debated, but it may derive from a word meaning "depression" or "ditch." It was a name borne by an important priestly family in Jerusalem in the first century.
G2533G.emploi: Caiaphas appears 9 times in the New Testament, almost always in connection with the trial and death of Jesus. He is mentioned in Matthew 26 during the arrest and trial of Jesus, in Luke 3:2 as a contemporary high priest of John the Baptist, and several times in the Gospel of John (chapters 11 and 18), where he is presented as the one who advises the Jewish authorities that Jesus must be put to death. In Acts 4:6, he is cited among the religious leaders who interrogate the apostles Peter and John after Pentecost. His role grows as the narrative progresses: from a simple high priest, he becomes the main actor in the condemnation of Jesus.
G2533G.portee: Caiaphas illustrates the paradox of refusing to recognize Jesus by one who, by his position, should have been the first to receive him. His story also shows that God can use even the words of those who reject him to accomplish his plan: Caiaphas prophesies without wanting to. It invites the reader not to confuse religious power with knowledge of God, and to remain vigilant not to become blind to the signs that God gives, regardless of our responsibility.

sens: The firstborn son of Adam and Eve, murderer of his brother Abel
An example of one who acts according to the flesh and not by faith
A model of rebellion against God and destructive jealousy
G2535.detail:
1. Cain is the first son born to Adam and Eve (Genesis 4:1). He killed his brother Abel out of jealousy, because Abel's sacrifice was accepted by God while Cain's was rejected. This story of the brother's murder has remained famous in the Bible and in human memory as the first fratricide.

2. In the letter to the Hebrews, Cain embodies one who did not act by faith: while Abel offered a "more excellent" sacrifice because he acted by faith, Cain acts only according to his own will and his works are evil (Hebrews 11:4). It is a contrast: faith opens the heart to God, the absence of faith hardens the heart.

3. In 1 John 3:12, Cain is described as "of the evil one" — he belongs to the one who has chosen lies and rebellion. His fratricidal act reveals a deep rebellion: not only did he reject God's judgment, but he killed the one who shamed him. The apostle Jude uses his name to designate all those who walk according to their fleshly passion, far from God.
G2535.origine: The Hebrew name קַיִן (Qayin) probably means "smith" or "one who shapes," suggesting a man of action and work. This name evokes the image of an active and creative person, but history reveals that this activity, without faith, becomes destructive. Cain is the first named person born naturally in the Bible (Eve says, "I have acquired a man"), marking his importance in human history.
G2535.emploi: Cain appears only three times in the New Testament. In each occurrence, he is cited as a counter-example or a warning: in Hebrews 11:4, he illustrates one whose sacrifice was not accepted due to lack of faith; in 1 John 3:12, he personifies one who acts under the influence of the evil one and commits murder out of jealousy; in Jude 1:11, he designates a spiritual current of rebellion that runs through history. Each time, Cain represents a break with God: rejection of divine judgment, envious jealousy, fratricidal violence, and distancing from faith.
G2535.portee: Cain serves as a warning for the Christian reader: mere religious or moral activity is not enough; it is faith that gives value to our acts before God. His story reminds us that jealousy and human pride can lead to crime, and that turning away from God places one under the influence of evil. By seeing Cain's fate, one understands that faith in God is the sine qua non condition for a righteous life.

sens: Son of Arphaxad in the genealogy of Christ
G2536G.detail: Cainan is a character in the genealogy of Jesus reported by Luke. He is presented as the son of Arphaxad (Luke 3:36). This name appears in the list of ancestors of Jesus established by Luke, which traces back to Adam, showing the continuity of the divine lineage throughout history.
G2536G.origine: The name Cainan comes from the Hebrew קֵינָן (Qéinân). This character appears in biblical genealogies, and the Greek form Καϊνάν or Καϊνάμ is used in Luke's genealogy to designate this ancestor of Jesus.
G2536G.emploi: Cainan is mentioned only once in Luke 3:36 in the New Testament, at the heart of the genealogy that Luke constructs to establish the identity and origin of Jesus. This genealogy traces from Jesus back to Adam, passing through the pre-flood and post-flood patriarchs, to show that Jesus is part of the continuous chain of God's people.
G2536G.portee: This genealogy reminds the reader that Jesus is truly a human being, rooted in the real history of God's people, and that he is the culmination of the divine promise pursued through the centuries. It emphasizes Jesus's solidarity with all humanity, from Adam.

sens: Son of Enosh in the genealogy from Adam to Noah
Son of Arphaxad in the genealogy of post-flood patriarchs
G2536H.detail:
1. Cainan is a character in the biblical genealogy, son of Enosh and father of Mahalalel. He appears in the lineage that descends from Adam to Noah, featured in the account of humanity's origins before the flood.
2. Another Cainan, son of Arphaxad, appears in the genealogy of peoples after the flood. This second mention is found in some ancient texts (such as the Greek Septuagint), although it is absent from the Masoretic Hebrew text.
G2536H.origine: The name Cainan comes from the Hebrew קֵינָן (Qenan), whose exact etymology is not definitively established. In Greek, the name has been transliterated in two ways: Καϊνάν and Καϊνάμ, reflecting the variations in the Hebrew text itself. The name belongs to the list of the ten pre-flood patriarchs, all ancient Hebrew names preserved through genealogical transmission.
G2536H.emploi: Cainan appears only in biblical genealogies. In Luke 3:37, he is cited in the genealogical lineage of Jesus tracing back to Adam. This verse places him as the son of Methuselah (or rather as part of this pre-flood genealogical chain). Genesis 5:9 also mentions him in Hebrew. There is a significant textual variant: some Greek manuscripts and the Septuagint include a second Cainan, son of Arphaxad, who does not appear in the Masoretic text of Genesis 10:24, reflecting a difference between the Hebrew and Greek traditions of ancient genealogical lists.

sens: That which has never been used, new and intact
That which is fresh, of superior quality to the old
That which is of a different form or nature, strange and surprising
That which changes the old order, inaugurating a new regime
That which is recent or newly appearing
That which renews internally, transforms the soul
G2537.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: an object or substance that has never been used. A new garment, a new wineskin that has no cracks (Matthew 9:17). A new tomb, where no one has been laid (Matthew 27:60).
2. That which is fresh and vigorous, in contrast to that which has become old and worn. New wine, tasty and alive, which cannot be poured into old and fragile wineskins: they will burst under its strength (Luke 5:38).
3. That which is of a species or quality unknown until now, which surprises by its difference. A new teaching, a doctrine that had never been heard (Mark 1:27). New tongues, an extraordinary phenomenon (Mark 16:17).
4. That which abolishes the old order and establishes something definitively different. The new covenant, which replaces the old (Hebrews 8:8), the new man in Christ who replaces the old nature (Ephesians 2:15).
5. That which appears for the first time in history. A new commandment: love one another (John 13:34), although it is as old as the Gospel itself.
6. That which transforms the heart and mind of the one who receives it. A new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), new heavens and a new earth (Revelation 21:1), the seal of a completely renewed life.
G2537.origine: The Greek word kainos comes from a root that evokes what is fresh and alive, free from wear. It stands in radical opposition to "palaia" (old, worn) and "archaia" (archaic, from another age). In Hebrew, it mainly translates "hadash" (new, fresh), which appears in Ezekiel. The Greek word emphasizes the new quality and form, while "neos" (young, recent) rather emphasizes the time elapsed since the origin. In the Bible, kainos carries the idea of radical transformation, of an order that breaks with the past.
G2537.emploi: The word appears 38 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and in the letters of Paul and John. It first denotes material realities: a new garment (Mark 2:21), new wineskins (Matthew 9:17), a new tomb (Matthew 27:60). Then it rises in theological significance: the new covenant sealed in Christ (1 Corinthians 11:25, Hebrews 8:8), the new man created in Jesus (Ephesians 2:15), the new commandment of brotherly love (John 13:34). In Revelation, it culminates: new Jerusalem, new heavens, new earth, everything is renewed in the consummation of the ages (Revelation 21:1-5). Paul uses it to describe the new creation that begins in every believer (2 Corinthians 5:17).
G2537.portee: This word illuminates faith by showing that God will not patch up the old world: He creates the new. New wine requires new wineskins; the Gospel cannot be confined within the old forms of the Law. For the Christian, being in Christ means becoming a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17): it is not an adjustment, but a total transformation. Biblical hope does not dream of a restoration of the old order, but of new heavens and a new earth where God will wipe away every tear.

sens: character of that which is new, unusual
quality of that which is fresh, alive, different from the past
G2538.detail:
1. The word first denotes that which is new, different from the old, that which has never existed before — it is the contrast between the worn and the unprecedented. But in Romans 6:4, Paul speaks not only of something recent: he speaks of "newness of life," this resurrected life of the baptized Christian that is completely different, alive, regenerated, because it is that of the risen Christ.
2. The second meaning emphasizes the living, fresh, dynamic quality of that which is new. In Romans 7:6, when Paul says that we serve "in a new spirit," it is not just about doing something different, but living with a new vitality, an inner renewal that contrasts with the old "letter" that "has grown old." It is the transition from something worn out, exhausted, to something alive and fresh.
G2538.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "new" (καινός) and takes the nominal form "novelty" (κ-αινότης). It expresses the idea of a break with the past, of innovation or renewal. In ancient Greek, the word designated the character of that which is unprecedented or surprising. In Pauline Christian thought, this term carries a spiritual significance: the novelty brought by Christ and the Gospel, the transformation of the believer's life.
G2538.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, exclusively in Paul's letter to the Romans. In Romans 6:4, it describes the new life of the baptized who rises with Christ: baptized in His death, the believer is destined to walk in "newness of life," that is, to live a radically transformed existence. In Romans 7:6, Paul uses it to contrast the service rendered in a "new spirit" with the service under the old law that has become rigid. The word captures the Pauline idea that the Christian does not simply do better in the old way: he lives according to an entirely new logic, that of resurrection and the Spirit.
G2538.portee: For the Christian, this "novelty" is not an abstract concept: it speaks of the concrete transformation of his existence through the death and resurrection of Christ. It affirms that the believer's life is not a simple adjustment of the old life, but a radical break, a deep renewal. It also reminds that the service of God is not based on conformity to fixed rules, but on a living relationship with the Holy Spirit. This truth frees the Christian: he is not a prisoner of what he was, but called to live in the freshness of new life in Christ.

sens: conjunction marking a concession: what follows is true despite what precedes
expresses a contrast or opposition between two facts
G2539.detail:
1. This Greek word connects two ideas in tension: one is true, but the other is also true, and they seem to oppose each other. In Hebrews 5:8, Jesus "learned obedience, although He was a Son": He is truly a Son, and truly He learned obedience — two things that seem contrary. The word signals: "even if you expect that... it is not an obstacle, it happens anyway."
2. Sometimes it emphasizes a surprising or seemingly contradictory remark. In Philippians 3:4, Paul says: "I too could have confidence in the flesh, however I do not do so" — he would have the credentials to do so, but he renounces it. In 2 Peter 1:12, the apostle insists on what they already know: "although you know it" — an insistence despite the apparent lack of need.
G2539.origine: It is a concessive particle formed from the conjunction "and" (kai) and the adverb "although, despite" (per). It expresses a tension or restriction: "and yet," "and however." It does not come from a verb, but is a small linking word, a logical tool of Greek.
G2539.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in the epistles (Philippians, Hebrews, 2 Peter). It generally accompanies a participle (a verbal form ending in -ing or -ed) to express a concession. The Segond sometimes translates it as "however," sometimes as "although," depending on the context. Paul uses it to nuance his statements (Philippians 3:4), the author of Hebrews to express important theological paradoxes (Jesus the Son learning obedience, Esau seeking the blessing without obtaining it), and Peter to reinforce his pastoral appeal.
G2539.portee: This word teaches to recognize the tensions of the Christian life: one can be a son although one must learn obedience, have fleshly qualifications although one does not rely on them, know the truth although one needs reminders. It invites not to flee from apparent paradoxes, but to accept them as true together.

sens: a determined period, marked by events or characterized by its own traits
the fixed or expected moment for something to happen or be done
the favorable instant, the right time to act
the era, the age, the moment in the course of time
G2540.detail:
1. **Determined period** — The word refers to a concrete span of time, a season, or a well-defined epoch. It is the "harvest" to which the owner of the vineyard sends a servant (Mark 12:2), or the time when Herod began to persecute the Church (Acts 12:1). The word depicts a time that has contours, a distinct identity.
2. **Pre-determined moment** — This is the time decided in advance, the expected moment for something to occur. Christ "died for the ungodly at the appointed time" (Romans 5:6): this is the moment that God had fixed. Similarly, "the time of the harvest" is that which the owner of the vineyard has established (Matthew 21:34).
3. **Favorable instant, opportunity** — This is the "right moment", the opportune time to do something. When it says to "redeem the time" (Ephesians 5:16), it means to seize the passing opportunity. Paul encourages the Galatians to "do good, do not grow weary; for in due season we shall reap" (Galatians 6:9): one must act at the opportune moment.
4. **Historical epoch or era** — The word also extends in a broader sense to a long period: a generation, a century. Jesus speaks of "those who will be in that time" (Luke 21:24), referring to that eschatological era.
G2540.origine: The Greek word καιρός comes from a root expressing the idea of "cutting, slicing, setting a limit." It originally denotes a "measured", "delimited" time. In classical Greek, it also evokes the right proportion, appropriateness. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew עֵת (et), which simply means "time" or "moment." The word καιρός distinguishes itself by emphasizing the opportunity and relevance of the moment, much more than its mere duration.
G2540.emploi: The word appears about 80 times in the New Testament, spread across all the major books. In the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John), it often designates concrete moments: the time of harvest, the time of passion, the hour of conspiracy. In the Epistles, particularly in Paul, the word takes on a more theological hue: it speaks of the "time" set by God for salvation (Romans 5:6), the present time in contrast to the one to come (Romans 13:11), the urgency to "redeem the time" (Ephesians 5:16). In Revelation, it characterizes the eschatological period. The meaning also sharpens according to the context: sometimes it highlights the divine determination of a moment ("my time has not yet come", John 7:6), other times the opportunity for human action (Galatians 6:10: "as we have opportunity").
G2540.portee: This word reminds the believer that time is not a succession of empty moments, but a reality directed by God. Each moment has significance, an "occasion" that God offers or that we can seize. It invites vigilance: to recognize the moment when God acts, to discern "the signs of the times" (Matthew 16:3), not to let the opportunity to do good pass by. For the Christian, living according to the καιρός means living in accordance with what God is doing now, rather than remaining a stranger to His present action.

sens: official title of the head of the Roman state
the reigning Roman emperor at a given time
the Roman imperial power
the political authority opposed to God
G2541G.detail:
1. The word "Caesar" is primarily an official title: it is the name held by the Roman emperors who ruled Rome and its vast empire. Luke mentions it when he historically situates the birth of Jesus: it is under "Caesar" Augustus, the emperor of Rome, that the decree was issued to census the whole earth (Luke 2:1).
2. In the New Testament, "Caesar" also refers to the reigning emperor at each moment of the narrative. Luke speaks of "Tiberius Caesar" to date the beginnings of the ministry of John the Baptist and Jesus (Luke 3:1), as one would say "under the reign of...".
3. The word also represents the entire system of Roman power: its authority, its laws, its empire. When the Pharisees ask Jesus whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, they question submission to political power.
4. Finally, in biblical thought, "Caesar" embodies human power that opposes or measures itself against the authority of God: this is why the question of the tax to Caesar becomes, for Jesus, an opportunity to distinguish what belongs to Caesar from what belongs to God.
G2541G.origine: The word "Caesar" comes from the name of the Roman Julian family, of which Julius Caesar was the most famous member. After him, all Roman emperors bore this title as a symbol of their supreme power. In Greek, the word was borrowed directly from Latin and became established in the New Testament to designate the emperor and his authority.
G2541G.emploi: The New Testament uses "Caesar" about twice to historically situate the reported events. Luke, in particular, uses this word to provide precise chronological markers: Augustus Caesar when Jesus is born, Tiberius Caesar when the ministry of John the Baptist begins. This choice is not neutral: Luke thus places Christ in the context of world history, under Roman domination. The word "Caesar" always represents a concrete political authority, the reigning emperor of the time.
G2541G.portee: For the readers of the New Testament, "Caesar" recalls an unavoidable reality: Jesus was born, grew up, and preached under Roman domination. The Church also arises within this empire. This word invites the Christian to think about the relationship between obedience to God and respect for political authority: Jesus does not respond with revolt, but with a clear distinction of orders. It also suggests that God is not in competition with the kings of this world: His kingdom, after all, is not of this world.

sens: the Roman emperor who reigns over the entire empire
the supreme authority of Rome, embodied in the person of the emperor
the Roman imperial court, where important cases are judged
G2541H.detail:
1. Caesar designates the reigning Roman emperor — the one who governs the entire empire. It is a title and a name that represents supreme political power. Luke uses it to speak of Augustus at the time of the census: "In those days, a decree went out from Caesar Augustus" (Luke 2:1).
2. The word evokes Roman authority itself, the power of the State. When Jesus' accusers shout, "We have no king but Caesar" (John 19:12), they acknowledge his political authority over Judea.
3. "Caesar" can also refer to the imperial court or the emperor as the final arbiter of justice. Paul appeals to Caesar (Acts 25:11) for his case to be judged by the emperor himself, not by local governors.
G2541H.origine: The Greek word Kaisar comes from the Latin name Caesar, which was originally the family name of Julius Caesar, and then became the title of all Roman emperors who inherited it. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, the closest word is אַדִּיר (addir, "mighty"), but the New Testament directly uses the Greek word borrowed from Latin, as Rome dominates the Mediterranean during Jesus' time.
G2541H.emploi: The word appears only in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Acts, particularly during Paul's trials before Roman governors. Matthew cites it once (22:17): "Tell us what you think: is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar?" It is also in the context of the government in Luke 2:1. The usages vary slightly: sometimes it designates the emperor himself as the supreme authority, other times his court or legal system. Paul refers to it three times (Acts 25:11-12, 26:32) as an appeal in last resort against the judgment of local governors. The expression "the knowledge of Caesar" (Acts 25:21) means: let the case be brought before the emperor so that he may be informed and judge it.
G2541H.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds that the early Church lived under a pagan power and that believers had to recognize the existing political order while remaining faithful to Jesus as the supreme king. Paul uses the Roman judicial system to defend the Gospel — which shows how disciples can use available legal resources. But the cry "We have no king but Caesar" also reveals the tragedy of those who reject the true King.

sens: Roman imperial title, held by the emperor
One who exercises political power and authority in the world
G2541I.detail:
1. Caesar is the title given to the Roman emperor, particularly during the time of Jesus and the apostles. It is the name of the imperial dynasty that became the symbol of absolute Roman power governing the known world at that time.
2. In biblical contexts, the word represents earthly political authority, the human power that rules over nations and citizens. When Paul greets "those of Caesar's household" (Philippians 4:22), he refers to the servants or officials of the Roman imperial palace.
G2541I.origine: The word comes from the Latin name Caesar, which became an imperial title held by all Roman emperors after Julius Caesar. In the Greek texts of the New Testament, it was simply transcribed into Greek, as the Roman Empire dominated the East and the Middle East, and local authorities answered to the Roman emperor.
G2541I.emploi: The word "Caesar" appears twice in the contexts noted in Pauline usage. In Philippians 4:22, Paul mentions "those of Caesar's household": he is likely speaking of Christians who worked in the service of the administration or the imperial palace, perhaps in Rome itself or in another major city. This term shows that the Gospel had spread to circles close to Roman political power. The presence of believers in Caesar's entourage illustrates the universal reach of conversion to Christ.
G2541I.portee: For the Christian reader, the word Caesar represents the power of this world — one that seems invincible and absolute. By mentioning "Caesar's household," Paul reminds us that the Gospel crosses social and political barriers, and that even in the palaces of the powerful, Christ is worshiped and confessed. This encourages the believer not to fear earthly authorities, but to recognize that Christ reigns above all emperors.

sens: The Roman emperor and the political power he represents
The sovereign authority of Rome over conquered territories
What legally belongs to the temporal government
G2541J.detail:
1. Caesar primarily refers to the reigning Roman emperor at the time of Jesus — it is an official title held by Roman sovereigns since Augustus. The word evokes absolute political power and Rome's domination over the known world. In the Gospels, it is simply referred to as "Caesar" without giving a personal name, as this title is sufficient to designate the supreme authority: it is like saying "the President" or "the King" to refer to the current power (Matthew 22:17).
2. The term also designates the political authority system itself, the Roman state with its demands and tributes. When asked if it is lawful to "pay taxes to Caesar" (Mark 12:14), it actually refers to the tax owed to the Roman government — a question of political legitimacy, whether a Jew can obey a non-Jewish master.
3. By extension, the word represents everything in the temporal, political, and economic realm, distinct from the spiritual and divine realm. This is precisely the meaning of Jesus' response: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (Matthew 22:21) — a distinction between obligations to earthly power and those to God.
G2541J.origine: Καῖσαρ comes from the Latin Caesar, the name of the Roman royal family that became the title of the emperor. The Greek form directly borrows from the Latin, as Greeks often do when they speak of Roman power. The word became established throughout the Empire as the official title of the sovereign, equivalent to "Lord" or "Supreme Master." Among Greeks and Jews, it designates less the individual person than the office and authority it represents.
G2541J.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. In the first three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke), it arises during the trick question about taxes (Matthew 22:17-21; Mark 12:14-17; Luke 20:22-25): Jesus' opponents attempt to compromise him by forcing him to choose between loyalty to Rome and loyalty to Israel. Jesus responds by distinguishing the two orders — Caesar for the temporal, God for the spiritual. In John, the word appears at the trial before Pilate, when the accusers shout, "We have no king but Caesar" (John 19:12-15), expressing their allegiance to Rome against Jesus. In Acts, the title reappears in the context of Paul's appeal to Caesar as a right of Roman citizenship (Acts 25:8 and following). The word changes little in meaning: it always embodies the external political authority against which the believer must discern their duty.
G2541J.portee: This word of Jesus — "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's" — gives the Christian a golden principle: it is possible to respect earthly authorities without renouncing faith in God. It frees the believer from the illusion that refusing political power is an act of consecration to God. But it also reminds that the primary duty remains towards God, not towards Caesar: the temporal is never absolute. For the disciple of Jesus, this means: obey civil laws in what is just, pay taxes, respect the established order, but without idolizing human power or sacrificing conscience to it.

sens: City in Palestine, on the Mediterranean coast, capital of the Roman governor
Region and city near Lebanon, north of Galilee
G2542G.detail:
1. Caesarea is an important coastal city in Palestine, built by Herod the Great to honor the Roman emperor Augustus (Caesar). It is the seat of the Roman governor and a major commercial crossroads. The apostle Peter preaches there and converts the centurion Cornelius, marking the opening of the Gospel to the Gentiles.

2. Caesarea Philippi is a mountainous region near Lebanon, north of Galilee, far from the Jewish religious center. It is there that Jesus poses the decisive question to his disciples: "Who do people say that I am?" (Matthew 16:13). This geographical location underscores the importance of the moment: in pagan territory, far from Jerusalem, Jesus brings his disciples to a moment of revelation and confession of faith.
G2542G.origine: The name Caesarea comes from the Latin "Cæsarea," which honors the Roman emperor Caesar or Augustus. Several cities in the ancient Roman world bore this name. In Palestine, Herod the Great founded the coastal city (around 25 BC) in honor of the reigning Caesar. The term literally means "city of Caesar."
G2542G.emploi: Two Caesareas appear in the Greek New Testament. Caesarea Philippi, located to the north near Lebanon, is mentioned in Matthew 16:13 and Mark 8:27 as the place where Jesus questions his disciples about his identity. Caesarea in Palestine, on the coast, is the center of several key events: Philip's preaching to unclean spirits and the lame (Acts 8:4), the conversion and refuge of Saul-Paul (Acts 9:30), the conversion of the centurion Cornelius by Peter (Acts 10), and several later passages of Paul through this city. It is a strategic point in the spread of the Gospel to the Gentiles.
G2542G.portee: Caesarea reminds us that the Gospel unfolds geographically and socially, reaching regions and populations far from the temple in Jerusalem. Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi remains the foundation of the Church. The conversion of the centurion at Caesarea in Palestine shows that the Holy Spirit opens access to salvation beyond the borders of Judaism. These places embody the universality of the Christian message.

sens: Coastal city of Palestine, capital of the Roman province
Roman administrative and military center in Judea
Place where the Gospel spreads beyond Jewish borders
Seat of the Roman governor of Judea
G2542H.detail:
1. Caesarea is a port city built on the Mediterranean coast of Palestine, founded by Herod the Great and named in honor of Emperor Caesar Augustus. It served as the administrative capital of the Roman province and housed the governor's residence (Acts 23:33, 25:1).
2. The city was a center of Roman power: it is where the centurion Cornelius, a military officer of the occupying army, resided (Acts 10:1), and it is to Caesarea that Paul was sent for his safety (Acts 9:30).
3. Biblically, Caesarea represents the meeting point between the Jewish world and the pagan world. It is here that Peter receives the vision of the sheet filled with unclean animals and understands that the Gospel is also for the Gentiles, through the conversion of Cornelius (Acts 10).
4. The city frequently appears in Acts as a port of arrival and departure for missionary journeys: Philip preaches there (Acts 8:40), and Paul lands there during his travels (Acts 18:22, 21:8).
G2542H.origine: The name Kaisareia (Caesarea) derives directly from the Latin Caesar, meaning the Roman emperor. Herod the Great founded this city in the 1st century BC and named it to honor Emperor Augustus. It is an example of how the Greeks and Romans imposed their institutions and cults in the Mediterranean world.
G2542H.emploi: Caesarea appears 15 times in the New Testament, exclusively in the book of Acts, except for mentions in Matthew 16:13 and Mark 8:27 of Caesarea Philippi. It is a strategic center for the expansion of the Church: Philip preaches there after the persecution in Jerusalem (Acts 8:40), Cornelius the centurion converts there (Acts 10:1), and Paul stays there several times during his missionary journeys (Acts 21:8, 21:16). The city also holds legal significance: it is where Paul appears before Governor Festus during his trial (Acts 25:1-6). Thus, Caesarea symbolizes the transition of the Gospel from the Jewish world to the Gentile world.
G2542H.portee: Caesarea shows that the Gospel does not stop at the religious or cultural borders of Israel, but is addressed to all men, even those who serve the Roman Empire. The account of Cornelius and his household's conversion reminds the reader that God does not accept people based on their nationality or social status, but based on faith. This is a powerful encouragement for every Christian: regardless of your background or position, the Gospel is for you.

sens: To light a flame, to make a lamp burn
To be consumed by fire
To be filled with a burning passion, an intense feeling
G2545.detail:
1. To light a lamp or fire: to set something on fire so that it illuminates or is consumed. In Matthew 5:15, Jesus speaks of someone who "lights" a lamp to give light. It is the concrete action of creating a flame.

2. To be consumed, destroyed by fire: when this word is used in the passive (suffered form), it describes what is burning or disappearing in the flames. John 15:6 shows this: the branches that do not remain in Jesus "burn" when they are thrown into the fire. It is the progressive destruction by fire.

3. To burn with a feeling or passion: used figuratively, the word evokes an inner fervor that consumes, an emotion that ignites the soul. In Luke 24:32, the disciples say: "Did not our heart burn within us?" — it is the spiritual fervor in response to the words of Christ. In John 5:35, John the Baptist is called "the burning lamp": he is filled with the zeal of God.
G2545.origine: The Greek verb καίω comes from an ancient root meaning "to burn, to ignite." In Hebrew, this sense is found in several words such as בָּעַר ("to burn"), יָקַד ("to ignite"), and שָׂרַף ("to burn"). The word carries the image of fire that spreads and consumes, whether seen physically (a lamp is lit) or spiritually (the heart is ignited).
G2545.emploi: This verb appears about a dozen times in the New Testament, mainly in John and Revelation. It unfolds along two axes. First, the concrete axis: lighting a lamp (Matthew, Luke) or burning in fire (John 15, Revelation). Then the figurative axis: the burning of the heart by a feeling (Luke 24:32 with spiritual joy, John 5:35 with zeal). In Revelation, it takes on an eschatological tone: heavenly symbols burn (4:5, 8:10) and the final judgment consumes the wicked (21:8). The word thus navigates between material fire and spiritual fire, never losing its image of intensity and transformation.
G2545.portee: This word invites the believer to two meditations. First, it reminds that faith must "shine" (Matthew 5:15) — it is not to be hidden, but to be let shine so that others may see the light. Secondly, it shows that encountering Jesus "ignites" the heart (Luke 24:32): faith is not cold, but alive, burning with love and desire. The future judgment also burns (Revelation 21:8), calling for vigilance.

sens: Lack of moral quality, corruption of character
Malicious intent or disposition, will to do harm
Malignity, cruelty, absence of goodwill
Sorrow, affliction, misfortune (secondary sense)
G2549.detail:
1. Wickedness is primarily a failing moral quality, the opposite of character excellence. It is the corruption that settles in the soul when one strays from righteousness. In Romans 1:29, Paul lists wickedness among the vices that fill the heart of one who refuses to glorify God.
2. It is also malicious intent, the active desire to do harm to others. In 1 Corinthians 5:8, Paul urges the Corinthians to celebrate the Passover without this leaven of wickedness, that is, without this disposition of heart that corrupts the community, just as leaven corrupts dough.
3. Wickedness manifests as cold malignity, the absence of compassion. In 1 Corinthians 14:20, Paul invites believers to remain children in this regard — that is, simple, pure, without malicious calculation — even if they must be mature in their judgment.
4. In late Greek writings, the word also takes on the meaning of sorrow or affliction: in Matthew 6:34, Jesus says that each day has sufficient trouble, speaking of the misfortune or difficulty inherent in each day.
G2549.origine: The word comes from κακός ("bad"), a fundamental adjective in ancient Greek. The root expresses the idea of a defective quality, either physically (poor health) or morally (bad character). The suffix -ία forms an abstract noun to designate this quality as a permanent state or disposition. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew רָאָה (ra'ah, "evil"), linking the Greek notion to the richness of this biblical concept.
G2549.emploi: The word κακία appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's epistles and in the epistle of James. It typically denotes a repugnant moral state that must be shed: Ephesians 4:31 lists it with bitterness, anger, and slander, as what must disappear from among believers. In 1 Peter 2:1 and 2:16, it is a vice to abandon for spiritual growth. In Acts 8:22, Simon the magician is called to repent of his wickedness. In Matthew 6:34, the meaning nuances towards "affliction" or "trouble": the idea of inevitable daily misfortune. The usage always revolves around the contrast between this corruption and the purity, truth, or holiness to which believers are called.
G2549.portee: This word reminds the believer that wickedness is not a mere mistake or a passing weakness, but a deep corruption of the soul that infects the entire character. Its omnipresence in lists of vices shows that it is one of the major enemies of the Christian life. Recognizing this spiritual reality pushes the believer not to treat it merely as an issue of external behavior, but to ask the Holy Spirit to purify it from their heart, as Paul invites the Ephesians. It also gives weight to Jesus' exhortation in Matthew 6:34: in the face of the real troubles of life, trust in God is not naivety, but mature faith.

sens: To experience physical pain or affliction
To endure difficulties with perseverance
To bear trials related to faith
G2553.detail: 1. To suffer means to experience pain or mistreatment: it is a physical harm that affects us. Paul in 2 Timothy 2:9 speaks of suffering to the point of being imprisoned as a wrongdoer for proclaiming the Gospel. 2. To endure means to bear with tenacity, to stand firm in the face of coming trials. In 2 Timothy 4:5, Paul urges Timothy to endure suffering — it conveys the idea of holding on, not giving up despite the pain. 3. To suffer can also refer to general affliction, the misfortune that weighs upon us. James 5:13 asks: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray — this encompasses all forms of trial, not just physical pain.
G2553.origine: The Greek word comes from the combination of two elements: "kakos" (bad, harmful) and "pathos" (suffering, passion). It literally denotes the experience of the bad, that which wounds or afflicts. The root "pathos" is found in other words of the New Testament such as "apopathos" (which in Greek means to be affected by). In Hebrew, the underlying word is often "amal" (hard labor, affliction), which expresses the idea of a burden imposed upon us.
G2553.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the New Testament. Paul uses it in 2 Timothy to speak of his own fate: he suffers because of his preaching of the Gospel, but the word of God cannot be chained (2:9), and he asks Timothy to endure the sufferings that accompany the committed Christian life (4:5). James uses it in a pastoral exhortation: when a Christian suffers, his resource is prayer (5:13). The word always applies to the trials that disciples experience, never to the punishments inflicted on God's enemies.
G2553.portee: This word reminds the believer that suffering is not abnormal in the Christian life: it often accompanies faithful service to God. Paul and James do not deny the reality of pain, but they place it within a spiritual perspective where prayer and perseverance help us through affliction. Understanding this word helps the Christian see that suffering for the Gospel is not a sign of abandonment by God, but a normal part of discipleship.

sens: To cause harm, suffering to someone
To commit an action contrary to morality or the will of God
To act with malice or wickedness
G2554.detail:
1. The most direct meaning is to cause harm or suffering to others: it is the act of inflicting damage. Jesus asks the question on the Sabbath: "Is it lawful... to do evil, to kill?" (Mark 3:4), where doing evil is contrasted with saving a life.
2. The word also denotes morally wrong action, that which contravenes righteousness and justice. In 1 Peter 3:17, it is better to "suffer for doing good than for doing evil": this encompasses all reprehensible acts before God.
3. By extension, it is to act with intentional malice: "He who does evil has not seen God" (3 John 1:11), for doing evil reflects a heart turned away from God and His love.
G2554.origine: The word combines two Greek elements: kakos (bad, harmful) and poieō (to do, to produce). It literally means "to produce evil." The Hebrew word it often translates in the Greek Old Testament is raa (to do evil, harm), particularly in its intensive form. The family of kakopoieō also includes kakopoios (one who does evil, wrongdoer) and kakon (the evil itself).
G2554.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in Luke and the Catholic epistles. Jesus uses it twice in a Sabbath controversy (Mark 3:4 and Luke 6:9) to highlight the paradox: if the Law forbids doing evil on the Sabbath, how can it prohibit doing good? In 1 Peter 3:17 and 3 John 1:11, the context becomes ethical: Peter recommends suffering rather than the guilt of wrongdoing, and John encourages imitating good, not evil. The meaning remains constant: it is the bad action, considered in its execution.
G2554.portee: This word invites the Christian to clearly distinguish good from evil in their actions, not just in their thoughts. It emphasizes that doing evil is not a mere mistake, but a rupture with God: "He who does evil has not seen God" (3 John 1:11). For the believer, choosing to suffer rather than do evil becomes an act of faithfulness to Christ and a confession that only God can judge what is right.

sens: One who does evil, who commits bad or criminal acts
A person guilty of an offense or crime in the eyes of the law
Unjustly accused of wrongdoing
G2555.detail:
1. A wrongdoer is one who acts against good: it is a person who willingly does evil. The Greek word combines "bad" and "to do," literally portraying the criminal in action. In 1 Peter 4:15, the apostle lists the types of wrongdoers: murderers, thieves, and those who meddle in others' affairs — in other words, those whose actions violate the law or morality.
2. Before the government, a wrongdoer is the person to be punished: it is the criminal in the legal and public sense. In 1 Peter 2:14, governors are "sent by [God] to punish wrongdoers" — they execute justice by repressing those who commit crimes.
3. Sometimes, someone who is innocent is unjustly accused of wrongdoing: pagans slander Christians by calling them wrongdoers, even though they are not (1 Peter 2:12 and 3:16). The word then designates one who is defamed, falsely accused.
G2555.origine: The Greek word arises from two simple roots: "kakos" (bad) and "poieo" (to do). It literally means a "doer of evil." The word already appears in ancient Greek translations of the Old Testament, particularly to render Hebrew words meaning "to do evil." The fundamental idea is that of a malevolent or criminal action.
G2555.emploi: The word appears four times in the first epistle of Peter, always in the nominative or accusative, and always with the meaning of criminal or accused. Peter uses it to urge Christians not to be wrongdoers (1 Peter 4:15), to accept the punishment of wrongdoers by governors (1 Peter 2:14), and especially to patiently endure the slanders of pagans who wrongly label them as wrongdoers (1 Peter 2:12 and 3:16). The pastoral emphasis is constant: do not be wrongdoers, and if you are treated as such, let your blameless conduct speak for you.
G2555.portee: This word reminds the believer of a constant tension: on one side, never to do evil, to flee real guilt; on the other, to endure gracefully false accusations. Peter teaches that the strongest testimony of the Christian in the face of a hostile world is a blameless conduct — not to justify oneself, but to glorify God and let the truth shine through itself.

sens: Of poor quality, defective, worthless
Contrary to morality, wicked, perverse
Causing harm, damage, harmful
Unpleasant, difficult to endure
G2556G.detail:
1. First, the word designates what lacks quality or value: that which is defective, of poor quality. Matthew 21:41 speaks of "miserable" vine growers, where the Greek word literally means people of bad sort, worthless.

2. Next, it applies to moral evil: that which offends God's law and harms others. It is the wicked man who commits evil (Romans 3:8), the bad thoughts that arise from the heart (Mark 7:21), the guilty actions that divine justice condemns (Romans 13:4). Evil can also be a carnal desire, a vile ambition (Colossians 3:5).

3. The word also describes what is harmful, what brings damage or suffering. James 3:8 says that the tongue is "a evil that cannot be restrained," because it hurts. Acts 28:5 reports that Paul was not harmed by a venomous snake (literally "bad").

4. Finally, it can qualify what is unpleasant or difficult: Hebrews 5:14 speaks of discerning "what is good and what is evil," also designating what is repugnant to the moral sense of the believer.
G2556G.origine: The Greek word κακός is an ancient adjective, related to Indo-European roots meaning "to weaken," "to be insufficient." In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), it primarily translates the Hebrew רַע (ra'), which carries the same idea: that which is bad in the broadest sense, from defective to morally repugnant. The word opposes ἀγαθός (good) and καλός (beautiful, honest). It is a universal term to express evil in all its aspects.
G2556G.emploi: The word κακός appears 39 times in the New Testament. It is first used to judge people: a wicked man, a false apostle (Revelation 2:2, Philippians 3:2). Then to describe what emanates from moral evil: bad thoughts, bad words (Mark 7:21), bad company (1 Corinthians 15:33). Very often, the text speaks of "doing evil" or "committing evil": it is an action, a concrete choice (Romans 3:8, 13:4). Saint Paul also uses it for what harms the conscience or brotherly love (Romans 12:17, 1 Thessalonians 5:15). Finally, from a legal perspective, the magistrate punishes "the one who does evil" (Romans 13:4). The word always retains a pejorative connotation and designates what the Christian faith condemns.
G2556G.portee: Understanding that κακός encompasses both moral sin and its concrete effects — the bad intentions of the heart and actions that harm others — helps the believer see that evil is never an abstraction, but always a reality to be fought against. Knowing that the magistrate bears the sword to punish "the one who does evil" (Romans 13:4) reminds us that social order rests on the distinction between good and evil. Finally, learning to "discern what is good and what is evil" (Hebrews 5:14) is a mark of spiritual maturity: it is the fruit of a conscience educated by the Word and by obedience.

sens: Physically harmful, damaging
Morally reprehensible, contrary to good
Pernicious, malevolent, causing harm
G2556H.detail:
1. Evil first designates what causes suffering or physical pain. Lazarus experienced evils during his life (Luke 16:25) — illness, poverty, misery. A snake bite can do harm (Acts 28:5), a malignant sore wounds the body (Revelation 16:2).
2. On a moral level, evil qualifies what opposes God and good: bad thoughts that spring from the heart (Mark 7:21 in the source definition), corrupt conversations, or covetousness. Love does not suspect evil (1 Corinthians 13:5), meaning it does not seek to discover the bad side in others.
3. Evil is also used to describe wicked acts and the harm inflicted. Alexander the coppersmith did much evil to Paul (2 Timothy 4:14) by persecuting him. It is also the action of doing evil — what believers are called not to practice (Romans 3:8 in the source definition).
G2556H.origine: The Greek word kakos is the direct opposite of the words agathós (good) and kalós (beautiful, noble). It designates what is vile, worthless, or corrupt. In Hebrew, it primarily translates the word ra, which evokes both moral evil and misfortune or distress. This root thus covers both the ethical domain and that of suffering.
G2556H.emploi: The word appears six times in the provided Segond uses, always to designate a concrete or moral negative reality. In Luke 16:25, Acts 28:5, and Revelation 16:2, it pertains to physical evils — suffering, absence of injury, painful sores. In 1 Corinthians 13:5 and 2 Timothy 4:14, it concerns moral evil or harmful acts. Acts 16:28 is a borderline case: "Do not harm yourself" refers to the suicide the jailer might have committed, a mix of bad intention and bodily harm. Everywhere, the word situates evil at the heart of fallen human condition and the obstacles opposing the new life in Christ.
G2556H.portee: Understanding evil in its three dimensions — suffering, moral rebellion, deliberate harm — helps the Christian grasp the extent of what Jesus comes to conquer. This word reminds us that evil is not just an abstract idea, but a reality experienced in body and heart. That is why the love stated in 1 Corinthians 13 is so demanding: refusing to suspect evil is choosing trust despite appearances.

sens: A person who commits criminal acts, wrongs
Criminal sentenced to death
One who acts badly, who practices evil
G2557.detail:
1. A wrongdoer is primarily someone who commits wrongs, harmful and criminal acts. The Greek word combines the idea of "evil" (kakos) and "action" (ergon): it is one whose works are bad. In Luke 23:32-33, two wrongdoers are led to death alongside Jesus; they are death row inmates, criminals.
2. The word particularly designates the criminal, one who has committed a serious crime justifying capital punishment. When one of the two crucified wrongdoers insults Jesus (Luke 23:39), we see a man paying for his guilt with death.
3. More broadly, it refers to anyone who practices evil — who acts against the law and justice. Paul writes that he suffers "bound as a wrongdoer" (2 Timothy 2:9): even innocent, he bears the treatment reserved for criminals.
G2557.origine: The Greek word kakourgos is composed of kakos ("bad," "evil") and ergon ("work," "action"). The image is that of a person whose actions are bad. This simple and direct composition reveals how the Greeks thought of crime: not as a secret intention, but as a visible manifestation of evil through actions.
G2557.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, all in the later gospels and pastoral epistles. Three occurrences concern the two criminals crucified alongside Jesus (Luke 23:32, 33, 39): this is its main context, where it designates men sentenced to death for their crimes. A fourth occurrence in 2 Timothy 2:9 uses it figuratively: Paul, though innocent, is treated as a wrongdoer because he proclaims the Gospel. The word always retains a judicial nuance: it is an official criminal, recognized and punished.
G2557.portee: This word reminds us that the Son of God chose to die between two criminals, taking the place of the wrongdoer and bearing the judgment he deserved. It raises the question: who is truly guilty? The two wrongdoers acknowledge their guilt (Luke 23:41), while Jesus, treated as a criminal, is innocent. For the Christian reader, this illustrates substitution: the just for the unjust.

sens: To harm someone, to injure them, to make them suffer
To treat someone with cruelty or violence
To subject someone to mistreatment
G2558.detail:
1. The verb denotes the action of causing physical or moral harm to a person: to injure them, to cause them suffering. In Hebrews 11:37, those who were "mistreated" suffered tortures and persecutions that damaged their bodies and dignity.
2. It is to treat someone with cruelty, without regard for their life or well-being. The passive form of the verb shows that the persecuted believers were the victims of this cruelty: they were struck, tortured, rejected.
3. More broadly, "mistreat" means to subject someone to undignified or oppressive conditions. In Hebrews 13:3, the term invites Christians to remember those who endure such treatment, as if they were enduring it themselves.
G2558.origine: The Greek word κακουχέω (kakoucheō) is composed of κακόν (kakon, "evil, bad") and ἔχω (echō, "to have, to hold"). The basic image is that of "holding evil," that is, causing harm to someone. This verb translates the Hebrew עָנָה (anah) in the sense of "to afflict, to torture, to mistreat." The family of words "kakos" (bad) is very rich in New Testament Greek and always denotes what is contrary to good and to the will of God.
G2558.emploi: The verb κακουχέω appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Hebrews, and always in the passive voice ("to be mistreated"). In Hebrews 11:37, in the catalog of heroes of faith, it describes the extreme sufferings endured by Old Testament believers: physical torture and social exclusion. In Hebrews 13:3, the apostle uses it to urge readers to sympathize with prisoners and the persecuted. The context is always that of religious persecution and suffering for faith. The word emphasizes the reality of the inflicted evil, without euphemizing it.
G2558.portee: This word reminds Christians that persecution is a reality that has marked the history of faith, from the Old Testament to the early days of the Church. By using this term, the epistle to the Hebrews invites its readers to compassion for those who suffer for their faith, and to recognize their dignity despite the mistreatment they endure. It is a call to identify with their pains and not to forget them.

sens: To treat someone with brutality, to subject them to physical or moral mistreatment
To embitter someone, to provoke hostility or malice against them
To cause harm or damage to someone
G2559.detail: 1. Mistreat means to treat someone with cruelty or harshness, to inflict suffering on them. This is the most concrete and common sense: the Egyptians "mistreated" the Israelites by enslaving them and forcing them into exhausting labor (Acts 7:6, 19). King Herod "mistreated" the members of the Church by persecuting them (Acts 12:1). 2. To embitter means to provoke malice or hostility: the unbelieving Jews "embittered" the minds of the pagans, that is, they poisoned them, turning them against the brethren (Acts 14:2). It is the same action, but viewed from the side of the attitude and feelings that are provoked. 3. To cause harm or damage is the most general sense: "no one will lay a hand on you to do you harm" (Acts 18:10) refers to anything that could harm someone, without distinction between direct violence and provoked hostility.
G2559.origine: The Greek word comes from the adjective κακός (kakos), which means "bad" or "evil." By adding the suffix -οω (-oō), it becomes a verb: "to make bad," "to treat badly." It is a simple and direct formation. In Hebrew, this verb primarily translates רָעַע (ra'a') in the causative form, which means "to do harm," and עָנָה (anah) in the intensive form, which means "to afflict." The central idea is one of harming or causing suffering.
G2559.emploi: This verb appears six times in the New Testament, all in Acts and 1 Peter. It describes situations of persecution and mistreatment: the oppression of the Israelites in Egypt (Acts 7:6, 19), the persecution of the Church by Herod (Acts 12:1), the hostility provoked against the disciples (Acts 14:2), and the promise that the Lord will protect Paul (Acts 18:10). In 1 Peter 3:13, the apostle poses a rhetorical question: who will dare to mistreat those who are zealous for good? The word always expresses an unjust action, either physical or moral, directed against believers or the righteous.
G2559.portee: This verb reminds the believer that the malice of the world can take many forms—direct violence, provoked hostility, systematic oppression. But the uses of the word in Acts and 1 Peter also show that the Lord does not leave His people unprotected, and that those who seek good should not fear those who might do them harm. It is a call to trust in God's providence in the face of persecution.

sens: To be in poor physical health, to suffer from an illness
To be tormented or cruelly afflicted by illness or demonic possession
To act, speak, or pray in a morally bad, unjust manner
G2560.detail:
1. The primary sense is purely physical: someone who "is unwell" is afflicted by illness. Jesus constantly encounters people suffering from various ailments (Matthew 4:24: "all who were suffering from diseases and pains"), and He heals them. It is the state of the sick in contrast to the healthy.

2. Illness can be particularly severe or humiliating: Jesus heals those who are "cruelly tormented" (Matthew 15:22), a young girl harassed by demonic possession. The adverb emphasizes the intensity of suffering and disorder.

3. In a moral sense, "to be unwell" means to act or speak with wickedness, injustice, or impiety. In John 18:23, Christ asks the servant who struck Him: "If I have spoken wrongly, show what is bad; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?" It is a question of just or unjust conduct.
G2560.origine: The word comes from the Greek κακός (kakos), which means "bad" in the broadest sense: that which is vitiated, deteriorated, morally bad. The adverb κακῶς adds the idea of manner, of doing something defectively. This family of words traces back to a root denoting deterioration or degradation. In ancient Hebrew, Greek translators often rendered verbs meaning "to curse" or "to belittle" (אָרַר, קָלַל) with this term.
G2560.emploi: The word appears about 16 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels of Matthew and Mark. Its most frequent use is physical: "to be unwell" or "to be sick," particularly in healing narratives where Jesus encounters the sick and heals them. Matthew and Mark use this expression to describe the crowd of infirm people pressing around Jesus. On a few occasions (John 18:23, Acts 23:5, James 4:3), the word takes on a moral sense: to speak wrongly, to do wrong, to make a bad request to God. The context clearly determines whether one is speaking of a physical illness or morally reprehensible conduct.
G2560.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus approached the sick, the suffering, the marginalized. His first public act is a massive healing (Matthew 4:24). This shows that compassion for the sick body is at the heart of His ministry. In a moral sense, the word challenges us regarding our words and actions: to speak wrongly or to act wrongly is to fall into the "evil" that Christ came to conquer. He invites the believer to seek true health, both physical and moral, by turning to Jesus.

sens: State of mistreatment, harsh or cruel treatment
Miserable condition of an oppressed people
Experience of pain and distress
G2561.detail:
1. The word refers to the act of being mistreated, treated harshly, with cruelty. It is the suffering that arises from the violence or injustice one endures — not a mere pain, but an affliction caused by others.
2. It specifically applies to the condition of an entire people burdened by oppression. When God says to Moses, "I have seen the suffering of my people who are in Egypt" (Acts 7:34), He speaks of the Hebrews enslaved and forced into hard labor.
3. It is the distress one experiences in this situation: the groans that God hears go hand in hand with this suffering, like the cry of one who bears the weight of servitude.
G2561.origine: The word comes from the verb κακόω (to do harm, mistreat), which itself is derived from κάκος (bad, harmful). In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it translates the Hebrew עָנִי, which means affliction, misery, the condition of the poor and oppressed — the state of one who is crushed under a weight.
G2561.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:34. It is Stephen who quotes it while recounting the words that God spoke to Moses at the burning bush: "I have seen the suffering of my people." This is a quotation from the Old Testament (Exodus 3:7), which speaks of the servitude of the Hebrews in Egypt. The context is God's call to free His people from oppression: suffering is the visible symptom of an injustice that calls for divine intervention.
G2561.portee: This word reminds us that God sees and hears the suffering of the oppressed. He is not indifferent to the injustices and mistreatment that people endure. For the Christian reader, it is an assurance: when one suffers under oppression, one can cry out to God — He does not remain deaf, and He is the deliverer of those who are burdened.

sens: Straw or chaff, residue of the harvest left in the fields or used as material
Material of little value, easily consumable
G2562.detail:
1. Straw refers to the stalks of grain that remain in the field after the harvest or that can be gathered. It is a common and low-value material used for bedding, heating, or basic construction. In 1 Corinthians 3:12, Paul mentions straw alongside hay among the low-cost materials that can be used to build on the solid foundation that is Jesus Christ.
2. Straw also symbolically represents what is fragile and easily destructible. Unlike gold, silver, or precious stones that endure, straw burns easily and does not last — an image of what has no eternal value. Paul uses it to evoke human works that do not align with God's plan.
G2562.origine: The Greek word καλάμη comes from the family of κάλαμος ("stalk, reed"). It literally refers to dried and cut stalks. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew קַשׁ ("straw"), which is notably seen in Exodus 5:12 when the Egyptians refuse to give straw to the Hebrews to make bricks. The image is that of the harvest: what remains after threshing the grain.
G2562.emploi: The word appears only once in 1 Corinthians 3:12, in the famous comparison of building materials. Paul depicts a contrast: some build with precious and durable materials (gold, silver, stones), while others use wood, hay, and straw — cheap and perishable materials. This is not a moral condemnation of straw itself, but an image of the spiritual quality of works: straw symbolizes what will not survive God's judgment. It is a teaching on the eternal consequences of our actions.
G2562.portee: This image of straw calls the Christian to reflect on the true value of their works: not on their appearance or immediate success, but on their spiritual solidity and conformity to God's will. It also invites humility: recognizing that it is easy to build superficially, but only what is founded on Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit will endure. For those who meditate on this word, it is a call to invest their lives not in the ephemeral, but in the eternal.

sens: Aquatic plant with hollow and flexible stems
Pipe or stick made of reed
Musical instrument: reed flute
Stick or stem used for striking
Measuring rod made of reed or gold
Writing instrument: quill or calamus
G2563.detail:
1. The reed is a plant that grows by the water's edge, with a hollow and flexible stem that sways in the wind. Jesus refers to it when speaking of John the Baptist: "What did you go out to see in the wilderness? A reed shaken by the wind?" (Matthew 11:7). The image suggests fragility and instability.
2. By its shape, the reed stem becomes a practical object: a stick or a rod. Roman soldiers use it to strike Jesus, mocking Him: they put a crown of thorns on Him and place "a reed in His right hand" (Matthew 27:29), then "one of them ran and filled a sponge with vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave Him to drink" (Mark 15:36).
3. The hollow reed can become a flute or a musical instrument when holes are pierced in it. This is one of its most well-known ancient uses, although it does not explicitly appear in these passages.
4. As a stick, the reed serves as a weapon or instrument of punishment: soldiers wield it to strike Jesus during His passion, thus ridiculing Him.
