5. The long and straight reed can serve as a ruler to measure distances. In Revelation, the angel measures the heavenly city "with a golden reed" (Revelation 21:15), transforming the humble instrument into an object of precision and glory.
6. The ancient writing quill was a cut and split piece of reed, dipped in ink. John writes to Gaius: "I have much to write to you, but I do not want to do so with pen and ink" (3 John 1:13), meaning without resorting to the ordinary instruments of written correspondence.
G2563.origine: The Greek word κάλαμος comes from the Mediterranean world where reeds grow abundantly near lakes and rivers. In Hebrew, the word קָנֶה (qanèh) designates the same plant; it literally means "stem" or "reed." The Greek word captures this common plant reality and broadens its meaning to all objects made from this material: pipe, stick, instrument. The reed was so common in antiquity that it became synonymous with any hollow, flexible object or tool.
G2563.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the New Testament. It first refers to the plant itself (Matthew 11:7, Luke 7:24). Then, it describes the objects made from it: Roman soldiers use a reed as a weapon of mockery against Jesus (Matthew 27:29-30, Mark 15:19), and as a handle to dip a sponge in vinegar (Matthew 27:48, Mark 15:36). In Revelation, the reed becomes a sacred measuring instrument: the angel measures the temple (Revelation 11:1) and the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:15-16) with a golden reed, symbolizing both the ordinary instrument elevated to holiness and the precision of the divine plan. Finally, in 3 John 1:13, the "pen" is the calamus of reed, the quintessential writing tool. The meaning thus varies from the concrete (the plant) to the symbolic (divine measurement), but the word always retains the same material root.
G2563.portee: The reed, a fragile plant swayed by the wind, invites the Christian to meditate on weakness. Jesus seems to say that John the Baptist is not a reed, but something more solid — a moral strength. Conversely, the reed in the hands of the soldiers mocking Jesus becomes an instrument of despicable humiliation, reminding us that mockery is a weapon of the world. But in Revelation, the golden reed in the hands of the angel is transformed into an instrument of divine revelation: what was ordinary becomes extraordinary. Finally, the reed pen evokes the power of the written word, a faithful witness to the truth.

sens: To bring someone to oneself by addressing them or giving them an order
To invite someone, especially to a meal or a celebration
To give someone a name, to name them
To designate someone for a role, a mission, or a life with God
To qualify someone as such or such (to treat them as)
G2564G.detail:
1. To call means to bring someone by addressing them or commanding them to come. At the time of the final judgment, the master "called" his servants to entrust them with his goods (Matthew 25:14): it is a simple command to appear. It is also to bring someone to oneself for a particular reason.

2. To invite means to call someone to participate in a celebration or a meal. The owner "called" the workers of his vineyard to pay them (Matthew 20:8). In the parables of the wedding feast, Jesus speaks of those who are "called" or "invited" to the feast of the Kingdom (Matthew 22:3, 9). This is a warmer form of calling, marked by hospitality.

3. To name someone means to give them a name or to designate them by a name. Jesus saw Simon and said to him: you shall be "called" Cephas, that is, Peter (John 1:42). A child receives their name through this act: the parents "called" them by such a name.

4. In spiritual language, "to call" means to choose someone, to invite them to enter into a relationship with God and to live according to His will. God "calls" the nations to be His people (Romans 9:25). He who has "called" you is faithful (1 Thessalonians 5:24): it is God who summons you to faith and eternal life. This divine calling transforms a person.

5. To qualify or to treat someone as something is also to "call". One "calls" someone blessed by recognizing them as such. It is to give someone a status or an identity: "you will be called children of God" (Matthew 5:9) means that you will receive this title and dignity.
G2564G.origine: The verb καλέω comes from a root that evokes the idea of shouting or making noise to attract attention. In Hebrew, it often translates קרא (qara'), which also means "to call" or "to shout". This root is enriched in the New Testament with a spiritual dimension: to call becomes to invite to a covenant with God. Several compounds of this verb exist (προσκαλέω, "to call to oneself", μετακαλέω, "to recall") and share this central idea of summoning and relationship.
G2564G.emploi: The verb καλέω is one of the most frequent in the New Testament (132 occurrences). It first appears in its concrete sense: to bring someone (Matthew 25:14), to invite to a meal (Luke 14:16, John 2:2), to give a name (Luke 1:32, John 1:42). But Paul and Peter mainly use it in a theological sense: the "call" of God that summons believers to faith and holiness (Romans 8:30, 1 Corinthians 1:9, Galatians 1:6, 1 Thessalonians 2:12, 1 Peter 1:15). Those who are "called" form the people of God. The past participle "the called" or "the invited" regularly designates the elect (Matthew 22:8, Hebrews 9:15). The word "call" itself (κλῆσις, or by extension of κλητός, "called") becomes a central concept to describe the Christian vocation.
G2564G.portee: For a Christian, understanding "to call" in depth means grasping that God does not remain distant: He personally addresses you, just as Jesus called His disciples. This vocation is not a punishment or an arbitrary obligation, but a warm invitation to enter His family and participate in His Kingdom. Knowing that "He who has called you is faithful" (1 Thessalonians 5:24) gives confidence in the face of trials. Finally, being "called" to holiness means that your life has meaning and a destiny, sealed by God Himself.

sens: To bring someone by addressing them or summoning them
To invite someone to a meal or a celebration
To give someone a name, to name them
To designate someone by a title or a role
In religious language, to invite someone to participate in the blessings of the Kingdom of God
G2564H.detail:
1. To call means to bring someone by addressing them or summoning them. It is to shout after someone to come to you or to join you. In Matthew 20:8, the master of the house calls the workers to pay them: he summons them to gather.

2. To call can also mean to invite someone to a meal or a celebration. When you are "called" to a meal, you are invited to come and participate. In Luke 14:16, the master of a large house "calls" many people to a feast: these are invitations extended to guests.

3. To call means to give someone a name, to name them. It is to establish someone's identity by assigning them a name. In Luke 2:21, the parents "give" the name Jesus to the child, which means they call him Jesus.

4. To call can designate someone by a title, a nickname, or a role. In Acts 7:58, a young man is "named" Saul: he is identified by this name; in Acts 10:1, a cohort is "called" Italian, that is, designated or referred to as such.

5. In religious language, to call means to invite someone to participate in the blessings of the Kingdom of God, to respond to God's call. God "calls" the faithful to holiness (1 Peter 1:15), to peace (Galatians 5:13), to hope: it is a call to enter into His grace and to receive His promises.
G2564H.origine: The Greek word kaléō comes from an ancient root that evokes the idea of making noise, shouting to bring someone. It often translates the Hebrew qara, which also means to shout, to call, to summon. The same root has given rise to words like klèsis (call, vocation) and eklektós (elect, chosen). It is a very lively word that encompasses everything related to the action of bringing someone or assigning them an identity through speech.
G2564H.emploi: The verb to call appears about 150 times in the New Testament. It is first used concretely: to call someone, to summon them to come (Luke 19:2 where Zacchaeus is "called" Zacchaeus, meaning known by this name). It is used to name, to give a name to someone (Luke 2:21 where the name Jesus is given to the child; Luke 22:3 where Judas is "named" Iscariot). It then designates the invitation to a meal (Luke 14:16, Revelation 19:9). But its use becomes deeper in Pauline theology: God "calls" believers to holiness, to peace, to hope (Romans 8:30, Galatians 1:6). This divine call is not merely a temporal summons, but an invitation to enter into an eternal relationship with God and to share in His blessings. God's call is effective: those He calls are destined to be saved and transformed.
G2564H.portee: This word invites the believer to understand that their relationship with God is born from a call. God "calls" us not for a human reason, but by His sovereign grace. Responding to this call means recognizing that God names us, identifies us as His own, and invites us to a new life in communion with Him. It also means understanding that salvation is not a solitary endeavor, but a response to God's personal and transformative call.

sens: Cultivated olive, selected for its quality of fruit
In contrast: well-tended olive, improved by human cultivation, opposed to wild olive
In imagery: that which is naturally excellent or benefits from the heritage of election
G2565.detail:
1. It is the cultivated olive, the one found in gardens and plantations, carefully tended to produce a better harvest of fruit. Unlike the wild olive, which grows freely without intervention, this one benefits from long selection and thoughtful cultivation. In Romans 11:24, Paul compares the Gentile believers to branches cut from a "wild olive" (that is, foreign to God's plan), which are grafted onto a "cultivated olive": the metaphor refers to the people of Israel and their heritage of blessing.
2. The contrast is striking: the cultivated olive represents natural excellence, the tree that has received the care of the one who has cultivated it, while the wild olive grows without favor. Paul uses it to remind that the Israelites by birth enjoy a privilege — they belong to the good branch — but that God's grace can extend this blessing to Gentiles who had no natural right to it.
G2565.origine: The Greek word "kallielaios" (literally "beautiful olive") is composed of "kallos" (beauty) and "elaios" (olive). It is a rare word, used here to clearly distinguish the cultivated olive from the wild olive. In the Mediterranean, the cultivated olive was highly prized: a productive shrub, a symbol of peace and prosperity. No Hebrew word specifically designates this distinction, but the Greek translators of the Old Testament were well aware of the contrast between the improved olive and the olive of the forests.
G2565.emploi: Paul uses this word only once, in Romans 11:24, at the heart of his reflection on the salvation of the Gentiles. It is an agricultural parable: the Israelites are the cultivated olive, the Gentiles are branches of wild olive that are grafted onto the good tree. This choice of vocabulary emphasizes that it is not "natural" for non-Jews to be grafted into the heritage of Israel — but God intended it this way. The agricultural culture of the time made this image clear and striking for its readers.
G2565.portee: This image teaches us that our place in the people of God is never a right, but a gift. Believers from the nations have been "grafted" by grace: we are not born into the good branch, and yet we enjoy its riches. This should inspire humility and gratitude — and also respect for the Jewish roots of our faith.

sens: In an appropriate, correct manner, in accordance with what is suitable
In a pleasant, satisfactory, commendable way
Successfully, effectively
Exactly, justly
G2566.detail:
1. The word describes an action or word that takes place in the right way, that which is suitable for the situation. It is to do or say what is necessary, at the right moment and according to the rules — like Paul who rightly acknowledges before Governor Festus that he must appear before Caesar's tribunal, which is exactly the expected legal procedure (Acts 25:10).
2. It is also to accomplish something in a pleasant or commendable way, in a manner that deserves approval. When one acts well, it is done with wisdom and justice.
3. The word can also express effectiveness: a well-built foundation withstands the assault (Luke 6:48), a structure that lasts because it has been built correctly and solidly.
4. In some contexts, it emphasizes that something is done justly, precisely as it should be, without deviation or error.
G2566.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "kalos," which means beautiful, good, noble. The adverb "well" naturally derives from it: it is the beautiful or good way of doing things. The comparative "kallion" (much better, very well) reinforces this idea: not only good, but better or excellent. In Hebrew, this word often translates roots related to "being good" or "being right."
G2566.emploi: This word appears only once in the Segond in the comparative form in Acts 25:10, where Paul states that he will appear very well (or quite well) before Caesar's tribunal — it is the procedure that is suitable and just. The word "well" (in the simple positive form) is much more frequent in the New Testament: it describes a manner of acting that is correct, right, worthy of approval. It can qualify a just word, a wise action, a solid construction. Its use changes according to the context: ironic when one pretends to approve what is wrong, sincere when one truly praises what is good.
G2566.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of the importance of how we act and speak. It is not only the result that matters, but also the manner: speaking well, acting well, honors God and respects those we have before us. It is a call to righteousness and wisdom in all circumstances of life.

sens: one who teaches what is good and useful
master whose teaching leads to virtue and piety
G2567.detail:
1. It is primarily one who imparts knowledge, instruction that bears fruit. The Greek word is composed of "good" (kalos) and "one who teaches" (didaskalos). The emphasis is on the quality of the teaching: it is not just any teacher, but a master whose words and example guide towards good, towards the wisdom of God. In Titus 2:3, Paul asks older women to play this role with younger women by instructing them in Christian virtues.
2. Figuratively, it means someone whose message transforms the heart and behavior. A good teacher does not simply accumulate knowledge; he shapes the character and conduct of those who listen to him. This is why the role is entrusted to those whose lives themselves testify to holiness.
G2567.origine: The word unites two Greek terms: "kalos" (beautiful, good, suitable, useful) and "didaskalos" (one who teaches, master). The starting image is that of a master whose word is good, effective, beneficial. It is a rare compound in the Greek Bible, formed to describe the ideal teacher in the Christian community.
G2567.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 2:3. Paul uses it when he describes the role of older women in the Church: they must be "good teachers." This context shows that the emphasis is on the moral integrity of the one teaching — her sobriety, her distance from slander, her holiness — which guarantees the quality of her teaching to younger women. The word summarizes the ideal of Christian mentoring: a transmission not only of ideas but of wisdom and virtue.
G2567.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that any teaching worthy of the name must lead towards good and transform the listener. It is a call to those who teach — whether they are pastors, parents, or elders — to ensure that their words are not only just but life-giving. It also highlights the importance of mentoring by the elders: their experience and spiritual maturity are a treasure for the Church.

sens: To accomplish good, just, and honest actions
To persevere in moral uprightness without becoming discouraged
To act with excellence and honor in one's conduct
G2569.detail:
1. The verb "do good" refers to the action of accomplishing what is good, just, and worthy. It involves performing morally right and honest acts that reflect virtue. When Paul writes "do not grow weary in doing good" in 2 Thessalonians 3:13, he speaks of those just and good works that Christians must continue to perform.
2. The meaning is enriched by a nuance of perseverance: "doing good" is not an isolated act, but a lasting attitude. The Greek emphasizes continuity — not giving up, not becoming weary from doing what is good. It is an encouragement to remain faithful in righteousness despite obstacles and moral fatigue.
3. There is also the idea of acting with excellence and honor, conducting oneself in a worthy and commendable manner. The word evokes an active virtue, an excellence of life that honors the one who practices it and honors God.
G2569.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: "kalos" (beautiful, good, of moral quality) and "poieō" (to do, to accomplish). This combination creates the literal meaning "to do the beautiful/good." In Hebrew, the idea corresponds to the concept of doing good (tob = good), which is also found in Genesis when God sees that His creation is "good." The Greek verb emphasizes voluntary and moral action: it is not passive beauty, but beauty in action.
G2569.emploi: The verb "do good" appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Thessalonians 3:13. Paul uses it to exhort Christians to persevere in good works. The context shows that some risked becoming discouraged or weary in the face of difficulties; the apostle calls them not to yield to this temptation and to continue accomplishing what is just and good. The expression "to do good" (kalón poiein) also appears in Galatians 6:9, where Paul encourages the Galatians not to grow weary in doing good, knowing that they will reap at the proper time. This verb fits into Paul's theology of perseverance and the moral life of the Christian.
G2569.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Christian life consists not only in believing but also in acting with righteousness and goodness, day after day. It calls them to moral perseverance: even when fatigue threatens, even when progress seems slow, they are called to continue doing good. It is an encouragement against discouragement and the abandonment of just works. It also affirms that this "beautiful conduct" has value in God's eyes and carries a deep dignity.

sens: Beautiful, pleasant to see or hear
Well suited for its purpose, effective, useful
Excellent in quality
Morally right, honest, noble
Beneficial, desirable
G2570G.detail:
1. This word primarily describes what is pleasing to the sight or senses: beautiful stones (Luke 21:5), excellent wine (John 2:10). It refers to an attractive appearance, that which catches the eye.
2. It then applies to what functions well, perfectly fulfilling its role. A good tree produces good fruit (Matthew 7:17-19); good soil receives the seed and makes it grow (Luke 8:15); good salt seasons effectively (Mark 9:50).
3. It designates superior quality, excellence: good pearls (Matthew 13:45), a good shepherd who knows his sheep (John 10:11). It is the best of its kind.
4. It takes on a moral dimension: a good deed pleases God (Matthew 5:16), a good conscience is pure (Hebrews 13:18), doing good is always commendable (Galatians 6:9). It is what is just and honorable.
5. Finally, it expresses what is fitting, what is advantageous: it is good to do this rather than that (Matthew 15:26). It is the judgment of an act or situation as desirable.
G2570G.origine: This Greek word comes from an Indo-European root originally denoting appearance or suitability. The biblical language relates it to the Hebrew "tob" (טוֹב), which shares this dual meaning: what is beautiful or pleasant to see, and what is useful or beneficial. Unlike another Greek word "agathos" (agathôs, "good") which emphasizes internal or moral goodness, "kalos" focuses on what is visible, functional, or suitable. This is why the two terms are often used together: what is true at heart must also manifest through beautiful actions.
G2570G.emploi: This word is very frequent in the Gospels and the epistles, with about 90 occurrences. The Gospels use it richly: Jesus speaks of good trees, good seed, good soil to describe what produces the fruits of the Kingdom. Mark and Luke use it to qualify His works and teachings. Paul primarily uses it in a moral and practical sense: doing good, being rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:18), not growing weary in doing good (Galatians 6:9). The pastoral epistles frequently mention it to define the Christian life and ministry: a good reputation (1 Timothy 3:7), a good conscience (Hebrews 13:18), a good confession of faith (1 Timothy 6:12-13). The meaning nuances according to the context: physical with fruits and soil, moral with works and conscience, practical with ministry and management.
G2570G.portee: This word invites the Christian to a dual vision: first, that good must be visible and beautiful, that it be seen in actions (Matthew 5:16) — faith is not hidden, it expresses itself. Secondly, that everything we do must be truly useful, genuinely good for something: no hollow zeal, but works that bear fruit. Finally, it reminds us that what is good to God also naturally pleases man, for good carries its beauty with it. For those who meditate on Scripture, this word encourages seeking good and recognizing it, not only in word but in action.

sens: Small harbor bay in Crete
G2570H.detail: Fair Havens (literally "fair" in Greek) is the name of a small natural cove on the southern coast of Crete. The name designates a coastal shelter where ships could anchor. In the account of the storm that drives Paul to Rome (Acts 27), the ship arrives at this location, near the city of Lasea, but this anchorage proves insufficient for the winter: Paul advises to stay in port, but the centurion and the shipowner decide to continue on and ultimately find themselves caught in a violent storm.
G2570H.origine: The Greek name κάλος (kalos) literally means "beautiful, excellent." It is a common adjective in the New Testament to describe what is beautiful in appearance or suitable for its use. Applied to this harbor, it reflects that it was a place offering recognizable shelter, likely appreciated by sailors in antiquity.
G2570H.emploi: Fair Havens appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 27:8, during Paul's journey to Rome as a prisoner. The ship arrives at this location after having navigated difficultly along the coast of Crete. Although this harbor is named "Fair Havens," it proves insufficient to face the winter storms, which shows that even a seemingly safe place may not offer the expected protection against the elements. It is in this context that Paul demonstrates wisdom by warning of the danger.
G2570H.portee: This passage reminds believers that appearances or promising names do not guarantee safety. Fair Havens also illustrates how God governs circumstances — even a storm becomes an opportunity to show divine protection and the Lord's faithfulness to His children, even in the midst of danger.

sens: Fabric or object that covers and conceals something
Obstacle that prevents seeing or understanding
Spiritual screen that veils the truth of Christ from unbelievers
G2571.detail:
1. The veil is primarily a fabric placed over something to cover or hide it: Moses wore a veil over his face so that the Israelites would not see the fading glory (2 Corinthians 3:13). It is a physical barrier, a material object that conceals.
2. The veil then becomes an image for anything that hinders understanding: "the same veil remains when reading the Old Testament" (2 Corinthians 3:14), meaning that something invisible obstructs access to the true meaning. The veil is no longer physical, but acts as an intellectual and spiritual barrier.
3. Finally, the veil signifies the spiritual obstacle that hides the glory and truth of Christ from those who do not believe: "a veil is thrown over their hearts" (2 Corinthians 3:15). This veil is lifted when one turns to the Lord (2 Corinthians 3:16). It represents the blindness of sin or unbelief in the face of divine revelation.
G2571.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb « kalyptô » which means « to cover » or « to hide ». It is a technical term for anything that veils, covers, or masks. In Hebrew, the Bible speaks of « masswé » (the veil of Moses) or « mékassé » (a covering), which the Greek translates with the same term « kalumma ». The image is that of a fabric placed over something to obscure it.
G2571.emploi: The word « veil » appears only four times in the New Testament, all in 2 Corinthians 3:13-16, a passage where Paul spiritually interprets the veil that Moses wore. He begins with the physical meaning (the veil over the face), then unfolds it into spiritual meanings: the veil that prevents understanding of the Old Testament (verses 14-15), and the veil that covers the hearts of unbelievers in the face of the Gospel. Each time, the veil is an obstacle to spiritual vision. Paul shows that what was a physical and temporary barrier becomes an image of the lasting blindness of those who do not receive Christ, but that this veil can be removed by conversion.
G2571.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on what prevents us from seeing the glory and truth of God. It is not only an external barrier but often an internal one: our prejudices, our unbelief, our religious habits without the Spirit. Understanding Paul's veil means recognizing that without Christ and the action of the Holy Spirit, the Word of God can remain veiled, misunderstood. And it is also a promise: this veil can be removed; it does not remain "when the heart turns to the Lord."

sens: To cover something by placing something over it
To shelter, protect
To conceal, hide
To veil, render invisible or incomprehensible
To forgive, erase (in the sense of sin)
G2572.detail:
1. To physically cover: to place something over another thing to protect or hide it. In Matthew 8:24, during the storm on the lake, the waves "cover" the boat, meaning they flood and submerge it.
2. To shelter or hide something so that it cannot be seen. In Luke 8:16, one does not "cover" a lit lamp with a jar, as it would be against its purpose.
3. To voluntarily conceal or hide what could be discovered. The word evokes both the action of hiding and the state of being hidden.
4. To veil or obscure: to render something invisible to the intellect or spiritual perception. In 2 Corinthians 4:3, the Gospel may remain "veiled" to those who do not believe: its true meaning is hidden from them.
5. To forgive in the literal sense of "to cover": by extension, love "covers a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:8 and James 5:20), meaning it forgives, erases, forgets the wrong without disclosing it. It is the image of a veil thrown over sin so that it is no longer visible.
G2572.origine: The verb καλύπτω (kaluptō) comes from a root meaning "to hide, to veil". In classical Greek, it is rare in ordinary prose. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint translated into Greek for Greek-speaking Jews), it almost always translates the Hebrew verb כָּסָה (kâsâ), which also has the dual meaning of "to physically cover" and "to forgive, to forget sin". This dual meaning comes from the biblical image: to forgive is to put a veil over sin so that it is no longer seen or pursued. The word belongs to the same family as the noun κάλυμμα, "veil" or "covering."
G2572.emploi: The verb appears seven times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke and Paul, with a progressive nuance. The concrete, physical meaning ("to cover", "to cover over") appears in moments of danger or concealment: the boat covered by the waves (Matthew 8:24), the lamp that should not be covered (Luke 8:16). The meaning of "to hide" or "to veil" appears in the Lord's words (Matthew 10:26) and in Paul (2 Corinthians 4:3), where the "veiling" concerns spiritual or divine clarity. Finally, the meaning of forgiveness—the love that "covers a multitude of sins"—returns twice (1 Peter 4:8, James 5:20) as a biblical image of mercy: Christian charity makes sin disappear by refusing to disclose it or to take advantage of it.
G2572.portee: This word teaches that God truly forgives: He does not merely forget our sins; He "covers" them, meaning He hides them forever, as if we had confessed and rejected them. It is the image of total remission. For the Christian, "covering the sins of others" means exercising charity by forgiving without recalling the wrong or exposing it: it is to imitate the divine love that has covered us. This image also reminds us that we are not called to judge or expose the sins of others, but to cover them with love and forgiveness.

sens: In a suitable, appropriate, correct manner
In an excellent, successful manner
In a moral or ethical manner, with righteousness
With approval, an expression of agreement or satisfaction
G2573.detail:
1. The word primarily describes an action carried out correctly, according to what is fitting: speaking rightly, responding appropriately (Mark 12:28: "knowing that Jesus had answered well to the Sadducees"), managing a household orderly (1 Timothy 3:4). It conveys the idea of doing things properly, according to rule or reason.

2. It can also emphasize the excellent quality of an act or result: building a house on the rock "well" so that it withstands (Luke 6:48). Here, it is less about correctness and more about the perfection or success of what is undertaken.

3. The word takes on a moral dimension when it comes to acting with righteousness: doing good to those who hate you (Matthew 5:44), leading with integrity (1 Timothy 5:17). Here, "good" expresses virtue, the right action in the eyes of God.

4. As an exclamation or reaction ("well!"), the word expresses approval and satisfaction: recognizing that one has spoken rightly, validating a true statement (Mark 12:32: "You have spoken well"). It is a positive judgment made about something heard or observed.
G2573.origine: The Greek word "good" (kalōs) comes from the adjective "beautiful" or "excellent" (kalos). This is why it carries the idea of order, harmony, what is seen and pleasing. In Hebrew, the original text often used the verb "to be good" (ṭōb) to express an action carried out correctly or successfully. The Greek "good" takes up this same nuance, enriching the meaning towards the idea of suitability and moral beauty.
G2573.emploi: This word appears 37 times in the New Testament. It is commonly used with action or speech verbs: speaking well, responding well, building well. The Gospels often place it in the mouth of Jesus or in questions that recognize his wisdom. The epistles use it to describe how to accomplish a task with excellence: leading a church, serving, praying. Sometimes, the meaning shifts towards "correctly" or "justly" (Acts 28:25: "the Holy Spirit spoke rightly"). Rarely, in an ironic context, "well" can mean "supposedly" or "so-called," as when Paul criticizes those who act as false apostles (2 Corinthians 11:4).
G2573.portee: For the believer, this word calls for quality and righteousness: doing things not just out of obligation, but with excellence and integrity. Whether speaking, acting, leading, or loving, biblical "good" is not limited to good intentions; it demands faithful execution and true morality. It is an invitation not to settle for the superficial, but to seek what honors God and builds up others.

sens: large desert animal, with one or two humps, capable of carrying burdens and enduring long periods without water
garment or fabric made from camel hair
the impossible or absurd in an exaggerated comparison
G2574.detail:
1. The camel is a well-known domesticated animal in the Middle East, renowned for its ability to traverse deserts and endure extreme conditions: John the Baptist wore its hair as clothing, a sign of an austere and Spartan life (Matthew 3:4).
2. Camel hair, coarse and brown, was used to weave rough garments: it was an ordinary fabric, worn by prophets and ascetics who renounced comfort (Mark 1:6).
3. In the mouth of Jesus, the camel becomes a symbol of the absurd or the impossible: passing through the eye of a needle is as ridiculous as a camel passing through that same eye, illustrating the impossibility for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God without renouncing their wealth (Matthew 19:24). Jesus also uses it to criticize those who make meticulous distinctions about minor details while committing major absurdities, like one who "strains out a gnat and swallows a camel" (Matthew 23:24).
G2574.origine: The Greek word κάμηλος (kamēlos) comes from the Hebrew גָּמַל (gamal), which designates the camel. It is a borrowing from Semitic, since the animal was unknown in classical Greece, and has no true Greek etymology. The camel was ubiquitous in the life of biblical Middle Eastern culture, hence the direct transition of the Hebrew word into the Greek vocabulary of the Bible.
G2574.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, exclusively in the first three Evangelists (Matthew, Mark, Luke). It first describes the real camel: John the Baptist wears a garment of camel's hair (Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6), a detail that underscores his prophetic and desert lifestyle. Then Jesus uses the camel in three parables or parallel moral teachings (Matthew 19:24, Mark 10:25, Luke 18:25): the camel passing through the eye of a needle symbolizes the impossible, making the image memorable and absurd to strike the minds. Finally, in Matthew 23:24, Jesus criticizes the hypocrisy of religious leaders who nitpick on insignificant matters (the gnat) while ignoring the essentials (the camel), a metaphor of inverted proportion.
G2574.portee: The camel teaches the reader two lessons. First, the example of John the Baptist invites simplicity and spiritual asceticism: material deprivation fosters listening to God. Second, Jesus' words about the camel and the needle remind us that attachment to wealth is a formidable obstacle to the Kingdom, not out of moralism, but because money diverts the heart from God. It is a call to break with the illusion of material power.

sens: Structure where intense heat is applied, for firing ceramics or melting metal
Place of extreme heat and suffering
Image of divine wrath and judgment
G2575.detail:
1. A furnace is primarily an oven, a place built to produce very high temperatures — it is used to fire bricks and pottery, and to melt metals. It is a place of intense and controlled fire. Revelation 1:15 evokes it when it describes the feet of the risen Christ "as if they had been burned in a furnace": the image is that of metal glowing in the fire.
2. In the New Testament, the word takes on a figurative sense: a furnace becomes a place of punishment and pain. Matthew 13:42 and 13:50 speak of casting the wicked "into the fiery furnace, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth" — it is the image of the final judgment, where destruction is total and suffering extreme.
3. By extension, the furnace represents divine wrath itself, the destructive power of God. Revelation 9:2 describes smoke rising "like the smoke of a great furnace" when the abyss opens: it is the symbol of cosmic judgment and the end of times.
G2575.origine: The Greek word κάμινος comes from a root that evokes the hearth and fire. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, we find כִּבְשָׁן (kibshan, "oven") and כּוּר (kur, "furnace"), particularly for potters' or metallurgists' furnaces. The Greek word retained this practical meaning before becoming an image of judgment in apocalyptic visions.
G2575.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in Matthew and John (Revelation). Matthew 13:42 and 50 use it in both parables of the harvest: at the end of times, the Son of Man will send his angels to gather from his kingdom all scandals and those who commit iniquity, and they will cast them into the fiery furnace. It is a stark image of the final judgment. In Revelation, the word takes on a more cosmic dimension: in 1:15, it describes the glory of the risen Christ, and in 9:2, it symbolizes the opening of the abyss and the judgment of the final times. Each time, the furnace embodies a reality of destruction and definitive separation.
G2575.portee: For the Christian, the furnace in Jesus' teaching is not an arbitrary threat, but the logical consequence of rejecting God. It reminds us that judgment is real and serious, and that there is an eternal difference between those who accept Christ and those who reject him. In Revelation, the image also reveals the power of the risen Christ: his judgment is as absolute as the fire of a furnace. It is a call to take Jesus' words seriously and to choose to belong to him.

sens: Physically close the eyelids
Refuse to see, to acknowledge a truth
Deliberately choose to remain blind to spiritual reality
G2576.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the physical action of closing the eyes, shutting the eyelids. It is the simple and concrete gesture of someone who closes their gaze.
2. However, in the Bible, "closing the eyes" primarily means refusing to see — not wanting to acknowledge what is nonetheless visible and true. In Matthew 13:15, the ears are hardened and the eyes are closed: it is the refusal to welcome the message of Jesus, even when it is heard.
3. This closing of the eyes is an act of will: it is choosing to remain blind rather than accept the spiritual reality and the conversion that God offers. In Acts 28:27, Paul uses this imagery when speaking of Israel: they do not want to see, hear, or understand with their hearts.
G2576.origine: The Greek word comes from an abbreviated form of "katamuō," which combines the idea of "closing" with that of "completely shutting." It translates the Hebrew "shagaʿ" (to blind, to obstruct) and "ʿatzam" (to close, to block). The verb belongs to the family of words that describe obstruction or closure. This imagery — closing the eyes — is borrowed from Isaiah 6:10 and 29:10, where it expresses God's judgment on a people who refuse to listen to His call.
G2576.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in parallel passages that quote or refer to Isaiah. In Matthew 13:15, Jesus uses it to explain why the crowds do not understand his parables: their hearts have become insensitive, they have hardened their ears, they have closed their eyes — it is a spiritual refusal, not a physical inability. In Acts 28:27, Paul addresses the same words to the Jews in Rome, showing that this same refusal to see and hear the word of God continues through generations. The verb thus expresses a voluntary act of rejection: one chooses to close their eyes rather than be challenged.
G2576.portee: This word reminds the reader that spiritual blindness is never an accident: it is always a choice. Closing the eyes means deliberately refusing to see the truth that God reveals. For the Christian, it is a warning: do not become like those crowds who intentionally closed their eyes to Jesus. It is also an invitation to vigilance: remain open to what God wants to show us, rather than locking ourselves in our prejudices and unbelief.

sens: to accomplish a task, an action
to become tired, exhausted from prolonged effort
to lose courage, to give up in the face of difficulty
to be sick, weakened
G2577G.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the Greek word κάμνω is that of physical work: to accomplish a task, to labor. It is the image of one who acts, who is active.
2. From this sustained work naturally arises fatigue: κάμνω then means "to be weary," to be tired, exhausted from continuous effort. This is what Hebrews 12:3 describes, where Paul exhorts Christians to consider Jesus "so that you do not grow weary and lose heart" — physical fatigue here becomes spiritual and moral fatigue.
3. The word can also express the abandonment of courage, the state of one who, exhausted, ceases to persevere. In Revelation 2:3, Jesus praises the church of Ephesus: "you have not grown weary" — it has not ceased to endure and resist despite trials.
4. In some ancient texts (cited in the definition), κάμνω can mean "to be sick," the physical weakening of the body. This is a natural extension: one who works too much becomes tired, and one who is tired becomes sick.
G2577G.origine: The word κάμνω comes from an Indo-European root that evokes work and effort. In ancient Greek, it retains this connotation of fatigue linked to prolonged action. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it notably translates the Hebrew קוּט (qût), which expresses weariness and disgust. The family of the word includes other Greek terms related to fatigue and suffering.
G2577G.emploi: The verb κάμνω appears 2 times in the New Testament according to the provided usages. In Hebrews 12:3, Paul uses it to encourage persecuted Christians not to be disheartened by contemplating Jesus who endured opposition from sinners: "do not grow weary" is an exhortation to persevere despite spiritual fatigue. In Revelation 2:3, Jesus commends the church of Ephesus because it "has not grown weary" — it has maintained its vigilance and faithful work. In both cases, the context is that of Christian perseverance under pressure: it is not mere physical fatigue, but the trial of courage and faith.
G2577G.portee: This word speaks to every believer confronted with spiritual exhaustion. It recognizes that the Christian life requires sustained effort and that fatigue is a reality one can experience. But it calls us not to "grow weary" by keeping our eyes fixed on Jesus and seeking in Him the strength to persevere. It is a word of encouragement for those who feel at the end of their strength in their walk of faith.

sens: to work tirelessly
to be exhausted from fatigue
to suffer from a bodily illness
G2577H.detail: 1. The word first evokes the action of working hard and long. 2. From this fatigue of prolonged work arises exhaustion: to be weary, unable to continue, spiritually downcast — as when one must persevere in effort despite fatigue (Hebrews 12:3 says not to "grow weary" by contemplating Jesus). 3. Bodily illness is the most concrete meaning: James 5:15 speaks of "the one who is sick" in the community, the one called to be healed through the prayer of faith.
G2577H.origine: The Greek word κάμνω comes from a root that means "to toil, to sweat." It is found in Greek words related to fatigue and effort. The Greek Old Testament uses it to translate the Hebrew קוּט (to be weary): what burdens the body also burdens the soul. The original meaning is physical — work that exhausts — but it extends to the moral and the bodily.
G2577H.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament in common French: James 5:15, where it refers to the sick person in the community to whom the elders come to lay hands and offer a prayer of faith. But the broader Greek context (in the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament) shows a range of meanings: from work that tires to the exhaustion of the heart to illness. In James, it clearly refers to physical illness — not just a feeling of fatigue, but an infirmity that justifies the intervention of the elders and collective prayer.
G2577H.portee: This word invites us not to hesitate to seek the help of the Church when illness overwhelms us. It reminds us that bodily weakness is not a shame and that communal prayer has the power to heal. It also links illness to forgiveness: prayer opens the door to both physical restoration and reconciliation with God.

sens: to bend, to fold (a member of the body)
to bow, to kneel (before someone)
to submit, to acknowledge someone's authority
G2578.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of physically bending or folding a part of the body, especially the knee. It is a visible and describable gesture (Ephesians 3:14: Paul says 'I bow my knees', a concrete image of his posture in prayer).

2. To bend the knee also means to bow or prostrate oneself before someone, as a sign of respect or honor. Romans 11:4 recounts that some Israelites 'did not bow the knee to Baal': refusing to bend the knee means refusing to submit or pay homage to a deity or authority.

3. By extension, bending the knee signifies submitting, acknowledging someone's authority or lordship. Philippians 2:10 proclaims that 'every knee shall bow at the name of Jesus': all beings, in heaven and on earth, will acknowledge the kingship and divine power of Christ.
G2578.origine: The verb κάμπτω (kamptō) comes from a Greek root that evokes the notion of bending or folding. It often translates the Hebrew כָּרַע (kāraʿ), which also means 'to bend the knee' or 'to kneel'. This vocabulary pertains to gestures of honor or submission in the ancient world: bending the knee is the attitude of the servant, the supplicant, or one who pays homage.
G2578.emploi: The verb κάμπτω appears four times in the New Testament, always with an important religious or theological meaning. It is first used to speak of the refusal to bend the knee before a false deity (Romans 11:4: the seven thousand who did not bow before Baal). Then, it describes the attitude of prayer or intercession (Ephesians 3:14: Paul bows his knees in prayer to the Father). Finally, it announces universal submission to Christ: Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:10 cite or echo a prophecy that every knee shall bow before the Lord. In all cases, the physical gesture (bending the knee) represents a spiritual reality (submission or honor).
G2578.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that bending the knee is not primarily an act of humiliation, but an act of honor and recognition towards God. Paul's prayer (Ephesians 3:14) shows that kneeling before God is a privilege and a strength, not a weakness. The prophetic passages (Romans 14:11; Philippians 2:10) remind us that every knee, willingly or ultimately, will acknowledge the lordship of Jesus Christ: it is an affirmation of Christ's victory and kingship.

sens: a town in Galilee where Jesus performed his first miracle
the place where Jesus turned water into wine
the location where Nathanael lived
G2580.detail: 1. Cana is a small town in Galilee, in Jewish territory in northern Palestine. It is the place where Jesus performed his first public miracle: turning water into wine at a wedding (John 2:1-11). 2. This first miracle, referred to as a 'sign' by John, manifests the glory of Jesus and strengthens the faith of his disciples (John 2:11). It is a foundational event in the Gospel of John. 3. Jesus later returned there to heal the son of a royal official from Capernaum, and this second miracle shows that Jesus was expected in this place (John 4:46). 4. Nathanael, one of the twelve apostles, was from Cana in Galilee, indicating that Jesus had already made himself known in this region before officially calling his disciples (John 21:2).
G2580.origine: The name 'Cana' appears exclusively in the Gospel of John, nowhere else in the New Testament. The town actually exists in Galilee, although its exact location has been debated over time by historians and archaeologists. The meaning of the underlying Hebrew or Aramaic name is not clearly established in ancient sources.
G2580.emploi: Cana is mentioned only four times in the Gospel of John: John 2:1 and 2:11 report the miracle of water turned into wine at the wedding, which is presented as Jesus' first miracle and the starting point of the revelation of his glory. In John 4:46, Jesus returns there to heal the son of the royal official, an event that demonstrates his power operating at a distance. In John 21:2, Nathanael is identified as being from Cana, making him the native disciple of this locality. These mentions grouped in John show that this small town played an important symbolic role in Jesus' Galilean ministry.
G2580.portee: For the reader of John, Cana represents the place where the hidden glory of Jesus first burst forth: it is where his disciples discovered who he truly was. This name reminds us that the revelation of Jesus did not begin in Jerusalem or in the great religious centers, but in a small village in Galilee, among ordinary people. It invites Christians to recognize that God often acts in humble places and reveals himself to those who have eyes to see.

sens: A disciple of Jesus nicknamed thus, likely because of his zeal or religious convictions
G2581.detail: 1. Simon the Cananite was one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus. The nickname 'Cananite' comes from a Hebrew word meaning 'zealous' or 'passionate' — it likely designated a man of great religious fervor, perhaps once associated with the Zealots, those Jews who refused to bow before the Roman occupier. Matthew 10:4 and Mark 3:18 name him when listing the twelve apostles.
G2581.origine: The Greek word 'Cananite' comes from the Hebrew 'qana'a', which literally means 'zealous' or 'ardent'. It does not refer to the ancient region of Canaan, but rather expresses a character trait: passion, fervor, zeal for God and the Law. In Greek, this nickname is rendered both as 'Cananite' and by the word 'Zealot' (ζηλωτής), which conveys the same idea.
G2581.emploi: Simon the Cananite appears twice in the Gospels, each time in the list of the twelve apostles. Both Matthew and Mark mention him, with slight variations in naming the group. He never intervenes in a specific narrative — we do not know his words or specific actions — but his presence among this small number of men chosen by Jesus testifies that Christ called to himself disciples of very diverse temperaments and passions.
G2581.portee: The presence of Simon the Cananite among the twelve shows that Jesus did not reject men of conviction and zeal, even those whom the religious and political system of the time might divide. It is a lesson of grace: the Lord calls and transforms human passions to turn them towards his kingdom, uniting around him men of different backgrounds and characters.

sens: Title of the queen of Ethiopia
G2582.detail: Candace is the honorific title held by the queens who reign over Ethiopia, in the ancient region of Nubia. It is somewhat like 'Pharaoh' for Egypt or 'Caesar' for Rome: this title designates the sovereign herself and her authority. In Acts 8:27, the apostle Philip encounters a high-ranking Ethiopian official who administered 'all the treasures' under Candace, showing that this queen was a powerful sovereign with an organized court.
G2582.origine: The name 'Candace' comes from the Ethiopian royal title that was held by several successive queens of Nubia and Ethiopia (ancient Upper Egypt). It was not a personal name but a royal dignity, like the title 'Cleopatra' in Egypt. Ancient Greek and Roman historians mention several Candaces; the one referred to in Acts 8 likely reigned in the first century.
G2582.emploi: Candace appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 8:27. Luke mentions her to socially situate the character of the Ethiopian minister: he is not a mere servant, but a high-ranking man in the service of a great power. This historical mention anchors the narrative in the geopolitical reality of the ancient world and shows that the Gospel extends to the distant powers of the southern known world.
G2582.portee: The mention of Candace reminds early Christian readers that the Gospel reached not only the Jewish people and the Greco-Roman centers but also the great distant royal courts. This Ethiopian eunuch who came to worship in Jerusalem and was converted by Philip illustrates how Jesus draws believers to himself from all peoples and social ranks, fulfilling the promise that the Gospel would be proclaimed to all nations.

sens: A rigid rod or bar, especially a measuring stick made of wood or metal
An instrument for measuring or drawing straight lines
A guiding principle, a standard to follow
A fixed limit, a domain or jurisdiction assigned to someone
G2583.detail:
1. Originally, the word refers to a concrete physical object: a rod, a bar, a measuring rule used to draw lines or check alignment. This is the primary image of the Greek word, inherited from the word for "reed."

2. By natural extension, it is the instrument that measures and delineates. From this comes the abstract idea of measure and standard: one evaluates according to a rule.

3. The most common figurative meaning in the New Testament: a "rule" in a moral or spiritual sense, a principle to which one must obey. In Galatians 6:16, Paul speaks of "following this rule" — it should be understood as living according to this principle, this established order.

4. By metaphor of the limits drawn by a rule, the word also designates a delineated area, a portion of territory or responsibility entrusted to someone. This is the meaning in 2 Corinthians 10:13-16: God has "assigned" to Paul "limits," that is, a field of action, a sphere where he can exercise his apostleship. The apostle must not boast beyond what is assigned to him.
G2583.origine: The Greek word κανών comes from the name of a plant: the cane or reed (Hebrew קָנֶה). The straight and flexible cane is its image: it is primarily an object that can be used for measuring or as a structural rod. From there, the word gradually rises from the concrete (the physical rod) to the abstract (the measure, the norm, the limit). It is a beautiful path of thought: from the real that we see to the law that we understand.
G2583.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament. Three times in 2 Corinthians 10:13-16, where Paul uses it in the sense of "limit" or "assigned domain": God has marked out a framework for him, a jurisdiction, and the apostle respects these boundaries so as not to unduly claim the work of others. Once in Galatians 6:16, where it means "rule" in the normative sense: "Peace be upon those who follow this rule" — those who conform to the stated principle. Once in Philippians 3:16 (not detailed here). Throughout these uses, the word always retains the idea of a limit, a measure, or an established order that one must not escape.
G2583.portee: This word teaches the believer two essential things. First, that God assigns each person a specific domain of service — a "share" — and that wisdom consists in remaining faithful to it rather than encroaching on the work of others. It is a lesson in humility and respect for each person's functions. Secondly, that there exists a "rule" — a moral and spiritual standard — to obey for peace and mercy. Accepting one's limits and following God's rule is to live in order and wisdom.

sens: City in Galilee, by the Sea of Galilee
Main center of Jesus' ministry in Galilee
Place of miracles and teachings of Jesus
Symbol of the rejection of divine grace
G2584.detail:
1. Capernaum is a city located near the Sea of Galilee, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matthew 4:13). It is a strategic port at the crossroads of trade routes, allowing for a life of fishing and commerce.

2. Jesus established the center of his public activity there after leaving Nazareth (Matthew 4:13). He spent a lot of time there, taught in the synagogue (Mark 1:21, Luke 4:31), and resided at Peter's house (Mark 2:1 implicit, John 2:12).

3. It is in Capernaum that Jesus performed several memorable miracles: the healing of the centurion's servant (Matthew 8:5), the healing of Peter's mother-in-law, and other signs (Luke 4:38 implicit). The city was a direct witness to divine power.

4. Despite these miracles and intensive teaching, Jesus prophesies that Capernaum will be "brought down to Hades" (Matthew 11:23, Luke 10:15) because its population rejected his grace and message, while even Sodom would have repented upon seeing these signs.
G2584.origine: The Hebrew name means "village of Nahum" ("Kéfar Nahum"). "Kéfar" means village; "Nahum" is a personal name or can mean "consolation." The Greeks transliterated this Hebrew name as "Kapernaum." It is an example of how Palestinian geographical names retained their original Semitic form in the Greek New Testament.
G2584.emploi: Capernaum appears 16 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the four Gospels (Matthew 4 times, Mark 4 times, Luke 4 times, John 4 times). It is not mentioned elsewhere in the New Testament, as it is specifically linked to the earthly life of Jesus and his Galilean ministry. The usages reveal its growing importance: first as the place where Jesus comes to dwell (Matthew 4:13), then as the seat of his regular teaching and miracles, and finally as the city from which Jesus pronounces judgment for its unbelief. It is in Capernaum that the vital activity of the Gospels concentrates during the Galilean period.
G2584.portee: Capernaum teaches the Christian a serious spiritual truth: proximity to Jesus and his wonderful works does not automatically ensure faith or salvation. The rejection of divine grace, even in the face of supernatural evidence, leads to terrible judgment. It is a call not to neglect or despise the revelation of Jesus that one has witnessed, but to respond with trust and obedience.

sens: To alter or distort something by mixing it with an inferior substance or corrupting it
To misrepresent or distort a message or word by presenting it dishonestly
G2585.detail: 1. The word first evokes the image of the dishonest merchant who mixes his goods with lower quality products to profit (like a wine seller who adds water): this is to falsify in the material sense, to alter for greater gain. 2. In a figurative sense, it designates one who distorts or misrepresents a message, particularly the word of God, by presenting it in a deceptive or self-serving manner: "For we do not falsify the word of God, as many do" (2 Corinthians 2:17), where Paul asserts that he proclaims the Gospel with sincerity, without corrupting it to please or gain personal advantage.
G2585.origine: The word comes from the Greek κάπηλος (kápēlos), which designates a small merchant, a reseller, or a peddler — often of bad reputation, as he was known for his dishonest practices. The verb κατηλεύω thus expresses the characteristic activity of these merchants: to traffic, to alter goods to increase profit. This dishonest commercial image has extended to moral and spiritual senses: to corrupt, to falsify, to distort.
G2585.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 2:17, where Paul defends his apostolic ministry against the accusation of preaching the Gospel in a self-serving or dishonest manner. Paul declares: "We do not falsify the word of God, as many do." He thus opposes those who, out of love for profit or desire to please, distorted the Christian message. The use of the word reveals that, from the early days of the Church, some were making a profit from faith by corrupting the Gospel for carnal motives.
G2585.portee: This word challenges the Christian regarding spiritual integrity and the authenticity of testimony. Paul lays the foundation for all faithful ministry: do not falsify the word of God, transmit it with sincerity rather than distorting it for personal gain. It is a call to moral uprightness and transparency in the life of faith, which resonates for every believer tasked with conveying the evangelical truth.

sens: Visible vapor that rises from a fire or combustion
Veil that obscures the air or vision
Image of the presence of God and His majesty
Sign of God's judgment on the world
Symbol of what rises to heaven
G2586.detail:
1. Smoke is primarily the vapor that rises from a fire. In Revelation 9:2-3, smoke rises from the abyss like that of a great furnace, obscuring the sun and the air. It is a concrete, visible, tangible image.

2. This smoke can veil light and obscure space: it fills the air and makes the atmosphere impenetrable, as when it rises from the abyss and obscures the sun (Revelation 9:2). It creates a veil between the visible and what is hidden.

3. Smoke rises to God with the prayers of the saints, carried by the angel: it becomes the symbol of what ascends to heaven, of worship and supplication that rise to God (Revelation 8:4). It is a poetic and spiritual image.

4. In the visions of judgment in Revelation, smoke accompanies the plagues: it comes out of the mouths of the war horses with fire and sulfur, killing a third of mankind (Revelation 9:17-18). It becomes the visible sign of divine judgment on the earth.

5. The smoke that rises eternally from destroyed Babylon (Revelation 19:3) symbolizes total and permanent ruin, annihilation that will never cease.
G2586.origine: The Greek word kapnos comes from the verb meaning to burn or smoke. In ancient Hebrew, the equivalent word (assân) designates the same reality: the vapor that rises from combustion. The word evokes a very concrete sensory image: what one sees when something burns. Smoke is what rises, what naturally ascends from fire to above.
G2586.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Revelation (9 times) and once in Acts. John uses it to describe the visual phenomena of eschatological visions: the smoke of worship rising to heaven (Revelation 8:4), the smoke of the abyss obscuring the earth (Revelation 9:2-3), the smoke coming from the fearsome horses (Revelation 9:17-18), and the smoke of ruined Babylon rising forever (Revelation 14:11, 15:8, 18:9, 18:18, 19:3). In Acts 2:19, Peter cites a prophecy from Isaiah announcing smoke as a sign of final judgment. It is a key word in apocalyptic imagery: smoke makes visible what is invisible, it manifests the divine and the terrible.
G2586.portee: For the Christian reader, smoke in Revelation reveals two realities. On one hand, it is the presence of God that cannot be seen directly: the smoke that rises with the prayers of the saints shows that our intercessions do not go unheard; they rise before God and heaven receives them. On the other hand, the smoke of final judgment is the visible sign that God does not leave evil and idolatry unpunished: destruction is real and irreversible. This invites trust in God and moral vigilance.

sens: Mountainous province of Asia Minor, corresponding to the central region of present-day Turkey
G2587.detail: Cappadocia is a historical region located in the central-southern part of Asia Minor. It is mentioned twice in the New Testament, both times in connection with the early Christians who were dispersed. At Pentecost, Peter addresses his message to "Parthians, Medes, Elamites" and to those who dwell in various regions, including Cappadocia (Acts 2:9), showing that the Gospel reaches even the faithful from these distant lands. Peter also writes to those who are "scattered" in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, and Asia (1 Peter 1:1), meaning the Christian churches spread across these provinces.
G2587.origine: The Greek name Καππαδοκία (Kappadokia) is the Greek adaptation of an ancient Persian or Anatolian name. The region was known in antiquity for its renowned breed of horses and mineral resources. It is part of what is called Asia Minor, a territory that encompasses modern-day Turkey.
G2587.emploi: Cappadocia appears twice in the New Testament. Acts 2:9 mentions it among the regions from which pilgrims came to Jerusalem during Pentecost, highlighting the geographical extent of the audience that hears Peter's message. In 1 Peter 1:1, it is one of the five provinces of Asia Minor where the recipients of the letter—dispersed Christians—are established. These two contexts show the importance of Cappadocia as a region housing an ancient Christian community.
G2587.portee: The mention of Cappadocia reminds readers that the Gospel quickly reached distant territories, far beyond Jerusalem. It illustrates how the early Christians, scattered far from their homeland, formed vibrant churches to which the apostle Peter personally addresses his exhortations.

sens: The physical organ that beats in the chest and sustains the life of the body.
The seat of thoughts, feelings, and intentions that are not visible from the outside.
The center of desires and passions — what one loves, what attracts us.
The home of moral and religious conscience — what determines if someone is righteous or guilty before God.
The deep center of a person, what truly defines their character.
The most intimate part of a thing (figuratively: the heart of the earth).
G2588.detail:
1. The word "heart" primarily refers to the organ of the body that beats and gives life. The Bible treats it this way when it speaks of physical life (Acts 14:17: "He has filled our hearts with joy").
2. But much more often, the heart is the seat of hidden thoughts that only God knows. When Jesus says that one cannot deceive Him, it is because He "knows the thoughts" of the heart (Matthew 9:4).
3. It is also where passions live: love, fear, joy, sadness. John 14:27 ("Let not your heart be troubled") shows the heart agitated by emotions.
4. The heart is especially, in the Bible, the place where moral decisions are born: what we do comes from the heart (Matthew 15:19: "For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks"). It is where our relationship with God is played out. Being pure in heart (Matthew 5:8) or having an unrepentant heart (Romans 2:5): everything depends on the heart.
5. The heart can be hardened — closed to God and deaf to His voice (Hebrews 3:10: "a heart that goes astray").
6. The expression "in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40) refers to the center, the deepest part.
G2588.origine: The Greek word kardia comes from a very ancient root designating the heart organ. In biblical Hebrew, the corresponding word is lèb or lèbab, which also means "heart." Both refer to the same reality: not only the physical organ but especially the inner seat of personal life, thoughts, and moral conscience. In both Greek and Hebrew, the heart is the center of all that makes a person — it is to the person what the source is to the stream.
G2588.emploi: The word "heart" appears 153 times in the New Testament and is used in almost all books. It is one of the key words of the Christian faith. In the Gospels, especially Luke and Mark, it expresses the interiority of spiritual life: what we think, believe, and truly want, hidden from view but transparent to God. In Paul, it emphasizes that true faith arises in the heart, not in words (Romans 2:5 contrasts the unrepentant heart with true repentance). The word thus encompasses both the seat of intellect (thinking), emotion (feeling), and will (wanting), but it especially emphasizes moral and spiritual depth: a pure heart, a sincere heart, a hardened heart.
G2588.portee: For the Christian, the heart is the issue of everything. Jesus teaches that what comes out of the heart defiles a person (Matthew 15:19), and that whoever wants to follow Him must love Him with all their heart (Matthew 22:37). This means that one cannot deceive God by playing appearances: He reads the heart. That is why faith begins in the heart — by receiving the word of God there, by allowing the Spirit to transform our desires and thoughts. To have a pure heart is to be in truth before God.

sens: The one who sees into the hearts of men, who knows their thoughts and secrets
The one who judges justly because he sees the hidden truth of the heart
G2589.detail:
1. The word designates one who possesses complete and direct knowledge of the human heart — not just surface feelings, but secret thoughts, true intentions, everything that lies deep within us. It is a powerful image: when Peter and the apostles pray in Acts 1:24, they address God as the only one who "knows the hearts of all" to ask for His help in choosing Judas' replacement. Only God sees what no one else can see.
2. This knowledge of the heart establishes a just and true judgment. In Acts 15:8, when the Bible says that "God, who knows the hearts, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit," it affirms that God judged the believers not on appearances, but on the reality of their faith. It is a term that reminds us that God is never deceived and sees beyond what we show.
G2589.origine: The Greek word combines two roots: "heart" (kardia) and "the one who knows" (gnōstēs). Together, they form "the one who knows the heart." In the Old Testament, this idea is expressed in Hebrew with phrases like "God who searches the hearts and the reins" (Jeremiah 11:20; 20:12 in Greek: "the one who knows hearts"). The heart in the Bible is not just the seat of emotions, but the hidden center of thought, will, and intention.
G2589.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, in both passages from the Acts of the Apostles. In both cases, it designates God Himself as the only one who truly knows the heart. In Acts 1:24, the apostles invoke Him to ask God to guide them in an important choice. In Acts 15:8, during the Jerusalem council, it is God who bears witness to the converted Gentiles by giving them the Holy Spirit, because He knows their hearts — He has seen their authentic faith, beyond any external question.
G2589.portee: This title reminds us that God sees in us with total transparency: no secret of the heart escapes Him, no hidden intention deceives Him. It is a call to honesty before God in prayer, and a source of peace: the one who truly judges us is never unjust, for He sees the truth. It also invites the Christian to cultivate integrity — since our heart is open to God, let us ask Him to purify it rather than pretending.

sens: What a tree or plant produces: apple, grape, grain, etc.
The harvest that one gathers from a field or vineyard
Figuratively: the result, the effect of something
The acts and works that show a person's character
The moral and spiritual qualities that arise from a new life
The benefit or profit derived from something
G2590.detail:
1. What a tree or plant produces: apple, grape, grain, etc. — The fruit is what the earth causes to grow and mature. Jesus speaks of the fruits of trees (a good tree produces good fruit, Matthew 7:17), and there are fruits of the vines that are harvested at the time of harvest (Mark 12:2).

2. The harvest that one gathers from a field or vineyard — It is the totality of what can be picked and harvested. When the grain has grown and "produced fruit," it was ripe for the harvest (Matthew 13:26). The vinedresser looks for fruit on the fig tree year after year (Luke 13:7).

3. Figuratively: the result, the effect of something — Just as fruit naturally grows from the tree, our acts naturally arise from who we are. Jesus asks people to "produce fruit worthy of repentance" (Matthew 3:8): to show that we have truly changed.

4. The acts and works that show a person's character — "You will recognize them by their fruits" (Matthew 7:20): what we do reveals who we are. A righteous life bears the fruit of righteousness (Philippians 1:11).

5. The moral and spiritual qualities that arise from a new life — The Holy Spirit produces in us love, joy, peace (Galatians 5:22). Those who believe in Jesus are called to bear spiritual fruit (John 15:16).

6. The benefit or profit derived from something — Work brings fruit, a reward (Philippians 1:22). What one sows, one will reap: the one who sows good will reap fruit (Romans 6:22).
G2590.origine: The word κάρπος comes from an Indo-European root related to the idea of "gathering" or "growing." In Hebrew, the corresponding word is פְּרִי (péri), which refers to both natural fruit and, figuratively, the result of an action or word. The Bible uses the image of fruit to speak of what comes naturally from us: just as a tree can only produce according to its nature (good or bad), a person produces acts that reflect their heart. It is a deeply Hebraic image: the quality of a thing is recognized by its fruit.
G2590.emploi: The word "fruit" appears about 56 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Paul's epistles. It primarily refers literally to the fruit of trees and vines (Matthew 21:34, Luke 13:7, Mark 12:2). But Jesus often uses it figuratively to speak of what we produce: our works, our words, our lives. The harvesters awaited fruit from the vineyard (Mark 12:2), and Jesus reproaches the fig tree for not bearing any (Luke 13:7). The moral sense dominates in Paul: the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), the fruit of righteousness (Philippians 1:11), the fruit of light (Ephesians 5:9). Everywhere, the image remains this: fruit comes from what is alive, it shows the true nature of the one who bears it, and it is meant to be harvested, shared, or presented.
G2590.portee: This word teaches the believer that their life must produce visible and lasting fruit. Jesus does not judge us on our intentions or words, but on our concrete actions — "you will recognize them by their fruits." For the believer, the fruit is not primarily the result of personal effort: it is the work of the Holy Spirit acting in us, just as sap flows in a branch (John 15:4-5). This gives freedom: it is not up to me to "manufacture" spiritual fruit, but to remain attached to Jesus so that the fruit comes naturally. And this fruit, according to Paul, is primarily moral and relational: love, patience, faithfulness, righteousness — qualities that benefit others and glorify God.

sens: Christian friend with whom the apostle Paul left belongings in Troas
G2591.detail: Carpus is a Christian from Troas (a city on the Aegean coast) who welcomed the apostle Paul. At the time Paul writes his second letter to Timothy from his prison in Rome, shortly before his execution, he asks Timothy to come to see him and to bring the cloak and the books he had to leave with Carpus during his previous visit. This was a mark of trust and Christian hospitality: Carpus carefully kept Paul's belongings, including precious scrolls that Paul deemed important to have with him.
G2591.origine: The name Κάρπος (Karpos) is of Greek origin. In Greek, "karpos" literally means "fruit," but it became a common personal name. Nothing in the biblical text tells us where Carpus got this name or what his exact origins were.
G2591.emploi: Carpus appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Timothy 4:13. He was evidently a member of the Christian community in Troas, someone trustworthy with whom Paul had stayed and left his personal belongings and books (notably scrolls, probably excerpts from Scripture). This passage shows the importance of the bonds of hospitality and sharing of resources in the early churches.

sens: To produce fruit, crops (in a physical sense).
To have success, effectiveness in one's actions.
To produce works or spiritual results (in a figurative sense).
To give birth to spiritual or moral fruits through faith and obedience.
G2592.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the concrete action of a plant or land that produces fruit: in Mark 4:28, the earth "produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear" — this is the natural cycle of the harvest.

2. In Jesus' parables, this physical sense becomes the image of a word sown that takes root and produces a harvest: in Matthew 13:23 and Mark 4:20, the one who receives the word "bears fruit, thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold," which means that the word has transformed their heart and changed their life.

3. In the spiritual and moral sense, the word denotes the Christian life that produces visible results. In Romans 7:4, Paul says that believers must "bear fruit for God" after being freed from sin — that is, to lead a holy life and act justly.

4. The verb can also evoke the act of "producing" what is bad: in Romans 7:5, without Christ, we "bore fruit for death," meaning that our actions distanced us from God and led to spiritual death.
G2592.origine: The Greek word is composed of "karpos" (fruit) and "pherō" (to bear, to produce). It literally describes the action of bearing or producing fruit, like a fruit tree. The image comes from Mediterranean agriculture: a plant that "bears fruit" is fertile, alive, and useful. The verb naturally applies to the results of anything that is sown — including a word or a life — while maintaining this notion of growth and harvest.
G2592.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Paul. In the first three Gospels, it is central to the parables of the sower (Matthew 13:23, Mark 4:20 and 4:28, Luke 8:15): Jesus uses it to show that the word of God, when well received, inevitably produces transformative results. In Paul (Romans 7:4-5, Colossians 1:6 and 1:10), the verb extends to the ethical and spiritual life of the believer: one "bears fruit" when growing in holiness, in knowledge of God, and in good works. The meaning varies slightly depending on the context — sometimes the emphasis is on abundance and multiplication, sometimes on the quality of the result and its relevance (fruit for God or fruit for death).
G2592.portee: This word teaches the Christian that faith in God is never barren: it naturally bears fruit, like a seed sown in good soil. It reminds us that our spiritual life must be visible in our actions, our relationships, and our moral transformation. It is also an invitation to examine whether our heart is truly "good soil" — that is, honest, receptive, and faithful to the word of God — and to persevere so that this fruit multiplies.

sens: Producing fruit, abundant harvests
Bringing prosperity and material well-being
Fecund, rich in resources and blessings
G2593.detail:
1. The word first describes what naturally bears fruit: a land, a fertile season produces crops and food in abundance. In Acts 14:17, Paul speaks of the "fertile seasons" that God gives from heaven, with the necessary rains for the harvest — this is the concrete gift of prosperous nature.
2. By extension, fertile designates anything that brings abundance and well-being: generous food, hearts filled with joy. Paul uses it to show how God, through nature itself, testifies to His goodness towards all peoples.
3. The word also evokes spiritual fertility: a blessing that fills and enriches. God fills hearts with joy through this visible fertility, showing His inexhaustible generosity.
G2593.origine: The Greek word is composed of "karpos" (fruit) and "phero" (to bear, to bring): literally "that bears fruit." It is the image of the fruitful plant that generously gives its harvest. The Hebrew "peri" (fruit) and "zera" (seed) convey this same idea of beneficial productivity: what comes from the earth to nourish.
G2593.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament (Acts 14:17). Paul uses it in his speech to the Lycaonians to show that God reveals Himself through His visible blessings: rain, prosperous seasons, abundant food. It is a proof addressed to those who do not yet know the Word, so that they may recognize the goodness of the Creator through nature itself. The context is one of "natural theology": God speaks to all men through fertile creation.
G2593.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that God never abandons His creatures: He sends rain and harvest, He fills hearts with joy. It is a call to gratitude towards divine Providence, visible in the cycles of nature. By seeing the fertile land, we see the generous hand of the Creator who wants to give us what sustains us and brings us joy.

sens: To remain unshaken in the face of a threat or difficulty
To hold on with patience and constancy
To show resolution and courage
G2594.detail:
