1. To be firm means to remain unshaken, not to bend under pressure or fear. It is to stand in the face of an external threat without wavering. In Hebrews 11:27, Moses "was firm" in the face of Pharaoh's anger: he did not give in to fear but maintained his determination.
2. The word also expresses a patient constancy, a capacity to persevere over time without giving up. It is not about brute strength, but a quiet and lasting firmness, that of someone who holds on despite trials.
3. It is a form of inner courage that arises from conviction: Moses was able to remain firm because he saw "him who is invisible," that is, because his faith in God gave him a strength that nothing could shake.
G2594.origine: The verb καρτερέω comes from a root that evokes strength and solidity. In Hebrew, it is related to חָזַק (hazaq), "to be strong, to be strengthened." The Greek word carries within it the idea of a firmness that holds on, of a patient resistance in the face of shocks. It is a less common verb than its compound relatives (like προσκαρτερέω, "to persevere"), but it shares the same essence.
G2594.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Hebrews 11:27, in the passage dedicated to Moses' faith. The author seeks to show how Moses was able to stand firm in the face of a superhuman authority — that of Pharaoh in all his power — without being paralyzed by fear. It is an illustration of faith in action: not a mere abstract belief, but a concrete firmness that changes behavior and gives courage to the heart.
G2594.portee: For the Christian reader, this word speaks of the possibility of remaining firm in faith even in the face of the powers of the world. Just as Moses was able to see beyond the visible threat (the king's anger) by contemplating the invisible (God), the believer can draw from their relationship with God an unshakeable strength. It is an invitation not to be intimidated by external obstacles, but to keep one's eyes fixed on God.

sens: small piece of dry wood, twig
dust, imperceptible grain
minor flaw, small fault
G2595.detail: 1. The word refers to a small piece of dried wood, a fine twig — something dry and brittle that is barely noticeable. This is why Jesus contrasts it with the beam, which is much more massive: in Matthew 7:3, you see the "straw" in your brother's eye. 2. More broadly, it is dust, a particle so tiny that it flies away or is barely visible — hence the image of something imperceptible and insignificant. 3. Figuratively, straw represents a slight defect, a minor fault, or a benign imperfection. Jesus uses it to illustrate the folly of the moralist who corrects others for their small faults while ignoring their own serious sins: "Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the straw from your brother's eye" (Matthew 7:5).
G2595.origine: The Greek word κάρφος comes from a root evoking something dry, brittle, stripped. In Genesis 8:11 (in the ancient Greek translation), the same word translates the Hebrew טָרַף (taroph), which means a new branch, a torn-off twig — the image of something light, fragile, that can be easily picked or carried away. It is a simple and concrete word, very common in spoken language to refer to small woody debris.
G2595.emploi: The word κάρφος appears 5 times in the New Testament, all in the same context: Jesus' teaching on judging others in Matthew 7:3-5 and its parallel in Luke 6:41-42. Jesus repeats the image three times to drive the point home: you see the straw in your brother's eye, you want to remove it, but you do not notice the beam in your own. The opposition between straw and beam (δοκός) structures the entire parable: the straw is the small defect, the beam is the serious sin. The word is not used anywhere else in Scripture; it is specifically chosen for its striking imagery of the trivial and the negligible.
G2595.portee: This image teaches humility and self-examination: before correcting others, the Christian must first recognize their own weaknesses, often much more serious than they believe. The straw versus the beam reminds us that a hasty judgment of others reveals a blindness to our own sins. It is an invitation to mercy and personal clarity: correct your brother only if you have first worked on yourself.

sens: in the direction of, towards
across, throughout
against, in opposition to
according to, in accordance with
in relation to, concerning
as, by distribution
G2596.detail:
1. Spatial direction: the word indicates movement towards a direction, a crossing. "They departed, and went from village to village" (Luke 9:6): the idea is to pass through successive villages.
2. Progression or passage: movement that crosses, traverses an area. "In a dream" (Matthew 1:20): the angel appears in the space of the dream, which becomes the place of the vision.
3. Hostile opposition: placement against someone or something, like a fight. "I opposed him to his face" (Galatians 2:11): Cephas and Paul are face to face, in disagreement.
4. Conformity with a rule or model: what is in agreement, following a given measure. "According to the flesh" (Romans 8:12): this is acting according to the principle, the carnal logic.
5. Relation or reference to something: perspective under which a subject is considered. "According to his will": we appreciate something in light of a particular will.
6. Distribution or allocation: successive assignment, by groups or portions. "Each man according to his work": giving each their distinct share.
G2596.origine: The Greek word κατά comes from a root indicating movement downwards or forwards. It is a fundamental compound word in the language: in composition, it gives rise to hundreds of verbs (to descend, to conquer, to accuse, etc.). In the translation of the Old Testament into Greek, it often corresponds to the Hebrew עַל ('al), which also carries several meanings related to direction, position, and relation. This word has retained this remarkable flexibility: Greek uses it with two different cases (genitive and accusative), each nuance varying the meaning according to the context.
G2596.emploi: This word is among the most frequent in the New Testament (436 occurrences). It appears in all books, but particularly in Luke, Paul, and Hebrews. Its uses vary considerably according to the context. With the spatial sense (direction, place), it is found in narratives like Luke 9:6 (going from village to village). With the sense of opposition, it accompanies hostile verbs: to resist, to accuse, to conspire (Galatians 2:11, Matthew 26:59). With the sense of conformity, very frequent in Paul, it introduces a measure or standard: "according to the flesh", "according to the law", "according to the Law". In Luke as well, it marks timing or distribution: "each year" (Luke 2:41), "from feast to feast". The word plays on its versatility to express very varied relationships: movements, conflicts, principles, rhythms.
G2596.portee: For the Christian, this word helps to grasp how the Bible expresses spiritual conflicts (the struggle against the flesh, against evil) and how it invites to live "according to" principles other than those of the world (according to the Spirit, according to grace). It also reminds us that a faithful life is not random, but ordered "according to" God's will and promises. This humble and common word carries the biblical teaching: every act, every direction of life is measured and evaluated according to some principle or standard.

sens: Move downwards, go or come down
Leave a high place for a lower one
When speaking of a person, move in a direction or towards a specific goal
When speaking of a spiritual or heavenly reality, lower oneself or intervene
When speaking of an object, fall or flow downwards
G2597.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply the movement downwards: going or coming from above to below. Jesus descends from the mountain (Mark 9:9), and Zacchaeus descends from his tree (Luke 19:5). This is the physical, concrete movement that we see every day.

2. The word is also used to leave a raised place or position: to descend from a cross (Matthew 27:40) or from a roof in case of immediate danger (Mark 13:15). The idea is always to change level or locality.

3. Sometimes it simply describes a direction or a route without emphasizing height: the disciples descend to the shore to embark (John 6:16), or the apostle Peter descends to join visitors (Acts 10:20). The movement can be horizontal, guided by a purpose.

4. When speaking of heaven or divine realities, the word takes on a spiritual force: the Holy Spirit descends on Jesus (Matthew 3:16), the Son descends from heaven (John 6:38), and Christ descends to the lower regions (Ephesians 4:9). It is the voluntary lowering of the divine.

5. Applied to inanimate things, the verb designates what falls or flows: rain descends (Matthew 7:25), a violent wind descends upon the lake (Luke 8:23), or fire from heaven descends upon the enemies (Luke 9:54).
G2597.origine: The Greek word κατα-βαίνω is composed of κατά (kata, "down, according to") and βαίνω (bainō, "to walk, to go"). It regularly translates the Hebrew יָרַד (yarad), which carries the same idea of descent. This simple verb, formed from a very ancient root meaning "movement downwards," is used throughout Greek to describe any movement from high to low.
G2597.emploi: The verb "descend" appears 82 times in the New Testament, largely in the four Gospels and Acts. It first describes ordinary physical movements: Jesus descends from the Mount of Transfiguration (Mark 9:9), Peter descends from the house (Acts 10:20). It also qualifies natural phenomena: the rain that falls (Matthew 7:25) or the wind that strikes the lake (Luke 8:23). In a higher spiritual register, it expresses the intervention of heaven: the Spirit descends in the form of a dove (Matthew 3:16), the heavenly Jerusalem descends from heaven (Revelation 21:2). In John in particular, it designates the coming of the Son from heaven to earth (John 6:38), a movement that summarizes the entire Incarnation. The word can also depict negative actions: accusers who descend to bring charges (Acts 24:1).
G2597.portee: This simple yet rich verb teaches that God does not remain distant: He descends, He lowers Himself, He intervenes in human history. The Spirit descends, the Son descends, and God seeks out His own. For the Christian, this affirms that their faith is not directed towards a closed heaven, but towards a God who draws near, who enters our lowly and humble places, just as He entered the house of the sinful Zacchaeus. It also reminds us that the path to true greatness passes through humility, as it did for Christ Himself.

sens: Throw someone to the ground, knock them down
Put an end to something, abandon it or set it aside
G2598.detail:
1. To knock someone down means to throw them to the ground, to overturn them, to prostrate them: it is the image of combat or physical defeat. Paul uses it figuratively in 2 Corinthians 4:9 to describe the trial of the persecuted Christian: although "knocked down" by tribulations, believers are not "destroyed," meaning annihilated or abandoned by God.
2. To lay down or put down also means to abandon something, to renounce keeping it or lifting it up. In Hebrews 6:1, it refers to not "laying again" (not lifting up or "putting down again") the foundation of the elementary doctrines of Christ, but to advancing towards spiritual maturity.
G2598.origine: The word is composed of κατά ("down") and βάλλω ("to throw"). In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often renders it with a form of the verb נָפַל ("to fall"), particularly in the sense of overturning someone. The combination of "down" + "to throw" evokes the idea of putting down or making fall, from which both physical and figurative meanings derive.
G2598.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In 2 Corinthians 4:9, Paul depicts the apostles as "knocked down" by persecution but not destroyed: it is an image of severe trial but not definitive. In Hebrews 6:1, the term takes on a different meaning: it refers to not "laying again" or "lifting up" the elementary foundations of the Christian faith, but to progressing. In both cases, the word expresses an action of laying down or abandonment, but applied differently depending on the context.
G2598.portee: This word invites the believer to distinguish between being tested and being destroyed: persecution may temporarily knock us down, but it does not have the final word. It also reminds us of the importance of not getting stuck on the foundational doctrines, but of advancing towards a deeper and more mature faith.

sens: Weigh heavily on someone
Impose a moral or material burden on someone
Be a burden to someone
G2599.detail: 1. The word literally evokes the action of weighing heavily, of making heavier — like a weight that adds to what one is already carrying. 2. Figuratively, it means to impose a burden on someone: to ask something of them that weighs on them, costs them, or embarrasses them. 3. When speaking of people, it means to be a weight for others, to cause them embarrassment or pain: "I was not a burden to you" (2 Corinthians 12:16) means "I did not impose a burden on you, I did not weigh you down."
G2599.origine: The word is composed of the prefix κατα (kata), which reinforces or marks an intense action, and the verb βαρέω (bareô), which comes from the root βάρος (baros) meaning "weight." This root is found in other Greek words: "barbarian" once referred to someone who spoke a heavy and incomprehensible language. The starting image is therefore that of weight — something that presses down, that imposes itself with force.
G2599.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:16. Paul mentions his visit to the Corinthians: even though he could have demanded to be supported (which was the right of apostles), he preferred to refuse this burden, so as not to weigh on the community. He therefore uses this verb to say "I did not impose the burden of feeding or helping me." It is an act of pastoral delicacy: Paul renounces his right to spare his people.
G2599.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to reflect on the weight we impose on others. Paul provides an example: a spiritual leader or a friend can choose to renounce certain rights to avoid burdening those they love. It is a lesson in humility and brotherly love — true strength often lies in lightening the burdens of others rather than increasing them.

sens: disposition à faire du mal de manière délibérée et sournoise
intention malveillante qui cherche à nuire
envie venimeuse, jalousie mesquine
G2550.detail:
1. Malice is the disposition of a person to commit evil, not out of simple anger or passion, but with a deliberate and sneaky intention. It is active malevolence, the kind that devises ways to hurt others. In Romans 1:29, Paul lists it among the vices of those who have rejected God: it adds to ordinary wickedness by mixing in a calculated form of perversion.
2. Beyond the evil committed, it is the state of mind that drives one to do so: a relentless will to harm, a patient malevolence. It differentiates the one who does harm in a fit of rage from the wicked who gossips, cultivates it, and seeks to take advantage of it.
3. It also takes on the aspect of a petty and venomous envy, one that cannot tolerate the good of others and opposes it by all means unfair: jealousy that damages reputation, resentment that plots revenge.
G2550.origine: The Greek word kakoētheia is composed of kakos ("bad") and èthos ("character, nature, morals"). It literally denotes bad nature or bad character—a malevolence inscribed in the deep dispositions of a person, not an isolated act. This formation shows that malice is not accidental: it is a matter of the heart, of the temperament one has forged.
G2550.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:29, where Paul enumerates the characteristic vices of humanity that has refused to know God. It is found in a catalog of sins of the heart and actions: injustice, wickedness, greed, malice, envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice. This Pauline enumeration draws from lists of vice in Stoic and Jewish morality to show the totality of corruption. Malice appears as a characteristic vice of the perverse heart, distinct from other vices by its deliberate and venomous aspect.
G2550.portee: For the Christian, recognizing malice as a specific vice, distinct from simple wickedness, invites introspection: do we not cultivate a deliberate envy, a patient resentment, a calculated will to harm? Paul places it among the fruits of distancing from God, reminding us that only the conversion of the heart can free us from it. The grace of Christ calls us to replace this malevolent disposition with kindness and generosity.

sens: Call down evil, a curse upon someone
Speak ill of someone, criticize or insult them
Declare something bad or unworthy
G2551.detail:
1. To curse is to call down evil or condemnation upon someone. This is what the Decalogue forbids: cursing one's father or mother resulted in death (Matthew 15:4, Mark 7:10). The image is that of pronouncing a powerful word that brings misfortune or destruction upon the one being cursed.
2. Speaking ill of someone means openly criticizing them, belittling them, or discrediting them in front of others. Jesus says that one cannot perform a miracle in His name and then immediately speak ill of Him (Mark 9:39): this is a contradiction.
3. To disparage something is to present it as bad or unworthy. In Ephesus, some disparage "the way of the Lord" in front of the crowd (Acts 19:9), meaning they denigrate it, publicly discrediting it.
G2551.origine: The Greek word κακολογέω comes from κακός (bad, evil) and λέγω (to say, to speak): literally "to speak evil." Its underlying image is that of a powerful word: to speak evil is to invoke or declare evil upon someone. In Hebrew, קָלַל (qalal) expresses the idea of cursing, often as a word that belittles or degrades. It is a serious word in the Bible, as the word has real power.
G2551.emploi: The verb κακολογέω appears 4 times in the New Testament. Two occurrences concern the commandment against blasphemy towards parents (Matthew 15:4, Mark 7:10, quoting Exodus): cursing father or mother is a capital sin. A third in Mark 9:39 establishes that no one can perform a miracle in the name of Jesus and at the same time speak ill of Him: this is incompatible. The last, in Acts 19:9, shows adversaries who disparage "the way of the Lord," meaning the Christian path, in front of the crowd. The word is used with the accusative of the person or thing being cursed or spoken ill of.
G2551.portee: Cursing is a serious offense: it violates the respect due to parents and to God. But this word also reminds us that our words carry weight — they can build up or destroy. Jesus sets a simple requirement: whoever follows Him cannot, with their mouth, curse or discredit Him. It is a call for consistency between faith and the words we speak.

sens: State of affliction, distress, physical or moral pains
Trial endured with patience and firmness
G2552.detail:
1. Suffering refers to the state of one who endures pains, troubles, and difficult trials. It is a distress, an affliction that weighs on the person. In James 5:10, Paul encourages believers to take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord as examples, because they accepted the sufferings inflicted upon them with patience.
2. The word carries the idea of patience and firmness in the face of these trials. It is not merely about enduring, but about enduring with courage and trust in God, as the prophets of the Old Testament did. This suffering thus becomes a testimony of faithfulness.
G2552.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: "kakos" (bad, evil) and "pathos" (what is suffered, suffering). The starting image is that of an evil that one suffers, a bad condition that one endures. In biblical Hebrew, this reality often corresponds to the word "tlâah" (fatigue, painful labor, affliction) encountered by the prophets in their difficult missions.
G2552.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 5:10, where the apostle encourages believers by inviting them to reflect on the fate of the prophets of the Old Testament. These prophets experienced suffering because they proclaimed the word of God, sometimes in the face of hostility and rejection. James uses this word to show that suffering and patience are inseparable in the life of a servant of God: one cannot preach faithfully without being prepared to suffer.
G2552.portee: This word reminds the believer that the prophets and servants of God throughout time have had to go through difficult trials. It is an invitation not to be surprised if we ourselves encounter suffering, but to accept it with the same patience and faith. The suffering endured for the cause of Christ is not a shame or a curse, but a mark of faithfulness and a sharing in the fate of the greatest servants of God.
